concepts/appearance-provider.title: Appearance provider
concepts/appearance-provider.content:
Appearance provider

In one sentence: the appearance provider is the one swappable object a solve creates to answer “what colour will this stack of filament layers be when backlit?”, so the solver and LUT builder never care which colour model is underneath.

The appearance provider is the forward-model boundary of the generator. Everything downstream of profile-loading — LUT construction, the solver, ΔE diagnostics, the luminance handler, palette suggestion — talks only to this interface. Swap the implementation and the colour model changes without touching any caller. There are two backends today, both in Prisma/generator/appearance_model.py.
How to drive it (for users)
You pick the backend with one config field, appearance_model_provider (server.py:408 default, server.py:594 typed field). The web UI exposes it as the #cfgAppearanceModelProvider selector (app/index.html:694, set in app/app.js:4629, read in app/app.js:6329). Two legal values:




















ValueBackend classWhat it ishistorical_spline (default)HistoricalSplineAppearanceProvider (appearance_model.py:82)The multiplicative spline model: a stack’s colour is the product of independent per-filament transmission curves. No extra artifact needed — it reads the spline profile JSONs you already have.photo_stack_bundlePhotoStackBundleAppearanceProvider (appearance_model.py:210)A context-aware model fit from photographed swatch stacks, loaded from a calibration bundle artifact.
The photo-stack backend needs two more settings:

photo_stack_bundle_path — a live calibration candidate directory or its runtime_bundle.json (appearance_model.py:229). It is mandatory for this backend; passing None raises immediately (appearance_model.py:232). Whenever the selected provider is anything other than photo_stack_bundle, the UI nulls this path so it can’t leak into a spline solve (app/app.js:6330).
use_corrections (server.py:407 default, server.py:593 typed field) — the direct-vs-corrected toggle described below.

These are per-run solve settings, not export presentation. Changing any of them produces a different solve fingerprint and invalidates a cached solve (see Solve fingerprint / stale-solve invalidation below).
The factory
create_appearance_provider (appearance_model.py:606) is the only construction path. It is called live on every solve at runner.py:670 and again for the palette-suggest white-rescale pass at server.py:3803 — both confirmed by grep, not dead code. It normalises the kind string and dispatches:

historical / historical_spline / spline → spline provider (appearance_model.py:618)
photo_stack_bundle → photo-stack provider (appearance_model.py:624)
anything else → ValueError("unknown appearance_model_provider: …") (appearance_model.py:629). The v2 rename dropped the old non_ml_photo_stack / v63 aliases, so those are now rejected here.

The constructed instance is stashed on the pipeline state as state.appearance_provider (runner.py:670, pipeline/state.py:236) and read back wherever appearance is needed.
The shared interface
Both backends expose the same method set, so callers stay model-agnostic. The contract methods and their live consumers:



































MethodReturnsLive caller(s)predict_stack_linear_rgb / _batchone/many stack colours, model-domain linear RGBprovider-LUT build lut.py:847, paper-white rescale helper solve.py:275predict_thickness_maps_linear_rgb / _srgbper-pixel predicted raster from the solved thickness mapsΔE diagnostic runner.py:188/runner.py:197, preview render facade.py:456/facade.py:832sample_white_cap_oklabOKLab samples for cap-thickness luminance controlluminance handler pipeline/luminance_handler.py:400fingerprint()a string identity of the modelLUT cache key lut.py:658, solve identity diagnostic runner.py:681, palette-suggest metadata palette/suggest.py:181model_kind (class attr)"historical_spline" or "photo_stack_bundle"branch selection in runner.py:798, staged_runner.py:6209, facade.py:454
StackRequest / Layer — the request shape
A Layer is just tuple[str, float] = (filament_id, thickness_mm) (appearance_model.py:33). A StackRequest (appearance_model.py:36, frozen dataclass) is one physical stack: white_base, a tuple of color_layers, and white_cap — all Layers. The batch methods take a Sequence[StackRequest]. The LUT builder builds a grid of them (lut.py:826) and scores the whole grid in one provider call (lut.py:847); the paper-white rescale helper builds a single white-only request at solve.py:267.

Disambiguation: StackRequest is the input to a prediction. It is a near-duplicate in spirit of VisibleRecipe / StackDefinition used elsewhere for recipe display, but those describe a result (what colours a region used), not a query. Do not conflate them.

The two backends, mechanically
Spline (HistoricalSplineAppearanceProvider). predict_stack_linear_rgb (appearance_model.py:106) assembles [(wb_profile, d_wb), (colour_profile, d)…, (wc_profile, d_wc)] and calls compose_stack (model.py:71 → lib.transmission.compose), which multiplies the per-layer transmission vectors. Layer order is irrelevant because multiplication commutes. Thickness-map prediction (appearance_model.py:171) precomputes per-step transmission LUTs and multiplies them pixel-wise. This is the model described on The Transmission Model.
Photo stack (PhotoStackBundleAppearanceProvider). Loads a runtime bundle (appearance_model.py:268) and builds a row-shaped predictor (appearance_model.py:271). Each StackRequest is collapsed (collapse_adjacent_layers, appearance_model.py:294) and turned into a model runtime row (appearance_model.py:296) the predictor can score. Off-grid thicknesses fall back to the row predictor; grid-aligned thicknesses go through a vectorized LUT evaluator (photo_stack_lut.predict_combo_model_linear_rgb, appearance_model.py:534). Because it is context-aware, it cannot be reduced to independent per-filament profile JSONs — that is the whole reason this boundary exists (appearance_model.py module docstring, line 1; verified against the code, not just the header).
Direct vs corrected toggle
The photo-stack backend has two flavours selected by use_corrections:

direct (use_corrections=False) — the raw bundle model output.
corrected (use_corrections=True) — the direct output with a separate correction_layer.json sibling artifact applied (apply_photo_stack_correction, appearance_model.py:404).

Corrections live in a separate sibling artifact on purpose, so you can compare direct against corrected without rebuilding the baseline bundle (appearance_model.py:215). Requesting corrections when no valid correction_layer.json is present raises rather than silently falling back to direct (appearance_model.py:261). The chosen flavour is baked into the fingerprint as direct or corrected:<hash> (appearance_model.py:273).
Fingerprints and stale-solve invalidation
Each provider exposes fingerprint() — a string that changes whenever the model’s meaning changes:

Spline: "historical_spline:" + hash(colour/wb/wc profiles) (appearance_model.py:97). Edit a profile JSON and the fingerprint moves.
Photo stack: "photo_stack_bundle:<bundle.fingerprint>:photo_stack_logic:<N>:<direct|corrected:hash>:<APPEARANCE_DOMAIN_VERSION>" (appearance_model.py:277). It folds in the bundle identity, the predictor logic version, the correction choice, and the domain-contract version.

APPEARANCE_DOMAIN_VERSION (appearance_model.py:79, currently "domain-pass-through-v1") is the lever for the pass-through change described below: bump it and every photo-stack fingerprint changes.
The fingerprint does two jobs:

LUT cache key — _build_luts_with_provider keys the cached .npz on provider.fingerprint() (lut.py:658, fed into _provider_cache_key at lut.py:680). A different model → a different cache file → no stale LUT reuse.
Solve freshness — the server’s _solve_owned_fingerprint (server.py:2035) mirrors the photo-stack predictor logic version (server.py:2080) and APPEARANCE_DOMAIN_VERSION (server.py:2089) into the solve-identity hash. So a code-only predictor change, or a domain-contract bump, marks existing solves/exports stale on swap/export — even though the provider instance doesn’t exist at config-hash time. This is checked at export (server.py:5444) and swap-instructions (server.py:5782).

The pass-through naming trap (read this)
This is the easiest thing to get wrong. After the 2026-06-12 projection-slot retirement, the photo-stack provider’s appearance-named methods return model-domain RGB, not display-domain. They are pure pass-throughs kept only for API-name stability:

predict_stack_appearance_linear_rgb_batch just calls predict_stack_model_linear_rgb_batch (appearance_model.py:423).
predict_stack_linear_rgb_batch is a “compatibility alias” for the same model-domain method (appearance_model.py:413).
project_model_linear_rgb_to_appearance returns its input unchanged — a “compatibility pass-through for the retired solve-domain conversion” (appearance_model.py:418).
predict_thickness_maps_appearance_linear_rgb forwards to predict_thickness_maps_model_linear_rgb (appearance_model.py:565).

So the word “appearance” in a method name does not mean display-converted output. Model-domain values are the flatfield-normalized model/correction output; conversion to display happens at the generator’s ingress/display boundaries, not here (appearance_model.py:218 domain-contract comment). The class docstring at appearance_model.py:210 documents this; the APPEARANCE_DOMAIN_VERSION = "domain-pass-through-v1" constant is the live proof the projection was retired. If you are looking for where model→display happens, it is not in this file — see Colour domains / docs/color_domain_doctrine.md.
Where it sits in a solve
The webapp solve runs the staged backend (run_staged_backend_path / staged_runner.py), not solve.py’s legacy “6-step” CLI engine. The staged runner still branches on state.appearance_provider.model_kind (staged_runner.py:6209, staged_runner.py:8257) and the runner picks the matching LUT builder: spline → _build_luts_raw (runner.py:799), photo-stack → _build_luts_with_provider (runner.py:815). So the provider choice also selects the Joint LUT builder, exactly as the solver path does.

Related: The Transmission Model · Joint LUT · Solve fingerprint · Colour domains · Photo stack model
Modules: generator.appearance_model · generator.model · lib.transmission · lib.photo_stack_model · lib.stack_geometry

concepts/gamut-mapping.title: Gamut mapping
concepts/gamut-mapping.content:
Gamut mapping

In one sentence: before the solver picks filament thicknesses, out-of-reach target colours are pulled onto the set of colours the palette can actually print — either by squeezing chroma (keeping lightness and hue) or by projecting onto the convex hull of achievable colours (allowing a small lightness shift).

The set of colours a chosen palette can reproduce when backlit is its gamut. A source image almost always asks for colours outside it (vivid saturated reds, deep blues). Rather than let the Joint LUT nearest-neighbour query chase an impossible target and return whatever LUT sample happens to be closest, the pipeline first remaps every out-of-gamut target onto (or very near) the achievable set, in OKLab space, on the solve grid. The solver then queries against targets it can actually hit.
Where it runs
Gamut mapping is stage 3 of 5 in the fixed pipeline spine (load → lut → gamut → solve → stats, with an optional group stage). The tracker advances the "gamut" stage at generator/pipeline/runner.py:832 and the work is done by _apply_target_gamut_mapping (generator/pipeline/runner.py:67), called at generator/pipeline/runner.py:833.
It runs after the LUTs are built (the hull and chroma checks both need the achievable colour cloud) and before the staged solve. The runner mutates state.solve_target_oklab in place (generator/pipeline/runner.py:146); the staged backend then reads that already-remapped cloud (generator/pipeline/staged_runner.py:759) and never re-runs gamut mapping itself.


                  
                  This is the webapp path 
                  
                

The live webapp runs the staged backend (run_staged_backend_path, invoked at generator/pipeline/runner.py:846). The remap happens once, in the runner, on the targets. solve.py’s solve_image (which embeds its own gamut step at generator/solve.py:472) is the legacy CLI engine — reached only through generator/pipeline_cli.py:634, not the web app. Both engines share the same two batch functions in solve.py, so the behaviour described below is identical regardless of entry point.


The three modes
The mode is the gamut_mode setting (PipelineConfig.gamut_mode, default "hull", generator/pipeline/state.py:75). The runner lower-cases and normalises it (generator/pipeline/runner.py:95); "none", "off", "disabled" all mean no remap; anything other than hull/chroma/none raises (generator/pipeline/runner.py:108-109).





























ModeWhat it doesPreservesImplementationhull (default)Projects each out-of-gamut point onto the convex hull of achievable OKLab colours — nearest point in full 3Dhue mostly; L* and chroma may both shiftgamut_map_hull_batch (generator/solve.py:180)chromaBinary-search chroma compression: scales a,b toward grey until the target is reachableL* and hue exactlygamut_map_batch (generator/solve.py:115)noneLeaves every target untouched; only the diagnostic header is writteneverything— (generator/pipeline/runner.py:96-107)
chroma — chroma compression (preserves L* and hue)
gamut_map_batch (generator/solve.py:115) first queries the LUT for every target and flags those whose nearest-achievable dE exceeds de_threshold as out of gamut (generator/solve.py:132-133). For each flagged pixel it runs a 12-step binary search (n_steps=12, generator/solve.py:119) on a single scalar s ∈ [0,1] applied to the chroma channels:
candidate = [L, a*s, b*s]

L is never touched (generator/solve.py:142 keeps L constant), and because a and b are scaled by the same factor the hue angle atan2(b,a) is preserved — only chroma (saturation) shrinks. The search narrows [lo, hi] toward the largest s whose candidate is within de_threshold of an achievable colour, and keeps the best-seen candidate even if no s fully lands in gamut (generator/solve.py:155-176). The whole batch is searched in parallel — all out-of-gamut pixels step together (generator/solve.py:151-163), which is the vectorisation that replaced the old per-pixel gamut_map_oklab (still present at generator/solve.py:89 but with no live caller — only used in the now-removed scalar path).
This mode is conservative: it never changes how light or dark a colour looks, only how vivid. The cost is that very saturated targets can compress to noticeably duller colours.
hull — convex-hull facet projection (allows a small L* shift)
gamut_map_hull_batch (generator/solve.py:180) works geometrically instead of by LUT query. The achievable colours form a point cloud; build_hull_from_luts (generator/lut.py:1295) wraps them in a scipy.spatial.ConvexHull (deduplicated to 4-decimal OKLab points, generator/lut.py:1306-1308). Each hull facet has a plane equation normal·x + offset; a point’s signed distance to a facet is positive when it lies outside.
Two subtleties, both verified in code:

What counts as out of gamut here is geometric, not LUT-distance. A point is flagged only if its maximum signed distance over all facets exceeds de_threshold (generator/solve.py:210-212). This deliberately differs from chroma mode: a target can sit inside the hull yet be farther than de_threshold from the nearest discrete LUT sample. Projecting such interior points to a facet would invent artificial saturated boundary colours, so hull mode leaves them alone (generator/solve.py:205-209).
Projection is iterated up to 4 times. Each pass subtracts the violation along the single most-violated facet’s normal (generator/solve.py:224-233). One pass handles points outside a single facet; the loop handles points outside several facets near a hull corner, where one projection can still leave the point outside a neighbouring facet.

Because the projection moves the point in full 3D OKLab, L* can shift (along with a and b). The docstring trade-off is real: hull mode produces lower total dE at the gamut boundary than chroma compression, at the price of letting lightness move a little (generator/solve.py:191-193).


                  
                  Hull-corner slight-outside is acceptable by design 
                  
                

Single-facet projection is an intentional approximation (generator/solve.py:195-197). After up to 4 passes a point near a hull corner may still land slightly outside the hull. This is fine because the downstream Joint LUT query (the solve stage) always snaps to the nearest achievable colour regardless — it can only ever return a real, printable LUT sample. The remap’s job is to get the target close, not to land it exactly on the surface.


none
No remap. The runner still records a diagnostic header with effective_mode = "none" and remapped_count = 0 (generator/pipeline/runner.py:98-107) and returns early, so the raw targets flow straight into the solve. Useful for diagnosis (seeing how far the solver drifts unaided) but generally leaves saturated regions chasing colours the print cannot make.
The optional white-point rescale (pre-step)
Independent of the mode, an optional white-point rescale runs first, gated by the gamut_white_rescale toggle (default False, generator/pipeline/state.py:76). When the toggle is off the block is skipped entirely and compute_paper_white_rgb is never even called (generator/pipeline/runner.py:79-83).
When on, apply_gamut_white_rescale_to_targets (generator/pipeline/target_cloud.py:106) computes the print’s paper white — the appearance of the thinnest printable white-only stack (white base + minimum-thickness cap, no colour layers) through the active Appearance provider (compute_paper_white_rgb, generator/solve.py:245). It then applies a per-channel von Kries adaptation of every OKLab target from source-white to that paper white (rescale_oklab_targets, generator/solve.py:282): round-trip OKLab → linear RGB, multiply channel-wise by the paper-white RGB, convert back to OKLab. Because OKLab↔linear is bijective, the only net change is the per-channel scale.
The rescale no-ops (returns None, no change) when there is no white base configured, or when the model’s paper white is effectively [1,1,1] (generator/solve.py:256, generator/solve.py:277). It runs before the mode is even inspected, so it applies whether the mode is hull, chroma, or none (generator/pipeline/runner.py:76-93). In hull mode the runner additionally does a diagnostic-only hull count pass on the pre-rescale targets to report how the rescale changed the out-of-gamut population (pre_rescale_out_of_gamut, generator/pipeline/runner.py:124-130).
Diagnostics and what reaches the UI
Two distinct gamut artefacts exist; do not confuse them:





























ArtefactWritten byMeaningSurfaced as__target_gamut_mapping__ (dict)runner, generator/pipeline/runner.py:149requested/effective mode, remapped_count, mean/max OKLab shift, white-rescale inforuntime diagnostic — listed in _RUNTIME_DIAGNOSTIC_KEYS (generator/server.py:2300)__target_gamut_mask__ (H×W raster)runner, generator/pipeline/runner.py:162which solve-grid pixels the pre-query remap movedper-pixel diagnostic map__gamut_mask__ (H×W raster)staged backend, generator/pipeline/staged_runner.py:763pixels whose final LUT-query dE still exceeds de_threshold after remapfeeds stats.n_out_of_gamut → UI “out of gamut” count (generator/server.py:2278)
The first two describe the remap; the last describes residual unreachability — colours so far outside the gamut that even after remapping the best achievable stack still misses by more than de_threshold. Because __gamut_mask__ is computed on the already-remapped state.solve_target_oklab, a non-zero count there is genuine: the palette physically cannot reach those colours. The remapped-pixel count shown in __target_gamut_mapping__ is usually much larger (everything that needed moving), while n_out_of_gamut counts only what remained unreachable.
The de_threshold knob
Both modes key off de_threshold (PipelineConfig.de_threshold, default 0.05, generator/pipeline/state.py:72). It is an OKLab Euclidean distance, where roughly 0.02 ≈ 1 JND (just-noticeable difference) per the in-code note at generator/solve.py:99. It sets two things at once: how far from achievable a target must be to count as out of gamut (and so get remapped), and — separately, at the solve stage — how far the final stack may miss before a pixel is counted in n_out_of_gamut. Raising it remaps fewer pixels but tolerates larger colour error; lowering it remaps aggressively.
How to drive it (users)

Leave it on hull unless you have a reason not to — it gives the lowest colour error at saturated boundaries.
Switch to chroma if you specifically need lightness preserved exactly (e.g. a portrait where you care more about correct brightness than correct saturation). It will never change how light/dark a region reads, only how vivid.
none is a diagnostic setting, not a production one.
gamut_white_rescale adapts targets to the print’s actual paper white; turn it on if the print reads with a colour cast relative to the source’s white. It is a no-op when there is no white base or the paper white is already neutral.

Related

How a Solve Works — the full 5-stage spine; gamut mapping is stage 3.
The Joint LUT and Staged Solve / Joint LUT — the nearest-neighbour query the remap feeds, and the source of the achievable colour cloud and its convex hull.
OKLab — the perceptual colour space all of this runs in.
Appearance provider — supplies the paper white for the white-point rescale and the colours that define the gamut.
Model-domain ingress — how source pixels become the OKLab targets that gamut mapping receives.
Architecture: generator.pipeline.runner (orchestration), generator.pipeline.target_cloud (target cloud + white-rescale helper), generator.lut (build_hull_from_luts), generator.pipeline.staged_runner (residual __gamut_mask__).

concepts/joint-lut.title: Joint LUT
concepts/joint-lut.content:
Joint LUT
The joint LUT is a precomputed lookup table that maps candidate layer recipes
to the colour they produce, letting the solve invert the
transmission model by nearest-match instead of by
formula.
It is joint because each entry fixes the white-cap thickness and the
colour-layer recipe together — cap and colour are chosen in one query, not in
separate passes. Each entry stores oklab(T_wb × T_wc(d_wc) × ∏ T_ci(d_ci)) for
budget-constrained combinations of (d_wc, d_c1, …, d_ck)
(Prisma/generator/lut.py:413).
Built by build_luts (lut.py:394) for the spline model, or
build_luts_with_provider (lut.py:630) for the photo-stack model; queried by
query_luts_batch (lut.py:946). Results are disk-cached by a content key
(lut.py:449).
Full explanation: The Joint LUT and Staged Solve. Module: generator.lut.

concepts/model-domain-ingress.title: Model-domain ingress
concepts/model-domain-ingress.content:
Model-domain ingress

In one sentence: the generator solves in the model domain (flatfield-normalized transmission RGB the calibration models were fit in), so it pulls source photos into that domain on the way in with an inverse Camera Transform (G), and pushes its predictions back out to display-encoded “lit appearance” with the forward Camera Transform (F) only when it bakes preview images.

This page covers the whole F/G round trip: how source colours get mapped in, what space the solve actually optimises in, the exact maths of the forward transform, and which PNGs get baked through F for the viewer.
Why two domains exist
The calibration app fits its appearance models against camera-captured swatch colours — what a strip of filament looks like when photographed on the lightbox and rendered to sRGB by the camera. Those colours are not plain display sRGB; they live in a “model domain” of flatfield-normalized transmission. The forward Camera Transform F is the bridge: it maps model-domain transmission RGB to that camera-rendered display sRGB (“what the lit lithophane will look like”). The inverse G = F^-1 goes the other way (lib/camera_transform.py:3).

























DomainWhat lives thereUsed forSource sRGBThe photo bytes on diskInput onlyModel domain (flatfield-normalized transmission, linear RGB in [0,1])Everything the solver touches: targets, predictions, dEThe solveDisplay-encoded appearance”What the lit print looks like”Preview PNGs baked through F
The solve never leaves the model domain. F is applied only at the very end, when baking preview images.
Ingress: pulling the source into the model domain (G)
image_to_target (generator/model.py:128) is the seam. With model_domain_ingress=True it runs the source image through the inverse 33³ LUT (G); with it off it falls back to a plain srgb_to_linear gamma-2.2 decode (generator/model.py:148-152).

On → _apply_model_domain_ingress_lut → apply_inverse_lut (generator/model.py:122-125, lib/camera_transform.py:356), a trilinear lookup into the baked 33×33×33×3 inverse LUT. The LUT already encodes the full-stack transmission oklab(T_wb × T_wc × ∏T_colour), so T_wb is not divided back out — it is baked into every LUT entry (generator/model.py:136-147).
Off → srgb_to_linear (generator/model.py:108-115), the legacy bit-identical path. Tests pin that the off path never even loads the LUT (tests/generator/test_model_domain_ingress.py:27).

The targets the solve aims at are built from the output of this step, via the OKLab conversion in pipeline/target_cloud.py:72 (the cloud builder calls image_to_target in the configured ingress mode, then to_oklab).
On by default, everywhere
model_domain_ingress defaults to True at every layer that holds the config:

























HolderAnchorPipelineConfig (pipeline state)generator/pipeline/state.py:77SolveConfig (facade)generator/facade.py:215Server _DEFAULT_CONFIGgenerator/server.py:421Server ConfigPayloadgenerator/server.py:607
The facade threads the toggle and LUT path straight through to image_to_target (generator/facade.py:644-646). It is also a solve-owned identity key — it appears in _SOLVE_OWNED_KEYS (generator/server.py:1978) and is persisted with Settings Profiles via _SETTINGS_PROFILE_KEYS (generator/server.py:2959), and it is echoed in the runner’s solve-identity diagnostics (generator/pipeline/runner.py:631), so toggling it changes a run’s fingerprint and old solves cannot masquerade as new ones.


                  
                  Artifact required 
                  
                

The Prisma/data/camera_transform/ artifact is required on the ingress-on path. It is git-ignored, so a fresh checkout without it fails solve work until it is present. Missing/invalid artifacts are a hard, loud error (CameraTransformError), never a silent fallback to raw transmission (lib/camera_transform.py:43, model_domain_display.py:11-13). The actionable message points to Rebuild via Calibration → Camera Transform (lib/camera_transform.py:34).


The webapp solves the staged backend
For developers: the live web solve does not run solve.py’s legacy “6-step” CLI engine. After the fixed Load stage builds the target cloud through compute_solve_target_cloud → image_to_target (pipeline/runner.py:779), the solve path dispatches to run_staged_backend_path (pipeline/runner.py:843-846, defined pipeline/staged_runner.py:10310). solve.py’s image_to_target callers (solve.py:337, :464, :607) are the legacy CLI/pipeline_cli.py engine.
The appearance provider that the staged backend predicts with is model-domain by construction after the 2026-06-12 projection-slot retirement: appearance_model’s appearance-named methods are pass-throughs that return model-domain RGB unchanged, not a separate display projection (generator/appearance_model.py:418-424 — project_model_linear_rgb_to_appearance literally return np.asarray(rgb); predict_stack_appearance_linear_rgb_batch just calls the model-domain batch). The contract version "domain-pass-through-v1" (generator/appearance_model.py:79) is folded into the provider fingerprint so a domain-contract change invalidates stale solves.
Egress: the forward Camera Transform F
The forward transform is implemented in two layers. generator/model_domain_display.py is the thin generator-side wrapper; lib/camera_transform.py holds the maths. apply_appearance_transform (model_domain_display.py:37) is a direct call to apply_forward (lib/camera_transform.py:259).
F is a v2 fit: a Finlayson degree-2 root-polynomial matrix followed by per-channel monotone PCHIP tone curves.
Step 1 — root-polynomial expansion + 3×6 matrix
Model-domain linear RGB (r,g,b) is expanded to a 6-feature root-polynomial vector and multiplied by a learned 3×6 matrix W (lib/camera_transform.py:244-251):
phi(r,g,b) = [r, g, b, sqrt(r·g), sqrt(g·b), sqrt(r·b)]
z = clip(phi @ W.T, 0, 1)

Negative inputs are clamped to 0 before the square roots (rp_features, lib/camera_transform.py:245).
Step 2 — per-channel monotone PCHIP tone curves
Each of the 3 output channels passes through its own PchipInterpolator over 10 knots on x ∈ [0,1] (lib/camera_transform.py:266-269, N_KNOTS = 10 at :26). The knot y-values are not stored raw — they are decoded from unconstrained params through a softplus-cumulative scheme that guarantees monotonicity (_decode_knots, lib/camera_transform.py:230-241): a sigmoid-scaled base, strictly-positive log1p(exp(·)) deltas, and a rescale so the top knot never exceeds OUT_MAX = 1.05. Output is clipped to [0,1] (lib/camera_transform.py:270).
The 18 matrix weights + 30 curve params give N_PARAMS = 48 (lib/camera_transform.py:31). unpack_params splits them into the 3×6 W and the 3×10 curve block (lib/camera_transform.py:254-256).
The inverse (G) is consistent with F
G exists in two forms. The baked 33³ LUT (apply_inverse_lut) is what ingress actually uses at runtime — fast trilinear lookup. There is also an analytic invert_forward (lib/camera_transform.py:279): it inverts the PCHIP curves (invert_curve_channel, :273), seeds t via the matrix inverse, then runs n_newton=4 Newton iterations against the root-polynomial Jacobian. This analytic inverse is what the calibration side bakes the LUT from; tests assert F(G(·)) is near-identity (tests/generator/test_model_domain_display.py:125).
The artifact: generation pinning + sha256
The Camera Transform is a versioned, hash-pinned artifact loaded by load_camera_transform (lib/camera_transform.py:201).

Generation pointer. A CURRENT text file names one local generation directory (gen-*); _read_current_generation reads it and rejects absolute paths or anything other than a single local name (lib/camera_transform.py:69-85).
Hash verification. When loading from a generation dir, _verify_generation_hashes reads manifest.json’s artifact_hashes and recomputes the sha256 of both camera_transform.json and inverse_lut_33.npz, erroring on any mismatch (lib/camera_transform.py:160-175). This is how a committed generation is guaranteed unmodified.
Provenance sha. Beyond the artifact-integrity hashes, load_camera_transform also computes the sha256 of the transform JSON bytes (lib/camera_transform.py:223) and returns it on the CameraTransform dataclass (:48-53). load_display_transform_params surfaces (params, sha256) (model_domain_display.py:31-34) so every baked image records exactly which transform produced it.
Schema gate. validate_camera_transform_payload requires schema == "camera_transform_v1", model_version == "v2", used_lattice falsy, and exactly 48 finite params / 10 knots (lib/camera_transform.py:178-198). Lattice transforms are explicitly unsupported.
Caching. Both the transform and the LUT are cached keyed on (resolved path, mtime_ns) and the cache is cleared on every fresh load (lib/camera_transform.py:209-227, :340-353).

The PNG encoding contract
This is the part most likely to bite a developer. The pixels move between domains and encodings in a fixed, test-pinned sequence (bake_view_domain_images, model_domain_display.py:73-125):

























ImageDomainEncoding writtenpredicted.pngmodel-domain transmissiongamma-2.2 sRGB (_srgb8_from_linear, appearance_model.py:70 → clip(rgb)**(1/2.2)*255)predicted_appearance.pngdisplay appearance (F applied)round(F · 255) — no extra gammatarget_transmission.pngmodel-domain target_srgb8_from_linear (comparable to predicted.png)
The recipe is:

Recover model-domain transmission from predicted.png as (png/255) ** 2.2 (model_domain_display.py:105). This undoes the gamma-2.2 encoding predicted.png was written with.
Apply F via apply_appearance_transform — its output is already display-encoded sRGB, so it must be written as round(F·255 + 0.5) with no further gamma (model_domain_display.py:106-109, contract pinned at :86-92).
Target image depends on the ingress toggle: ingress-on writes G(source) (the actual solve target this run aimed at) through _srgb8_from_linear; ingress-off byte-copies source.png (the decoded source was the target) so the frontend’s Appearance/Transmission rule stays unconditional (model_domain_display.py:111-120).

bake_view_domain_images returns a provenance dict (display_transform_path, display_transform_sha256) that the server folds into run.json as run_metadata["model_domain_display"] (generator/server.py:5141).
Which preview images get baked
The server bakes these inside _run_solve (loud failure = solve failure; a run without these assets must not render):

bake_view_domain_images (generator/server.py:4836) writes predicted_appearance.png + target_transmission.png. These back the Appearance / Transmission display toggle; the predicted-appearance URL is surfaced at generator/server.py (predicted_appearance_url).
bake_appearance_png (model_domain_display.py:47, called at generator/server.py:4859) writes the colour-only predicted render for the Recipe viewer’s Color Regions tab. The source is result.predict_image_color_only() (generator/facade.py:494) — the same forward composition as predict_image, but with the white-cap term (boundary + detail) zeroed via _cap_zeroed_thickness_maps() so the cap’s luminance shaping does not drown out the colour story. It is baked through the same F as the full appearance so the two viewer cards are comparable; it shares bake_view_domain_images’s exact encoding contract (recover (png/255)**2.2, apply F, write round(F·255)). Output: predicted_color_only_appearance.png, surfaced as predicted_color_only_appearance_url (generator/server.py:5162).



                  
                  Liveness 
                  
                

Both bakers are wired and live on master. bake_appearance_png and predict_image_color_only exist only in the merged-recipe-viewer state (the main checkout / master); some development worktrees predate that merge and lack them. Verified via git grep against the main checkout (generator/server.py:4855, :4859; generator/facade.py:494).


How to drive it

Leave ingress on. It is the default and matches how the models were calibrated. Turning it off reverts to a plain sRGB decode that ignores the camera’s colour rendering — useful only for A/B diagnostics. The toggle lives in the solve-owned settings (it changes the run fingerprint).
Keep the artifact fresh. If solves fail with a CameraTransform artifact … Rebuild via Calibration → Camera Transform error, the Prisma/data/camera_transform/ generation is missing or its hashes don’t match — rebuild it from the calibration app.
Reading the previews. In the viewer, Transmission mode shows the model-domain pair (predicted.png vs target_transmission.png); Appearance mode shows predicted_appearance.png — the print as it should look backlit. The recipe viewer’s colour-only card drops the white cap on purpose.


Related: How a Solve Works · Recipe viewer · Appearance vs Transmission view · Camera Transform · concept Flatfield normalization · architecture generator.model · generator.model_domain_display · lib.camera_transform · generator.appearance_model · generator.facade.

concepts/oklab.title: OKLab
concepts/oklab.content:
OKLab
OKLab is the perceptual colour space the generator optimises in. Distances
in OKLab track perceived colour difference far better than distances in RGB, so
the solver minimises OKLab distance (ΔE) between what a layer stack produces and
the target colour.
In the code, to_oklab (Prisma/generator/model.py:155) converts linear RGB to
OKLab. Targets are stored as OKLab on the observation and solve grids
(pipeline/state.py:247), the Joint LUT stores each recipe’s colour as
OKLab, and ΔE — the headline quality number — is the OKLab distance between
predicted and target (runner.py:245).
Used by: How a Solve Works · The Transmission Model ·
The Joint LUT and Staged Solve

concepts/thickness-map.title: Thickness map
concepts/thickness-map.content:
Thickness map

In one sentence: a thickness map is the solve’s core output — an (H, W) millimetre array per filament — and ThicknessMaps is the typed dict-like container that holds them, keyed by either a real filament id or a reserved __-prefixed sentinel.

A thickness map answers one question for one filament: how thick is this filament, in millimetres, at every pixel? A solve produces one array per colour filament, plus reserved arrays for the white cap and a couple of diagnostic layers. Export reads these arrays to build geometry; the Appearance provider re-predicts colour from them to compute per-pixel ΔE.
The container itself is ThicknessMaps (thickness_maps.py:77), a MutableMapping[str, np.ndarray] — see the generator.thickness_maps Architecture node. It is a compatibility-first typing wrapper around a plain dict[str, np.ndarray], not a semantic rewrite. Every key it stores is a plain str identical to the legacy magic-string convention, so any serializer, export bundle, or frontend payload built from it emits exactly the same keys and filenames as the pre-typed code did.
Two kinds of key
Every key in a thickness map is one of two kinds (thickness_maps.py:10-13):




















KindExampleSourceDynamic filament id"bambu-pla-basic-red"data value from config / palette / material ordering — cannot be enumerated ahead of timeReserved sentinel"__white_cap__"a fixed __-prefixed string, one per non-filament layer
The partition is purely the __ prefix. filament_ids() returns keys that do not start with __; the reserved keys all do (thickness_maps.py:147).
Reserved sentinels (MapKey)
The reserved keys are enumerated by the MapKey enum (thickness_maps.py:40-54). Each member subclasses str, so maps["__white_cap__"] and maps[MapKey.WHITE_CAP] resolve to the same slot:



































MapKey memberString valueMeaningWHITE_CAP__white_cap__combined white-cap thicknessWHITE_BOUNDARY_CAP__white_boundary_cap__the boundary/base portion of the capWHITE_DETAIL_CAP__white_detail_cap__the optional tonal-relief detail capDE__de__per-pixel ΔE (diagnostic)GAMUT_MASK__gamut_mask__which pixels were out of gamut (diagnostic)
MapKey covers exactly the webapp/facade reserved sentinel contract — the keys that the facade, export, and frontend payloads agree on. It is not an exhaustive list of every __-prefixed string a map may ever hold (see the filler sentinel below).
Where the diagnostic sentinels actually live
Important nuance the enum hides: __de__ and __gamut_mask__ being MapKey members does not mean the live solve stores them inside the thickness map. In the staged backend — the path the webapp actually runs — diagnostics live in PipelineState.diagnostics, never in thickness_maps (pipeline/state.py:266-272). __gamut_mask__ is copied straight from the compatibility bundle into diagnostics (pipeline/runner.py:567-568), and __de__ is written there by _recompute_de_diagnostics. Only the legacy CLI engine (solve.py:570-571, pipeline_cli.py:728-729) carries __de__/__gamut_mask__ inside thickness_maps.
MapKey.DE/MapKey.GAMUT_MASK remain enum members because the facade’s accessors read whichever home is populated: de_map/gamut_mask check diagnostics first and fall back to thickness_maps for diagnostics-less legacy results (facade.py:407-415). So the cap sentinels (WHITE_CAP, WHITE_BOUNDARY_CAP, WHITE_DETAIL_CAP) are the sentinels that genuinely live inside the live thickness map; the two diagnostic sentinels are dual-homed.
The legacy-string compatibility guarantee
The container’s whole reason to exist is to let typed code (MapKey enums) coexist with the historic string keys without changing one byte of any payload. The guarantee is enforced by _normalise_key (thickness_maps.py:60-74):

A MapKey member normalises to its .value (a plain str).
A plain str (or any str subclass) coerces to str.
Anything else raises TypeError.

Because every key is normalised on write (__setitem__, thickness_maps.py:101-102), the backing dict only ever holds plain strings. Iteration and serialization therefore yield the exact legacy strings — a serializer never sees an enum repr like MapKey.WHITE_CAP. Read-side helpers (__contains__, get) catch the TypeError and treat an un-normalisable key as “not present” rather than raising (thickness_maps.py:114-127), so dynamic loop variables of unexpected type degrade gracefully.
This is why export can key its mesh objects off MapKey.WHITE_CAP.value etc. (mesh/post_solve_export.py:47-49) and get the identical filenames the magic-string era produced.
Container API
ThicknessMaps is a full MutableMapping, so all the usual dict access (maps[k], k in maps, len, iteration, .get) works and tolerates MapKey / str interchangeably. Beyond the protocol it adds a few helpers:



































MethodPurposeLivenessfilament_ids()dynamic filament-id keys only (excludes __ sentinels)Live — backs SolveResult.filament_ids (facade.py:433)copy()shallow ThicknessMaps copy (arrays shared)Live — used to build the cap-zeroed maps for colour-only prediction (facade.py:483)filament_items()(filament_id, array) pairs, sentinels excludedTest-only callers in the current tree (tests/generator/test_thickness_maps_container.py); no production caller foundreserved_items()(sentinel, array) pairs for __ keysTest-only callers; no production caller foundas_string_dict() / to_plain_dictplain dict with exact legacy string keys (shallow)Test-only callers; to_plain_dict is an alias for as_string_dict (thickness_maps.py:142)
SolveResult.__post_init__ normalises any incoming maps into a ThicknessMaps (no-op when already wrapped), so every result — webapp, legacy CLI, or test-constructed — exposes the typed container with identical aliasing behaviour (facade.py:394-401).
ThicknessMaps is constructed at the producer sites: the staged finalize step (pipeline/runner.py:559), the grouping substitution paths (grouping/beam_search.py:660, grouping/greedy_optimize.py:76), blueprint-triage application (pipeline/blueprint_triage/application.py:63), and the legacy solve.py/pipeline_cli.py engines.
Retired and excluded sentinels
Two __-prefixed sentinels are deliberately not MapKey members, for different reasons:
__filler__ — CLI-only, excluded by design
__filler__ is written only by pipeline_cli.py on the opt-in --filler path (pipeline_cli.py:718). It is not part of the webapp/facade payload contract, so it is intentionally left out of MapKey (thickness_maps.py:15-18). ThicknessMaps still accepts it — it is just an ordinary __-prefixed string that flows through _normalise_key like any other. So __filler__ is live, but only on the legacy CLI engine; the staged webapp solve never emits it.
__translucent_underfill__ — retired, must never return
__translucent_underfill__ was retired by Task 2.3 and is deliberately absent from MapKey; the module header states it must never be reintroduced as a live key (thickness_maps.py:20-21, thickness_maps.py:46-47). Confirmed retired in product code: in server.py the literal string survives only as an explanatory comment (server.py:2714) inside _RETIRED_CONFIG_FIELDS, and the actual rejection guard (server.py:2766-2768) rejects the v2_translucent_underfill_* config family that used to drive the solve-time overlay — not the overlay key itself. The only other reference is the audit write-up at generator/docs/legacy_audit/06_DISABLED_TRANSLUCENT_UNDERFILL.md. No production writer emits it into a thickness map today.
Where it sits in the pipeline
Produced in: How a Solve Works (the Solve stage). The staged path builds the maps in pipeline/runner.py from the staged compatibility bundle (see generator.pipeline.staged_bridge). Consumed by: Exporting Print Files (geometry via generator.mesh.post_solve_export and generator.pipeline.material_exposure) and the Appearance provider (ΔE re-prediction). Diagnostics travel alongside in PipelineState.diagnostics, not inside the thickness map.
Related: generator.facade (SolveResult wraps the container), generator.thickness_maps (the module), Gamut mapping (__gamut_mask__ semantics), Joint LUT (what the solve composes before thicknesses are emitted).

conditioning/automatic-palette-suggestio.title: Automatic palette suggestion
conditioning/automatic-palette-suggestio.content:
Automatic palette suggestion

In one sentence: given your source image and a library of calibrated filaments, palette suggestion answers “which N colour filaments should I load to print this picture?” — it summarises the image as a handful of weighted OKLab colours, builds the colour cloud each filament (and each pair of filaments) can physically reach when backlit, and picks the subset whose reachable cloud sits closest to the image’s colours.

This page covers the concept and the gamut machinery — how the image is reduced to a colour signature, how filament gamut clouds are computed, and how a palette is scored by distance-to-nearest-gamut. The search, ranking, and swap-tier sweep that turn those scores into a ranked list live on Palette suggestion search and ranking. Backend node: generator.palette.suggest.

Trust the code, not the header. The module docstring at palette/suggest.py:8 still describes a 6-step “greedy → pairwise → local search → top-K” pipeline, and suggest_palettes still defaults search_mode="fast" (palette/suggest.py:1342). The web app no longer uses that path: the endpoint forces search_mode="thorough" (server.py:3875) and the “quality” mode raises if requested (palette/suggest.py:1412). Everything below is read from the live code.

How to drive it
Suggestion is a web-app feature on the conditioning side of the generator. The endpoint is POST /api/palette/suggest (server.py:3746); it kicks off a background thread and returns {"status": "started"} immediately (server.py:3938), and you poll GET /api/palette/suggest/status (server.py:3942) for progress and the final result. A POST /api/palette/suggest/cancel (server.py:3956) requests cancellation.
The request body is PaletteSuggestPayload (server.py:3511), which forbids unknown fields — stale clients that still send the removed search_mode/quality_weights get a loud 422 (server.py:3515):


















































FieldDefaultMeaningimage_pathrequiredimage under the generator’s images dir (server.py:3517)n_filaments7target palette size, colour filaments only (server.py:3518)top_k5how many candidate palettes to return (server.py:3519)filament_idsNonerestrict the pool; None = all profiled filaments (server.py:3520)max_swapsNoneif set, run the AMS swap-tier sweep instead of a single suggest (server.py:3521)palette_mode"standard""standard" or "luminance_detail" (server.py:3522)improvement_thresholdNoneswap-tier early-stop gain % (server.py:3523)force_all_tiersNoneswap-tier: evaluate every tier regardless of gain (server.py:3524)
palette_mode is normalised before validation (server.py:3526): "source"/"source_color"/"source_colour" all fold to "standard"; "luminance"/"detail"/"luminance-detail" fold to "luminance_detail"; anything else is rejected.
Two guardrails run before any work starts. The configured white base/cap are fixed inputs the suggester cannot drop, so if either is flagged exclude_from_model the endpoint refuses up front with a 400 (server.py:3766–3774). And colour candidates flagged exclude_from_model are stripped from the pool via excluded_filament_ids(...) (server.py:3886) so an excluded filament never appears in a suggestion.
The three-part idea

Colour signature — reduce the image to K weighted OKLab centroids (k-means). Each centroid is a representative colour; its weight is how much of the image is that colour.
Filament gamut clouds — for every filament, enumerate every printable (colour-thickness × cap-thickness) stack and convert the predicted backlit RGB into OKLab. That point cloud is everything that filament can reproduce. Pairs of filaments get their own sampled cloud to capture mixed colours (a green from cyan + yellow).
Score = distance to nearest gamut — for a candidate palette, every signature centroid looks up its nearest point across the union of the palette’s single and pair clouds. The weighted mean of those nearest-distances (plus, in robust mode, the tail) is the palette’s error.

Steps 1 and 2 are this page. Step 3’s search and ranking are on Palette suggestion search and ranking.
Step 1 — the image colour signature
The signature is a ColourSignature (palette/suggest.py:95): centroids (K×3 OKLab), weights (K, summing to 1), n_pixels, and a domain tag (default MODEL_OKLAB_DOMAIN, i.e. "model_oklab").
The web app does not cluster raw image pixels. It first runs the image through the same target-cloud path the solve runner uses, so the colours being matched are the colours a solve would actually try to hit. solve_target_oklab_for_signature (palette/suggest.py:323) calls compute_solve_target_cloud (pipeline/target_cloud.py:64) and returns its solve_oklab cloud, optionally applying the gamut-white rescale (palette/suggest.py:341). That cloud is then clustered by extract_colour_signature_from_oklab (palette/suggest.py:286), which runs k-means and turns per-cluster pixel counts into normalised weights (palette/suggest.py:307).

Why the solve-equivalent cloud, not raw pixels? The signature’s domain must match the gamut clouds’ domain, or scoring is meaningless. The endpoint asserts this — _assert_signature_gamut_domain_match (palette/suggest.py:467) raises if sig.domain != gamut_backend.domain (called from palette/suggest.py:1404). Routing the image through the solve target cloud guarantees both sides live in model OKLab.

The k-means itself (_kmeans_oklab, palette/suggest.py:589) is a hand-rolled implementation: k-means++ seeding via a running-minimum distance (palette/suggest.py:599), then up to 30 Lloyd iterations using a scipy.spatial.KDTree for the assignment step and np.bincount for vectorised centroid updates (palette/suggest.py:617–632). Fixed seed 42 (palette/suggest.py:593), so a given image yields a stable signature. The web app asks for 100 clusters in standard mode (server.py:3842).

Saturated-corner caveat (from the code). Both solve_target_oklab_for_signature (palette/suggest.py:330) and extract_colour_signature (palette/suggest.py:383) carry a docstring note: deeply saturated source pixels map to inverse-LUT corners that are extrapolated beyond measured swatch evidence and can shift between Camera Transform generations. Suggestion deliberately mirrors solve ingress for those pixels rather than promising stable precision — it leaves downstream gamut handling to the normal solve machinery. See Gamut mapping and Model-domain ingress.

Luminance-detail mode
When palette_mode == "luminance_detail", the endpoint swaps in extract_luminance_residual_signature (palette/suggest.py:482) with 120 clusters (server.py:3827). The premise (its docstring, palette/suggest.py:491): a luminance-detail solve lets the white cap carry most of the source’s lightness structure, so palette suggestion should chase chroma reach instead of fitting full source luminance as if the colour stacks carried all the detail.
It does two things differently:

L is down-weighted for clustering. _scale_oklab_l (palette/suggest.py:454) multiplies the OKLab L axis by a small luminance_weight (0.15, server.py:3822) before k-means, so clusters split on chroma, not lightness (palette/suggest.py:529).
Centroids are chroma-weighted. Each cluster’s centroid is a chroma-importance-weighted average of its members (palette/suggest.py:556), and a cluster’s weight is the sum of its members’ chroma importance (palette/suggest.py:561), where chroma importance is the member’s chroma normalised against the 90th-percentile chroma and clipped to [0,1] (palette/suggest.py:519–521). Low-chroma greys contribute little weight; vivid colours dominate.

There is a companion metric knob, gamut_luminance_weight, derived from the session’s chroma_weight as 1.0 / chroma_weight in standard mode and detail_l_weight / chroma_weight in luminance-detail mode (server.py:3820, 3823). This scales the L axis again at scoring time (see “How a palette is scored” below). It is distinct from the clustering luminance_weight above.

extract_colour_signature (palette/suggest.py:359) and extract_appearance_colour_signature (palette/suggest.py:434, a deprecated alias with no remaining callers) are convenience wrappers that load + downsample + cluster in one call. extract_colour_signature is exercised by the dev CLI (main, palette/suggest.py:1926) and tests, not the web endpoint, which assembles the signature step-by-step. Confirmed by grepping server.py: the endpoint imports extract_colour_signature_from_oklab / extract_luminance_residual_signature (server.py:3788–3789), never the wrapper.

Step 2 — filament gamut clouds
A filament’s gamut is the set of OKLab colours it can produce when backlit, across every printable stack. Two providers exist for these clouds, chosen by which colour model is active.
Which provider you get
_build_palette_suggestion_model (server.py:3656) resolves the backend from the session’s appearance_model_provider:




















Active colour modelGamut sourceranking_modehistorical_spline (default)the spline-profile functions in this module (server.py:3667)"mean" (server.py:3673)photo-stack providerPhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend (server.py:3696)"robust" (server.py:3722)
When the spline path is used gamut_backend is None, and suggest_palettes falls back to the in-module gamut functions. When the photo-stack model is selected the backend object is passed through and used instead — same scoring contract, different colour predictions. (Both report domain "model_oklab".) The photo-stack branch requires a calibration-fit bundle and 400s if none exists (server.py:3686).
Single-filament gamut
For the spline path, _compute_single_filament_gamut (palette/suggest.py:639) enumerates a 2-D grid: every colour-layer count 0..max_layers × every sampled cap thickness from d_wc_min up to d_wc_max (sampling every 4th cap step for speed — cap_step=4, palette/suggest.py:648). It batch-evaluates the white-base, white-cap and colour transmissions, multiplies them per the transmission model
T_total = T_wb · T_wc · T_colour (palette/suggest.py:684),
masks out any stack whose cap + colour height exceeds the budget t_max (palette/suggest.py:689), clips, and converts to OKLab (palette/suggest.py:697). The result is a few-hundred-point cloud per filament.
For the photo-stack path, PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend.single_gamut (palette/suggest.py:227) does the same enumeration but predicts RGB through a _PhotoStackGridEvaluator (palette/suggest.py:158, 247) instead of multiplying spline transmissions, then converts to OKLab via _gamut_oklab_from_model_rgb (palette/suggest.py:214). Single clouds are cached per filament (palette/suggest.py:229).
Pair gamut — capturing mixed colours
Two filaments stacked produce colours neither can reach alone (the canonical example in the code: green from cyan + yellow, palette/suggest.py:15). _compute_pair_gamut (palette/suggest.py:700) samples n_samples=10 evenly-spaced thicknesses per filament (palette/suggest.py:732) across a coarser cap grid (cap_step=8, palette/suggest.py:711), builds the full T_wb · T_wc · T_a · T_b product over the 3-D meshgrid (palette/suggest.py:741), budget-masks, and converts to OKLab. The photo-stack equivalent is PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend.pair_gamut (palette/suggest.py:253), cached per unordered pair.
Pairs are on by default (include_pairs=True, palette/suggest.py:1353). Pair clouds are precomputed for all C(N,2) filament pairs in _precompute_centroid_distances (palette/suggest.py:833–855), which is the dominant cost and the source of the “Computing pair gamuts i/N” progress messages (palette/suggest.py:839).
Whites are not colour candidates
The photo-stack backend’s supports(fid) (palette/suggest.py:187) returns False for any white filament (is_white(text), palette/suggest.py:193) and for filaments absent from the model’s curves. The white base and white cap are fixed parameters of every gamut (the T_wb/T_wc factors), never selectable members of the palette.
How a palette is scored (the bridge to ranking)
The gamut clouds feed scoring through one precomputation. _precompute_centroid_distances (palette/suggest.py:795) builds, for each filament and each pair, a per-centroid nearest-neighbour distance array: it scales both the gamut points and the signature centroids’ L axis by gamut_luminance_weight (palette/suggest.py:820, 827), builds a KDTree over the scaled gamut, and queries each centroid (palette/suggest.py:828). The result is dist_single[fid] and dist_pair[(a,b)], each a (K,) vector.
Given a candidate palette, _palette_distance_vector (palette/suggest.py:859) takes the element-wise minimum across the palette’s single distances and all its pair distances (palette/suggest.py:868–874) — for each signature centroid, the distance to the nearest reachable colour in the whole palette. From that vector _score_palette_metrics (palette/suggest.py:878) produces four numbers: weighted mean dE, max dE, % of image weight above the JND threshold, and weighted p90 dE (palette/suggest.py:892–895). The in-gamut threshold is SUGGESTION_COVERAGE_DE_THRESHOLD = 0.02 OKLab (~1 JND) (palette/suggest.py:61).
These four metrics collapse into one rank score by _palette_rank_score (palette/suggest.py:913):

mean mode (spline path): score = mean_de (palette/suggest.py:923).
robust mode (photo-stack path): score = mean_de + 0.35·p90_de + 0.15·max_de + 0.03·(pct_above/100) (palette/suggest.py:924–929) — penalises visible holes in coverage, not just the average.

The actual greedy/exhaustive/multi-start search over palettes, the top-k assembly, the swap-tier sweep, and the response shape are all on Palette suggestion search and ranking.
What comes back
The endpoint formats either a candidate list (single suggest, _format_candidate_response at server.py:3590) or a tier list (swap-aware, _format_tier_response at server.py:3620), each candidate carrying filament_ids, mean_de, max_de, and coverage (server.py:3600, 3632). Alongside the candidates it returns signature_stats (clustering + ingress provenance, server.py:3846) and model_metadata (gamut backend, domain, provider fingerprint, ranking mode, server.py:3855). Both palette_mode and metric_luminance_weight are echoed so the UI can label the scoring space honestly.
Related

Palette suggestion search and ranking — the search algorithm, top-k assembly, AMS swap-tier sweep, and HTTP response shape

conditioning/image-preprocessing-the-f1-.title: Image preprocessing the F1 slot
conditioning/image-preprocessing-the-f1-.content:
In one sentence: the F1 slot takes the loaded image, runs an ordered, contract-enforced chain of preprocessing operators (each declaring its own colour domain), and hands the result forward to target computation — inserting colour-space conversions at every domain boundary and refusing to start if the chain is mis-wired.

Image preprocessing — the F1 slot
The F1 preprocessing slot is the stage that conditions the source image after filament profiles are loaded and before the solve target is computed. It is a pure function over image data: raster plus read-only context in, transformed raster plus an audit trace out. The actual operators that do the conditioning live on Preprocessing operators; the F2/F3 shared services (palette metadata, protect masking) that some operators consume live on Palette metadata and protect masking. This page is about the runner that drives the chain and enforces the contract.
The slot runner is preprocessing/runner.py; its public types are preprocessing/types.py; the boundary converters are preprocessing/color_convert.py.
Where the slot sits in a solve
The slot is driven from the staged-backend pipeline runner, not the legacy CLI engine. run_pipeline (pipeline/runner.py:587) builds the LUTs and target cloud and then hands off to the staged backend at pipeline/runner.py:846 (run_staged_backend_path). The F1 slot executes inside run_pipeline, in between:















Before the slotThe slotAfter the slotProfiles loaded into state.profiles (pipeline/runner.py:663); appearance provider created (pipeline/runner.py:670).run_preprocessing_pipeline(...) called at pipeline/runner.py:761.compute_solve_target_cloud(image, ...) at pipeline/runner.py:779 computes the OKLab solve target from the post-preprocess raster.
Profiles load first so palette-aware operators can resolve their F2 context (pipeline/runner.py:701, resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain); the slot runs before target computation so the target OKLab reflects whatever conditioning the chain applied. This ordering is documented inline at pipeline/runner.py:689.
Liveness. The slot is live on the webapp solve path. The chain is resolved from live module state by _resolve_preprocessing_from_state (facade.py:602) and threaded into PipelineConfig.preprocessors (facade.py:763), which the webapp facade hands to run_pipeline (facade.py:906, facade.py:920). The whole F1 block is gated on if config.preprocessors: (pipeline/runner.py:695) — when no operators are enabled, the block is skipped entirely and the original raster flows through unchanged.
The runner contract — five things it does
run_preprocessing_pipeline (preprocessing/runner.py:210) does exactly five things, in order:

Sort enabled operators (preprocessing/runner.py:232).
Validate the chain shape before any work (preprocessing/runner.py:233).
Convert the raster at each operator’s input boundary (preprocessing/runner.py:247).
Run each operator and validate its output per-boundary (preprocessing/runner.py:252–253).
Preview: emit a per-operator snapshot frame, view-only (preprocessing/runner.py:273).

It returns (image, trace, accumulated_debug_maps) (preprocessing/runner.py:217): the post-preprocess raster in the last operator’s declared output domain, a list of one PreprocessingTraceStep per executed operator, and a dict of debug maps keyed <module_name>:<map_name> (preprocessing/runner.py:266).
1. Sort: (order, class qualname)
_sort_operators (preprocessing/runner.py:111) does a stable sort keyed on (float(getattr(op, "order", 1000.0)), f"{type(op).__module__}.{type(op).__qualname__}") (preprocessing/runner.py:117–123). So the primary key is the operator’s declared order (default 1000.0 on the base class, pipeline/base.py:94), and ties break deterministically on the fully-qualified class name — matching the registry’s lexical import-path discovery order.
Operators advertise their position with conventional order bands (documented at pipeline/base.py:80): Wing A 100–199, Wing B 200–299, Wing C 300–399, Wing D 400–499. For example, c2_soft_gamut_compress declares order = 330.0 (operators/c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:381), placing it in the Wing C band.
2. Validate the chain before running anything
_validate_chain (preprocessing/runner.py:126) enforces one rule: the last enabled operator must emit an sRGB output domain. It checks getattr(tail, "output_domain", None) against SRGB_OUT_DOMAINS (preprocessing/runner.py:136) and raises PreprocessingContractError otherwise (preprocessing/runner.py:137). SRGB_OUT_DOMAINS is frozenset({"srgb_u8", "srgb_f32"}) (types.py:35).
This check runs before any apply() call (preprocessing/runner.py:233, ahead of the loop at :243), so a mis-wired chain fails loudly with zero partial work. The error message is actionable — it names the offending operator and tells you to disable it or add a tail converter (preprocessing/runner.py:138–142). An empty chain is a legal no-op: _validate_chain returns immediately when not operators (preprocessing/runner.py:132), and the runner short-circuits with return image, [], {} for an empty sorted chain (preprocessing/runner.py:235–236).
3 & 4. Convert at boundaries, then run + validate per operator
The run loop (preprocessing/runner.py:243) carries a current raster and a current_domain. The ingress domain is inferred from the input raster’s dtype by _infer_ingress_domain (preprocessing/runner.py:189): uint8 → srgb_u8, float32 → srgb_f32 (preprocessing/runner.py:200–203); any other dtype raises PreprocessingContractError (preprocessing/runner.py:204). In practice the slot is entered from the post-load srgb_u8 raster, while many direct tests feed srgb_f32 (preprocessing/runner.py:194–197).
For each operator, the runner reads its declared input_domain (preprocessing/runner.py:244) and, if current_domain != in_dom, converts the raster to match (preprocessing/runner.py:247–248). The runner owns every boundary, including the very first one — the first enabled operator receives its declared input domain without normalizing inside apply().
After op.apply(...) (preprocessing/runner.py:252), _validate_apply_result (preprocessing/runner.py:146) enforces the per-boundary contract on what came back:








































CheckRaises if…AnchorTyperesult is not a PreprocessingResultpreprocessing/runner.py:152Image typeresult.image is not an np.ndarraypreprocessing/runner.py:158ShapeH/W differs from the input (img.shape[:2] != raw_input.shape[:2])preprocessing/runner.py:163Domaindeclared output_domain not in VALID_COLOR_DOMAINSpreprocessing/runner.py:169Dtypeactual dtype ≠ the domain’s expected dtype (_DOMAIN_DTYPE[declared])preprocessing/runner.py:174Finitenessany NaN/Inf in the outputpreprocessing/runner.py:179
_DOMAIN_DTYPE (preprocessing/runner.py:60) is the canonical dtype-per-domain map: srgb_u8 → uint8, the three *_f32 domains → float32. Every failure carries the offending operator’s name.
After validation the runner records one PreprocessingTraceStep (preprocessing/runner.py:256) with the operator’s name, input/output domains, cache_hit=False, and a copy of its metrics; then it merges the operator’s debug_maps into the accumulator (preprocessing/runner.py:265). Finally current and current_domain advance to the operator’s output (preprocessing/runner.py:287–288).

Note: PreprocessingTraceStep.cache_hit is hard-wired False here (preprocessing/runner.py:262); the runner itself does not cache operator outputs.

5. Preview emission — view-only
When a snapshot_publisher is supplied (preprocessing/runner.py:273), the runner canonicalizes the operator’s output to srgb_u8 via _to_srgb_u8_for_preview (preprocessing/runner.py:274) and publishes it under stage key preprocess/<module_name> (preprocessing/runner.py:281–283). This is view-only: the raster handed forward to the next operator stays in the declared domain (preprocessing/runner.py:287 advances current to result.image, not the previewed copy).
If the operator is palette-aware — "palette_metadata" in its required_context and the context actually carries metadata — the preview’s cache key folds in palette_metadata.request_fingerprint (preprocessing/runner.py:277–280) so the same module name under a different palette does not collide in browser cache. request_fingerprint is a real field on PaletteMetadata (palette_metadata.py:152).
The four colour domains
The slot speaks exactly four colour domains, defined as a Literal type (types.py:26) and enumerated in VALID_COLOR_DOMAINS (types.py:29):






























Domaindtype / rangeMeaningsrgb_u8uint8 [0, 255]sRGB primaries (Rec.709), D65, IEC 61966-2-1 transfer (types.py:5)srgb_f32float32 [0, 1]Same encoding as srgb_u8, normalized (types.py:7)linear_rgb_f32float32, nominally [0, 1]Same primaries + D65, linear light (no transfer); may exceed [0,1] for HDR-style ops (types.py:8)oklab_f32float32Ottosson OKLab, D65; L in [0,1], a/b in ~[−0.5, 0.5] (types.py:10)
Each operator declares an input_domain and output_domain from this set on the PreprocessingModule base class (pipeline/base.py:92–93, both default "srgb_u8"). The runner’s job is to bridge any mismatch between an operator’s output_domain and the next operator’s input_domain.
Per-boundary conversion
_convert (preprocessing/runner.py:70) is the boundary bridge. It is a no-op when src == dst (preprocessing/runner.py:76), routes the six adjacent pairs directly (preprocessing/runner.py:79–90), and two-hops every other pair through srgb_f32 (preprocessing/runner.py:92). So srgb_f32 is the single conversion hub; e.g. linear_rgb_f32 → oklab_f32 goes linear → srgb_f32 → oklab.
The conversion math lives in color_convert.py, and the runner imports exactly six helpers (preprocessing/runner.py:34–41):








































HelperDirectionNotessrgb_u8_to_srgb_f32u8 → f32divide by 255 (color_convert.py:22)srgb_f32_to_srgb_u8f32 → u8clamp [0,1], ×255, round half-to-even (color_convert.py:27)srgb_f32_to_linear_rgb_f32sRGB → linearIEC 61966-2-1 piecewise, sign-preserving, no clamp (color_convert.py:45)linear_rgb_f32_to_srgb_f32linear → sRGBpiecewise inverse, sign-preserving, no clamp (color_convert.py:62)srgb_f32_to_oklab_f32sRGB → OKLabtwo-hop via linear (color_convert.py:92)oklab_f32_to_srgb_f32OKLab → sRGBtwo-hop via linear (color_convert.py:97)
Two precision-relevant choices in color_convert.py:

It uses the true IEC 61966-2-1 piecewise transfer, not the **GAMMA approximation in model.py (color_convert.py:8), because round-trips through linear light must not bleed shadow precision near the project’s T_floor=0.003 noise floor (color_convert.py:11).
The sRGB↔linear helpers are sign-preserving and unclamped (color_convert.py:54, color_convert.py:70): HDR-style operators may temporarily exceed [0,1], and only the final emit to srgb_u8 clamps (color_convert.py:35). The OKLab conversions delegate to lib.transmission.linear_to_oklab / oklab_to_linear (color_convert.py:17), tying the slot’s colour math to lib.transmission.

The runner inserts at most one converter per boundary, and operators never call these helpers directly except in tests (color_convert.py:5).
Read-only context handed to each operator
Every apply() receives a frozen PreprocessingContext (types.py:50). The runner builds it once per solve at pipeline/runner.py:753 with:

config — the PipelineConfig (types.py:60)
image_fingerprint — from fingerprint_protect_mask_image(image) (pipeline/runner.py:700)
source_image — the pre-slot raster (pipeline/runner.py:757)
palette_metadata — the F2 service result, or None (types.py:64)
protect_mask — the F3 service result, or None (types.py:65)

An operator only sees palette_metadata / protect_mask populated if it opts in via required_context (pipeline/base.py:95) — otherwise these stay None. palette_metadata is resolved exactly once per solve and only when at least one operator requests it (pipeline/runner.py:696); the protect mask is resolved only when subject-protect is enabled and some operator advertises supports_protect_mask (pipeline/runner.py:714). These two services are documented on Palette metadata and protect masking. A concrete consumer: c2_soft_gamut_compress declares required_context = frozenset({"palette_metadata"}) (operators/c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:382).
The slot’s public types
All in preprocessing/types.py:

PreprocessingContractError (types.py:38) — the single exception type for every contract violation (wrong type/shape/dtype, non-finite output, illegal end-of-chain domain, ingress-dtype mismatch).
PreprocessingContext (types.py:50) — frozen, read-only, handed to every apply().
PreprocessingResult (types.py:68) — an operator’s return value: image, output_domain, optional debug_maps, optional metrics (types.py:76–79). Mutable (not frozen).
PreprocessingTraceStep (types.py:82) — one frozen audit row per executed operator; the list lives on PipelineState.

How to drive it (users)
You do not call the runner directly — you enable/order operators through the generator’s module management UI, which writes the live module state that _resolve_preprocessing_from_state reads (facade.py:602). Practical consequences of the contract above:

Order matters and is explicit. Operators run in order order, not enable order. If two operators tie, the class-name tiebreaker decides — see the Wing bands above.
A disabled chain is free. With no operators enabled, the whole F1 block is skipped (pipeline/runner.py:695) and the image passes through untouched.
The last operator must end in sRGB. If you build a custom chain whose final operator emits linear_rgb_f32 or oklab_f32, the solve aborts at chain-build time with a clear message (preprocessing/runner.py:137) — add a tail converter or reorder so an sRGB-emitting operator is last.
Previews are per-operator. Each enabled operator publishes a preprocess/<name> snapshot you can inspect; the previews are colour-canonicalized to srgb_u8 for display but do not affect the data flowing downstream.

Related

Palette metadata and protect masking — the F2/F3 services consumed via required_context
