generator.pipeline.runner — the staged-backend runner that drives the slot
lib.transmission — OKLab conversion math the slot’s converters delegate to

conditioning/palette-metadata-and-protec.title: Palette metadata and protect masking
conditioning/palette-metadata-and-protec.content:
In one sentence: two palette-aware preprocessing services — F2 palette metadata samples what colours the chosen filament stack can actually reach (an achievable-colour envelope), and F3 protect masking finds the photo’s subject (via rembg saliency, plus user brush/raster overrides) so that conditioning operators can soften their edits inside the subject and stay aggressive in the background.

These two services run in the generator.pipeline.runner F1 preprocessing slot, before the image is turned into a solve target and before the Staged backend does the actual layer solve. They are inputs that conditioning operators (C1, C2, B1, B3) consume — they do not themselves edit the image. Both are resolved once per solve and passed down through PreprocessingContext.

F2 = “what colours can this palette make?” → fed to operators that compress toward the gamut or remap tone.
F3 = “where is the subject?” → fed to operators as a per-pixel weight that blends an aggressive edit against a gentler one.

See also: Preprocessing chain, Conditioning operators, generator.preprocessing.palette_metadata, generator.preprocessing.protect_mask, generator.preprocessing.protect_blend.

How it wires into a solve
Both services are live and called from pipeline/runner.py inside run_pipeline, which the webapp/facade uses (facade.py:906 imports run_pipeline; run_pipeline later delegates the solve to run_staged_backend_path at pipeline/runner.py:843-846). Preprocessing happens in the if config.preprocessors: block (pipeline/runner.py:695) — that is, F2/F3 resolve and the chain runs before the staged backend ever sees the raster.



































StepCall siteWhat happensF2 resolvepipeline/runner.py:701resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain(...) → `PaletteMetadataF3 mask resolvepipeline/runner.py:718resolve_protect_mask_for_chain(...) → `ProtectMaskResultF3 weight resolvepipeline/runner.py:724resolve_protect_blend_spec(...) → shared ProtectBlendSpec for metricsHand to chainpipeline/runner.py:753-760both stuffed into PreprocessingContext(palette_metadata=..., protect_mask=...)Chain runspipeline/runner.py:761run_preprocessing_pipeline(...) runs each operator with that context
The runner-side resolve_protect_blend_spec call (pipeline/runner.py:724) is only for diagnostics/metrics (protect_weight_mean, protect_weight_p95, debug maps at pipeline/runner.py:733-752). Each operator independently re-derives its own blend weight from the cached mask (see F3 weight derivation below).

F2 — palette metadata (achievable-colour envelope)

Source: preprocessing/palette_metadata.py.

What it produces
resolve_palette_metadata returns a frozen PaletteMetadata with exactly four pinned fields plus a fingerprint (palette_metadata.py:140-152):



































FieldShapeMeaningachievable_black_oklab(3,) float32The darkest OKLab point the stack can reach (lowest L among sampled stacks) — palette_metadata.py:336achievable_white_oklab(3,) float32The lightest reachable OKLab point (highest L) — palette_metadata.py:337max_chroma_by_hue(n_bins,) float32Per-hue-bin maximum reachable chroma — palette_metadata.py:343hue_degrees(n_bins,) float32Hue-bin centres these chroma caps belong to — palette_metadata.py:344request_fingerprintstr32-hex digest of the producing request — palette_metadata.py:345
The black/white anchors are C1’s input; the per-hue chroma envelope is C2’s input (the module header at palette_metadata.py:11-14 calls these “the four pinned fields”, and the consuming operators confirm it — see below).
How the envelope is sampled
_candidate_oklab_points (palette_metadata.py:176) builds a cloud of OKLab points by composing transmission stacks within the print budget and projecting each to OKLab via compose + linear_to_oklab from lib/transmission.py (imported at palette_metadata.py:49; compose defined lib/transmission.py:146, linear_to_oklab lib/transmission.py:40). It is explicitly an envelope sampler, not a full polytope enumeration (palette_metadata.py:190-193).
The coverage strategy (palette_metadata.py:184-188):

White sandwich alone — white base + white cap, across three cap-thickness samples (d_wc_min, midpoint, d_wc_max; palette_metadata.py:196-200, palette_metadata.py:211-215).
Single-filament stacks — each palette colour at coarse thickness samples (palette_metadata.py:219-230).
Pairs (k=2) — every 2-combination, when k_max >= 2 (palette_metadata.py:233-250).
Triples (k=3) — every 3-combination, when k_max >= 3 (palette_metadata.py:253-273).

Thickness samples are coarse by design: at most _THICKNESS_SAMPLES_PER_LAYER = 4 per layer (palette_metadata.py:158), snapped to layer height by _layer_sample_thicknesses (palette_metadata.py:166-173). Each stack must fit the colour budget t_max - d_wb - d_wc (palette_metadata.py:208; pair/triple sums checked at palette_metadata.py:239 and palette_metadata.py:261). Corrections are applied to compose when use_corrections is set (palette_metadata.py:202-204).
From that point cloud:

black/white = argmin/argmax of L (palette_metadata.py:335-337).
chroma envelope = _chroma_envelope (palette_metadata.py:278) bins points by hue into _HUE_BINS_DEFAULT = 12 bins (30°-wide; palette_metadata.py:157) and takes the max chroma per bin, with empty bins set to 0 (palette_metadata.py:294-298).

If sampling somehow yields no points, the resolver falls back to the bare white-cap point for both anchors and an all-zero chroma envelope rather than failing (palette_metadata.py:317-333).
When it runs (opt-in) and how it is keyed
F2 is skipped unless some operator opts in. _chain_needs_palette_metadata (palette_metadata.py:349) returns True only if an operator declares "palette_metadata" in its required_context; otherwise resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain returns None and the chain sees context.palette_metadata = None (palette_metadata.py:375-378). The two opting-in operators are C1 (operators/c1_achievable_tonemap.py:229) and C2 (operators/c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:382) — both frozenset({"palette_metadata"}).
The request is the envelope-relevant slice of PipelineConfig, built by PaletteMetadataRequest.from_config (palette_metadata.py:90). It deliberately includes only fields that move the achievable envelope — palette (sorted, treated as an unordered set; palette_metadata.py:99), the white sandwich identities and thicknesses, t_max, k_max, layer_height, and corrections (palette_metadata.py:98-110). It deliberately excludes solver weights like de_threshold/gamut_mode/chroma_weight, grouping knobs, image resolution, and preprocessing params (palette_metadata.py:64-72). fingerprint() (palette_metadata.py:112) is a 32-char truncated SHA-256 over the rounded fields (palette_metadata.py:119-135); identical envelopes hash identically. This fingerprint is the palette-change invalidation key (header note palette_metadata.py:16-22).
How C1 and C2 consume it




















OperatorUsesBehaviour on degenerate / missingC1 achievable tonemapachievable_black_oklab / achievable_white_oklab L-endpoints to remap tone(anchor inputs per c1_achievable_tonemap.py:229 required_context)C2 soft gamut compresshue_degrees + max_chroma_by_hue as the per-hue chroma ceilingraises if metadata is None (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:441-444); returns an identity result if the envelope is empty / all-zero (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:456-461)
C2 reads the two envelope arrays at c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:446-453, then interpolates a per-pixel chroma bound around the hue circle via _query_chroma_bound (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:36) and soft-knee-compresses chroma toward it.

F3 — protect-subject masking

Sources: preprocessing/protect_mask.py (service + overrides), preprocessing/protect_mask_providers/rembg_u2net.py (saliency), preprocessing/protect_blend.py (weight + blend).

What it produces
ProtectMaskService.get returns a ProtectMaskResult (protect_mask.py:77): a final soft mask (HxW float32 in [0,1]), a confidence scalar, the provider name, a cache_hit flag, and debug_maps (protect_mask.py:396-402). The mask itself is just saliency-plus-overrides; it becomes an editing weight only after resolve_protect_blend_spec (below).
The provider: rembg / u2net saliency
The only registered provider is "rembg" (protect_mask_providers/__init__.py:18-21; unknown names raise KeyError at __init__.py:22). RembgU2NetProvider.predict (protect_mask_providers/rembg_u2net.py:21):

Lazily imports rembg and raises ProtectMaskUnavailableError with the install hint uv sync --group protect-mask-rembg if it is missing (rembg_u2net.py:22-28).
Runs remove(image, session=...) and takes the alpha channel as the soft mask (rembg_u2net.py:33-36). This is class-agnostic saliency — it segments the foreground subject, whatever it is.
Computes a confidence heuristic in _confidence_from_alpha (rembg_u2net.py:40) by penalising three things and averaging the penalties: too-little/too-much high-alpha coverage (rembg_u2net.py:43-46), high-alpha bleeding into the image border (rembg_u2net.py:48-55), and a fuzzy/uncertain boundary band measured via dilate-minus-erode (rembg_u2net.py:57-72). Final confidence = 1 - mean(penalties), clipped to [0,1] (rembg_u2net.py:74-77).

The provider protocol is (soft_mask, confidence) = predict(image) (protect_mask_providers/__init__.py:12-13); the service validates that shape/dtype/range contract (protect_mask.py:452-480).
The service: disk-cached, override-composited
ProtectMaskService (protect_mask.py:349) caches the auto mask only (not the override-composited result) keyed by image fingerprint + provider name. get (protect_mask.py:363):

Canonicalises the framed raster to srgb_u8 (protect_mask.py:364; canonicalize_protect_mask_input at protect_mask.py:86 accepts uint8 or float32 HxWx3).
Loads the cached .npz if present (protect_mask.py:372); on cache miss it calls the provider, validates, and writes the cache atomically via a .tmp rename (protect_mask.py:374-386, write at protect_mask.py:436-450).
Applies the user override on top of the (cached) auto mask — apply_protect_mask_override at protect_mask.py:390.

Cache files live under data/generator/protect_masks/{fingerprint}_{provider}.npz (DEFAULT_PROTECT_MASK_CACHE_DIR protect_mask.py:25-27; path built protect_mask.py:410-412). clear() deletes all cached .npz (protect_mask.py:404-408). The image fingerprint is content-hash of the canonical raster (fingerprint_protect_mask_image protect_mask.py:102, 32-hex). A module-level _DEFAULT_PROTECT_MASK_SERVICE singleton (protect_mask.py:483) backs the chain resolver unless a service is injected.
Overrides (Wing D editing)
The auto mask can be edited two ways, both transported as a solve-scoped ProtectMaskOverride (protect_mask.py:53):




















Override kindFieldCompositing ruleBrush strokesstrokes: tuple[BrushStroke, ...]protect strokes raise the mask (np.maximum), relax strokes lower it (mask * (1 - relax)) — protect_mask.py:335-343Full raster uploadmask_png_pathgrayscale PNG replaces the base mask entirely (protect_mask.py:322-328)
apply_protect_mask_override (protect_mask.py:310) returns the composited mask plus debug maps (override_raster_mask, override_protect_strokes, override_relax_strokes). A BrushStroke (protect_mask.py:45) has mode ("protect"/"relax"), a polyline of points, radius_px, and opacity; strokes rasterise to a canvas with cv2 circles/lines in _stroke_to_mask (protect_mask.py:261). parse_protect_mask_override (protect_mask.py:131) validates the JSON transport strictly — only protect/relax modes (protect_mask.py:158), finite points, radius_px > 0 (protect_mask.py:182), opacity in [0,1] (protect_mask.py:186). Raster filenames are constrained to a server-managed basename inside the override dir — absolute paths, drives, and traversal are rejected (_normalise_override_mask_filename protect_mask.py:220-239; _resolve_override_mask_path re-checks the parent at protect_mask.py:209-217). Override dir: data/generator/protect_mask_overrides/ (protect_mask.py:28-30).
When F3 runs (double gate)
resolve_protect_mask_for_chain (protect_mask.py:486) returns None unless both gates pass:

config.protect_subject_enabled is true (protect_mask.py:495).
At least one operator sets supports_protect_mask = True (protect_mask.py:497).

The operators that opt in are C1, C2, B1 print-scale bilateral (operators/b1_printscale_bilateral.py:110), and B3 TV flatten (operators/b3_tv_flatten.py:127). The runner repeats this same double-gate before calling the resolver (pipeline/runner.py:714-717). The provider name comes from config.protect_mask_provider (default "rembg", protect_mask.py:508; config field pipeline/state.py:158) and the override from config.protect_mask_override (protect_mask.py:505-507; field pipeline/state.py:159).
F3: the protect weight (resolve_protect_blend_spec)

Source: preprocessing/protect_blend.py.

The mask is turned into a per-pixel editing weight by resolve_protect_blend_spec (protect_blend.py:20). The formula (protect_blend.py:42-47):
confidence_gate = clip((confidence - floor) / (1 - floor), 0, 1)
weight          = clip(strength * confidence_gate * mask, 0, 1)

So the protect weight scales with three things: the user strength (protect_subject_strength, validated to [0,1] at protect_blend.py:38), a confidence gate that ramps from 0 at the floor to 1 at confidence 1.0 (protect_confidence_floor validated to [0,1) at protect_blend.py:36), and the soft mask itself. A low-confidence auto-mask therefore self-attenuates toward no protection. Config defaults: protect_subject_strength = 1.0, protect_confidence_floor = 0.35 (pipeline/state.py:156-157).
F3: the blend (blend_aggressive_and_gentle)
Each protect-aware operator computes two versions of its edit — an aggressive pass and a gentle pass — and blend_aggressive_and_gentle (protect_blend.py:60) linearly interpolates them per pixel by the protect weight (protect_blend.py:88-90):
out = aggressive * (1 - weight) + gentle * weight

Weight 0 (background) = full aggressive edit; weight 1 (confident subject) = gentle edit. The function validates both images are float32 srgb_f32 HxWx3 of equal shape with a matching HxW weight (protect_blend.py:70-86).
How each operator builds its gentle pass:






























OperatorAggressive vs gentleSkip-if-no-weight guardC1 tonemapgentle pass at C1_GENTLE_STRENGTH_RATIO = 0.50 of strength (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:24, :426)weight max < _MIN_PROTECT_WEIGHT = 1e-6 → return aggressive (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:22, :419-420)C2 gamut compressgentle pass at C2_GENTLE_COMPRESSION_RATIO = 0.50 of compression (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:26, :483-486)weight max < _PROTECT_WEIGHT_EPSILON = 1e-6 → return aggressive (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:23, :348-350)B1 bilateralblend at b1_printscale_bilateral.py:261gated at b1_printscale_bilateral.py:240B3 TV flattenblend at b3_tv_flatten.py:373gated at b3_tv_flatten.py:352
C1/C2 each re-derive the blend spec from the cached context.protect_mask themselves (C1 at c1_achievable_tonemap.py:407; C2’s helper _protect_blend_weight at c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:330), guarding on protect_subject_enabled + a non-None mask before doing the gentle pass.

Driving it (user-facing)

Reach a wider gamut warning / tone fit: enable C1 (achievable tonemap) and/or C2 (soft gamut compress). They self-resolve the F2 envelope; you do not configure F2 directly. Envelope width is determined by your palette, white sandwich, t_max, k_max, layer height, and corrections — those are the only knobs that move it (palette_metadata.py:64-72).
Protect the subject from heavy conditioning: turn on “protect subject” (protect_subject_enabled), which requires rembg installed (uv sync --group protect-mask-rembg). It only takes effect when at least one of C1/C2/B1/B3 is enabled.
Tune protection: raise protect_subject_strength toward 1.0 for stronger protection; raise protect_confidence_floor to ignore low-confidence auto-masks (the gate zeroes the weight below the floor).
Fix a bad auto-mask: paint protect/relax brush strokes, or upload a full-mask PNG. Overrides composite on top of the cached saliency mask, so re-running the same image is cheap (auto mask is cached; only the override re-composites).


Liveness summary

F2 (resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain) — LIVE. Called pipeline/runner.py:701; opted into by C1 (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:229) and C2 (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:382).
F3 service (resolve_protect_mask_for_chain / ProtectMaskService) — LIVE. Called pipeline/runner.py:718; double-gated on protect_subject_enabled + operator supports_protect_mask.
F3 blend (resolve_protect_blend_spec / blend_aggressive_and_gentle) — LIVE. Used by runner metrics (pipeline/runner.py:724) and by C1, C2, B1, B3 (grep-confirmed call sites above).
rembg/u2net provider — LIVE but dependency-optional; raises ProtectMaskUnavailableError if rembg is not installed (rembg_u2net.py:24-28). It is the only registered provider (protect_mask_providers/__init__.py:18-22).

conditioning/palette-suggestion-search-a.title: Palette suggestion search and ranking
conditioning/palette-suggestion-search-a.content:
Palette suggestion search and ranking

In one sentence: given an image’s colour signature and a pool of calibrated filaments, this picks the best small subset of colour filaments by greedily minimising weighted colour error against each filament’s printable gamut, then returns a requested number of distinct candidate palettes ranked by either mean error or a hole-penalising robust score.

This page covers the search (how palettes are explored) and ranking (how palettes are scored and ordered) halves of generator.palette.suggest. For how the image is turned into the colour signature that drives it, see Colour signature extraction. For the filament-gamut clouds the search scores against, see Palette gamut backends.
All code references are to generator/palette/suggest.py unless noted.

How to drive it (user-facing)
The generator web app’s Auto-suggest flow (POST /api/palette/suggest, generator/server.py:3746) takes these knobs from PaletteSuggestPayload (generator/server.py:3511):













































FieldDefaultEffectn_filaments7Target palette size (colour filaments, white not counted).top_k5How many distinct candidate palettes to return. This is a contract — see below.filament_idsnullRestrict the search pool; null = all profiled non-white filaments.max_swapsnullIf set, run the swap-tier sweep instead of a single-size search.palette_mode"standard""standard" or "luminance_detail" (chroma-emphasised). Validated at generator/server.py:3526.improvement_thresholdnullCoverage gain (%) required to justify another swap tier.force_all_tiersnullEvaluate every swap tier even if improvement stalls.
The web app always runs the thorough search. The endpoint hard-codes search_mode="thorough" (generator/server.py:3875); the old fast/quality switches were removed as user-facing complexity (generator/server.py:3755). The removed search_mode/quality_weights fields are now rejected loudly — the payload forbids extra fields (generator/server.py:3515) and search_mode="quality" raises inside suggest_palettes() (suggest.py:1411).
The job runs on a background thread; poll status at GET /api/palette/suggest/status (generator/server.py:3942) and cancel via POST /api/palette/suggest/cancel (generator/server.py:3956).

Two search modes
suggest_palettes() (suggest.py:1337) dispatches on search_mode after precomputing gamuts. Both modes share the same precomputed per-centroid distance tables (suggest.py:1448) so scoring a trial palette is a cheap np.minimum reduction, never a fresh KD-tree query.
Fast mode (CLI default, not used by the web app)
search_mode="fast" (the function default) runs a single deterministic pass (suggest.py:1485 onward):

Greedy build — repeatedly add the one filament that most lowers the rank score, until n_filaments are selected (suggest.py:1489).
Local search — repeatedly try swapping each selected filament for each unselected one; accept a swap only if it improves the score by more than 0.001 (suggest.py:1552). Capped at 20 sweeps (suggest.py:1521).
Alternatives — fill the remaining top_k slots with the best single-swap neighbours of the primary palette (suggest.py:1581), then double-swap neighbours if still short (suggest.py:1625), then sort (suggest.py:1670).

Thorough mode (web app default)
_thorough_search() (suggest.py:968) chooses between two strategies by combination count:

Exhaustive when C(n_available, n_filaments) <= 50_000 (suggest.py:1002) → _exhaustive_search() (suggest.py:1022) enumerates every combination and keeps the best top_k, periodically trimming the running list to top_k once it grows past top_k * 5 (suggest.py:1087).
Multi-start greedy otherwise (suggest.py:1012) → _multi_start_search() (suggest.py:1095). It seeds from the 8 best individual filaments (n_starts = min(8, len(ranked)), suggest.py:1130), runs the same greedy-build-then-local-swap procedure from each seed (suggest.py:1159 build, suggest.py:1196 swap loop), and dedupes converged palettes by frozenset (suggest.py:1254).


Trap: there are unrelated “greedy”/“beam-search” implementations elsewhere in the generator (post-solve grouping/scheduling). The greedy here is palette-selection greedy over filament subsets — it has nothing to do with layer grouping.


Ranking: mean vs robust
Every trial palette is scored from precomputed distances by _score_palette_metrics() (suggest.py:878), which returns (mean_de, max_de, pct_above_threshold, p90_de). The single scalar used to order palettes comes from _palette_rank_score() (suggest.py:913):




















ModeObjectiveCode"mean"mean_de onlysuggest.py:923"robust"mean_de + 0.35·p90_de + 0.15·max_de + 0.03·(pct_above_threshold/100)suggest.py:924–928
Robust mode deliberately penalises visible holes (a high 90th-percentile or worst-case centroid distance), not just the average — a palette with a great mean but one badly-missed colour region ranks worse than its mean alone suggests.
Default mode is data-driven (suggest.py:1405): "robust" when a gamut_backend is supplied (the model-backed web-app path), "mean" otherwise (legacy spline-gamut CLI path). Any value other than "mean"/"robust" raises (suggest.py:1408).
The component metrics:

mean_de — weight-averaged nearest-gamut OKLab distance across signature centroids.
max_de — worst single centroid distance.
pct_above_threshold — % of image weight whose nearest-gamut distance exceeds de_threshold (default SUGGESTION_COVERAGE_DE_THRESHOLD = 0.02, suggest.py:61, ~1 JND). Coverage surfaced to the UI is 100 - pct_above_threshold, computed in the response formatter (generator/server.py:3604); the swap-tier sweep computes the same quantity internally (suggest.py:1875).
p90_de — weighted 90th percentile via _weighted_percentile() (suggest.py:777).

The final candidate sort key is (rank_score, mean_de, max_de) (_candidate_sort_key, suggest.py:963) — rank score first, with mean and max as tie-breakers.

The requested-count distinctness contract
N requested = N distinct palettes whenever the pool allows. This is an explicit user contract, not a best-effort. The danger is that multi-start greedy converges to the same optimum from many seeds — and near-equal colour error is not user-equivalence (colour-distance metrics are not the final word; the right palette is the one the user picks). See Requested count is a contract and feedback-intuition-through-interaction.
When multi-start greedy returns fewer than top_k distinct palettes, _multi_start_search() fills the gap (suggest.py:1296–1331): it expands a frontier of the best single-swap neighbours of the palettes already found, skipping any subset already seen (suggest.py:1314), scoring each, and taking the best until top_k distinct palettes exist. The fast-mode alternatives generator does the analogous single-swap → double-swap fill (suggest.py:1581, suggest.py:1625).

Note: distinctness is by set of filament IDs (frozenset), not by recipe. Two palettes with the same filaments but different thickness assignments are the same candidate here — thickness is decided downstream by the solver, not by suggestion.


Swap-tier sweep
suggest_palettes_swap_aware() (suggest.py:1803) models the reality that an AMS unit only holds a few filaments at once, so reaching more colours means mid-print filament swaps. It sweeps tiers 0..max_swaps:

Tier t allows n_groups = t + 1 AMS loads (suggest.py:1854), so max_filaments = colour_slots_per_load * n_groups (suggest.py:1855), where colour_slots_per_load = slots_per_ams*n_ams_units - reserved_white - reserved_filler (suggest.py:1843).
For each tier it calls suggest_palettes() with that n_filaments and packages a SwapTierResult (suggest.py:1792) carrying the tier’s candidates, best mean dE, and coverage.
Early stop: after tier 0, if coverage improvement over the previous tier is below improvement_threshold (default 5.0%) it stops, unless force_all_tiers (suggest.py:1893).

Endpoint wiring
The /api/palette/suggest job (generator/server.py:3776) builds a common_kwargs dict once (generator/server.py:3874) — search_mode="thorough", white profiles, de_threshold, the excluded-filament set, and gamut_luminance_weight — then branches on max_swaps (generator/server.py:3891):

max_swaps set → suggest_palettes_swap_aware(...) (generator/server.py:3892), result formatted by _format_tier_response (generator/server.py:3903, defined at generator/server.py:3620).
max_swaps unset → suggest_palettes(...) (generator/server.py:3910), formatted by _format_candidate_response (generator/server.py:3916).

Two availability guards run before any palette is suggested: a configured white base/cap that is exclude_from_model raises 400 up front (generator/server.py:3768), and the colour pool is filtered through excluded_filament_ids(...) (generator/server.py:3886) so an excluded filament can never enter a suggestion. suggest_palettes() enforces the same drop internally (suggest.py:1400) and additionally filters to filaments the gamut backend supports() (suggest.py:1396).

Dead printability heuristics (flagged)
suggest.py defines three “printability metrics” under a # ── Printability metrics ── banner (suggest.py:1730):

























FunctionLocationLivenessestimate_fragmentationsuggest.py:1732Dead in productionestimate_grouping_costsuggest.py:1754Dead in productionestimate_swap_costsuggest.py:1776Dead in production
A whole-repo grep for these three names finds callers only in tests/generator/test_palette_suggest.py (lines 9–98) and their own definitions — no production code path imports or calls them. They are not wired into suggest_palettes(), suggest_palettes_swap_aware(), the rank score, or the server endpoint. None of the ranking objectives (suggest.py:913) reference fragmentation, grouping cost, or swap cost; ranking is purely colour-error driven. These are vestigial heuristics kept alive only by their unit tests.

Caveat: “dead” here means no production caller as of this audit. The functions still pass their tests and could be revived. Do not delete blindly — confirm the tests’ intent first.


Quick reference: key symbols




























































SymbolLocationRolesuggest_palettessuggest.py:1337Top-level entry; mode dispatch._thorough_searchsuggest.py:968Exhaustive-vs-multi-start chooser (50k threshold at suggest.py:1002)._exhaustive_searchsuggest.py:1022Enumerate all C(N,k)._multi_start_searchsuggest.py:10958-seed greedy + local swap + distinctness fill._palette_rank_scoresuggest.py:913Mean vs robust objective._score_palette_metricssuggest.py:878Mean/max/pct/p90 from precomputed distances._precompute_centroid_distancessuggest.py:795Per-centroid nearest-gamut distance tables.suggest_palettes_swap_awaresuggest.py:1803Swap-tier sweep with early stop.SwapTierResultsuggest.py:1792Per-tier result record.suggest_palettes_endpointgenerator/server.py:3746HTTP route (always thorough).
Related

Colour signature extraction — the OKLab centroid signature this search scores.
Palette gamut backends — PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend and single/pair gamut clouds.
Requested count is a contract — why top_k distinct results is non-negotiable.
generator.palette.suggest — module-level architecture node.
lib.photo_stack_model — the appearance predictor behind the model-backed gamut.

conditioning/preprocessing-operators.title: Preprocessing operators
conditioning/preprocessing-operators.content:
In one sentence: five self-registering image operators (A1, B1, B3, C1, C2) that condition the solve-grid raster before the solve — every one ships off by default — plus two shared helpers, feature_scale (a nozzle-derived spatial anchor) and hue_interp (circular hue interpolation).

Preprocessing operators
These operators live in the preprocessing slot, a chain that runs on the loaded image before the colour solve. They are discovered from the filesystem under preprocessing/operators/ (no hand-maintained name list — _discover_preprocessing_operators, pipeline/registry.py:33; the “no hand-maintained tuple” rationale is at pipeline/registry.py:101), self-register via the @register_preprocessing decorator (pipeline/registry.py:123), and each subclasses PreprocessingModule (pipeline/base.py:73).
The slot is executed by run_preprocessing_pipeline (preprocessing/runner.py:210), called once from the live solve path at pipeline/runner.py:761 — which is the same run_pipeline that hands off to the staged backend (run_staged_backend_path, pipeline/runner.py:846). So these operators are live in the webapp solve, not legacy CLI-only code. They run on the post-load_image() raster, before LUT construction and the solve.
Related: Feature scale anchor · Protect subject blending · preprocessing slot runner · PreprocessingModule contract · Module management
All five ship disabled
Every operator declares default_enabled = False on its class, and the shipped app/modules.json keeps all five false (app/modules.json:4-8). The default-state machinery reads this attribute (pipeline/modules.py:62). You turn them on per-run in the module manager; nothing here is part of the baseline pipeline.















































OperatorClass · nameorderNeeds palette?Protect-mask aware?A1 bilateral denoiseA1BilateralDenoise · a1_bilateral_denoise (a1_bilateral_denoise.py:37)120.0 (:76)nonoB1 print-scale bilateralB1PrintscaleBilateral · b1_printscale_bilateral (b1_printscale_bilateral.py:104)210.0 (:111)noyes (:110)B3 TV flattenB3TvFlatten · b3_tv_flatten (b3_tv_flatten.py:121)220.0 (:128)noyes (:127)C1 achievable tonemapC1AchievableTonemap · c1_achievable_tonemap (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:222)310.0 (:228)yes (:229)yes (:230)C2 soft gamut compressC2SoftGamutCompress · c2_soft_gamut_compress (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:372)330.0 (:381)yes (:382)yes (:383)
order controls chain position; the conventional bands are Wing A 100–199, Wing B 200–299, Wing C 300–399 (pipeline/base.py:80-82). So if you enable several, they run A1 → B1 → B3 → C1 → C2 regardless of the order you toggled them.
All five declare input_domain = output_domain = "srgb_f32" (e.g. a1_bilateral_denoise.py:74-75), i.e. float32 sRGB in [0, 1]. The Wing-C operators convert internally to OKLab and back (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:320, c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:77) but hand sRGB back out. Domain definitions: preprocessing types.

A1 — bilateral denoise (Wing A)

Edge-preserving denoise of the solve-grid raster via a single OpenCV bilateralFilter.

apply (a1_bilateral_denoise.py:108) runs cv2.bilateralFilter once with d = 2*radius_px + 1 (:123), sigmaColor = sigma_range, sigmaSpace = sigma_spatial (:124-129). It is the simplest operator: no palette, no protect mask, no OKLab — purely spatial sRGB smoothing.
It computes a “flat-region” mask up front (Rec.709 luma, local 5×5 std ≤ 0.02 — a1_bilateral_denoise.py:12-13, :30-32, :119) but uses it only for the reported metrics (flat-patch variance before/after, :141-142); the filter itself is applied globally, not gated by the mask.





























ParamDefaultRangeMeaning (from params, :39-72)radius_px31–8Bilateral radius in px; diameter is 2r+1.sigma_range0.040.005–0.25Range sigma in srgb_f32 units (intensity).sigma_spatial2.00.5–10.0Spatial sigma in px.
Constructor re-validates each param against the same bounds and raises ValueError on out-of-range (:85-92, :97-98). Emits debug_maps={"delta_abs_luma": ...} (:147) for the diff visualization.

B1 — print-scale bilateral (Wing B)

Bilateral flatten whose spatial sigma is tied to the printer’s physical feature scale, not a raw pixel count.

The key difference from A1: B1’s spatial sigma is derived in millimetres from the nozzle, then converted to pixels using the solver’s fine pitch. In _resolve_bilateral_params (b1_printscale_bilateral.py:57): sigma_spatial_mm = feature_scale_multiplier * feature_scale_mm (:63), then sigma_spatial_px = sigma_spatial_mm / solver_fine_pitch_mm (:64), clamped to [0.5, 15.0] px (:19-20, :66-71), and the kernel diameter is 2*round(sigma_spatial_px)+1 (:72). feature_scale_mm comes from resolve_feature_scale_mm(context) (:196) — see feature_scale below; solver_fine_pitch_mm defaults to 0.20 if absent (:197-199).
The filter can run multiple passes (:91-97), then clips to [0, 1] (:98).





























ParamDefaultRangeMeaning (:112-155)feature_scale_multiplier1.00.5–2.0Multiplies the shared nozzle-derived feature scale (2×nozzle). 1.0 = blur exactly at print-feature scale; <1 preserves detail; >1 flattens more.sigma_range0.050.005–0.25Intensity sigma on [0,1]. Set higher than A1’s because B1 is a flattener, not a denoiser.passes11–3Bilateral-filter passes; 2–3 strengthen flattening at the cost of edge softness.
Protect-mask path (supports_protect_mask = True, :110): when protect_subject_enabled and a protect_mask are present (:217-224), B1 runs a second, gentler variant whose multiplier is max(0.5, 0.5 * multiplier) (b1_printscale_bilateral.py:21-22, :249-252) and blends aggressive↔gentle by the resolved protect weight via blend_aggressive_and_gentle (:261-265). This protects the masked subject from over-flattening. See Protect subject blending. Reported metrics include the resolved feature_scale_mm, sigma_spatial_mm/px, kernel_d_px, and flat-region variance before/after (:304-320).

B3 — TV flatten (Wing B)

Total-variation (Chambolle) denoise that drives regions toward piecewise-constant patches, optionally in OKLab.

apply (b3_tv_flatten.py:324) runs denoise_tv_chambolle from scikit-image (:61, called through _tv_denoise). The wrapper reflectively adapts to the installed skimage API (max_num_iter/n_iter_max, channel_axis/multichannel) at :63-73, so it survives version drift.
Weight autoscaling is the Wing-B signature: with weight_autoscale=True, effective_weight = tv_weight * (feature_scale_mm / 0.40) (_effective_weight, :202-206; baseline _AUTOSCALE_BASELINE_MM = 0.40 at :24), then clamped to [0.005, 0.30] (:25-26, :207-209) with a warning if it clamps (:210-215). The 0.40 baseline is the default-nozzle feature scale, so at a 0.2 mm nozzle autoscale is a no-op and the weight you set is the weight applied.



































ParamDefaultRangeMeaning (:129-182)tv_weight0.040.005–0.40TV regularization weight; higher = stronger, more piecewise-constant.weight_autoscaleTrueboolScale weight by feature_scale_mm/0.40 so TV strength tracks the print-feature scale.channel_axisoklab_L_absrgb_rgb · oklab_L_ab · oklab_L_onlyColour space for TV: per-channel RGB; perceptual OKLab L+a+b (default); or OKLab-L only (flatten luminance, keep chroma).n_iter_max10020–500Chambolle iteration cap.
_run_tv (:218) branches on channel_axis: srgb_rgb denoises RGB directly (:226-233); oklab_L_ab converts to OKLab and denoises all three channels (:236-242); oklab_L_only denoises just L and re-attaches the original a/b (:244-250), then converts back to sRGB and clips (:251-255).
Protect-mask path: like B1, when a protect mask is active B3 runs an aggressive and a gentle pass (gentle effective weight = 0.35 * effective_weight, b3_tv_flatten.py:27, :369-372) and blends them (:373-377). Its _realized_metrics (:274) count small connected components (≤6 px) per quantized luma bin (:87-116) in protected vs background regions to quantify how much speckle was removed (:314-322).

C1 — achievable tonemap (Wing C)

Palette-aware tonal compression: remaps source luminance (OKLab L) into the range the chosen filament palette can physically reproduce.

C1 is the first operator that requires palette context (required_context = frozenset({"palette_metadata"}), c1_achievable_tonemap.py:229); it raises ValueError if context.palette_metadata is None (:314-317). The palette supplies the achievable black/white L (:324-325).
How it works: source is converted to OKLab (:320); shadow/highlight anchors are taken as percentiles of source L (:327-330); a 3-anchor PCHIP curve maps [shadow, midpoint, highlight] source L onto [achievable_black, midtone_target, achievable_white] (_build_core_curve, :41-61), where the midtone target is placed via 0.5 ** midtone_contrast (:49). Pixels outside the anchor range are extended by linear tails using the curve’s end slopes (_linear_tail_remap, :64-105), then clamped into the achievable range. The remap is blended with the original L by strength (_tonemap_pass, :168-171), and only the L channel is rewritten — a/b are preserved (:173-174).



































ParamDefaultRangeMeaning (:231-272)strength1.00.0–1.0Blend between source L and the achievable-range remap.shadow_percentile0.50.0–10.0Source-L percentile treated as the shadow anchor.highlight_percentile99.590.0–100.0Source-L percentile treated as the highlight anchor.midtone_contrast1.00.5–2.0Three-anchor PCHIP midpoint placement (0.5**contrast).
The constructor additionally requires shadow_percentile < highlight_percentile, raising otherwise (:294-297). Degenerate guards: C1 returns the input unchanged in two cases — if the achievable range collapses (white <= black + 1e-4, with a degenerate_palette metric, :332-341) or if shadow/highlight L coincide (no degenerate_palette flag, :343-351); both route through _zero_result (:187). C1 declares a preview_key (:223) so it can drive a preview tile. Protect-mask path mirrors B1/B3 (gentle strength = 0.5 * strength, :24, :422-432). Debug maps: delta_L, clamp_mask (:384-387).

C2 — soft gamut compress (Wing C)

Hue-preserving soft-knee chroma compression: pulls over-saturated pixels in toward the palette’s per-hue maximum chroma without shifting their hue.

Also palette-required (required_context = frozenset({"palette_metadata"}), c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:382). It reads two arrays from palette metadata: hue_degrees (bin centres) and max_chroma_by_hue (the per-hue chroma envelope) (:446-453). For each source pixel it computes OKLab hue + chroma (_hue_and_chroma, :48-53) and queries the chroma bound at that exact hue via circular interpolation (_query_chroma_bound → interpolate_circular_degrees, :36-45) — see hue_interp.
The soft knee (_run_compression_pass, :88): compression starts at knee_start_ratio * chroma_bound (:94); above the knee, output chroma follows a tanh curve filling the remaining “room” up to the bound (:109-112). The code comment at :107-108 pins this exact tanh form (“Consensus R6 pins this tanh form exactly; do not substitute”). Hue is preserved by scaling a/b uniformly (chroma_scale, :128-144); L is untouched (:146-149).























ParamDefaultRangeMeaning (:384-411)knee_start_ratio0.850.50–1.00Fraction of the hue-local chroma bound at which soft compression begins.knee_softness0.500.05–1.50Soft-knee curvature; higher spreads the transition across a wider input-chroma range.
Degenerate guard: if the palette supplies no hue/chroma samples (or all bounds ≈ 0) C2 returns identity with degenerate_palette (:456-461, _identity_result at :259). Protect-mask path runs a gentle pass (gentler knee via _gentle_knee_start_ratio, :322-327) and blends, then runs a 2-pass re-projection (_resolve_output_chroma, :275) that enforces zero pixels over-bound after blending (:284-319, enforce_zero_over_bound=True at :497). Debug maps: chroma_scale, over_bound_mask (:251-253).

feature_scale — the Wing-B spatial anchor

A single helper that turns the active nozzle diameter into a millimetre “print-feature scale” so B1 and B3 share one definition of “blur at print scale.”

resolve_feature_scale_mm(context, explicit_mm=0.0) (feature_scale.py:45) returns:

explicit_mm verbatim if > 0.0 (a per-call override; :65-66);
otherwise nozzle_diameter * 2.0 — the constant _FEATURE_WIDTHS_PER_NOZZLE = 2.0 (:37, applied :72-73), encoding the heuristic that a reliably reproduced feature is ~2 bead widths wide;
otherwise (missing / non-numeric / non-positive nozzle) the fallback _DEFAULT_FEATURE_SCALE_MM = 0.40 (:42, returned :71, :74).

So at the default 0.2 mm nozzle, feature scale = 0.40 mm (2 × 0.20). Callers are exactly the two Wing-B operators (b1_printscale_bilateral.py:8, b3_tv_flatten.py:14) and the evaluation harness — confirmed via grep. The module header notes printer_min_line_width_mm is deliberately not the anchor (it’s the extrusion floor, ~0.8×nozzle, a different quantity; feature_scale.py:15-17). This 0.40 mm value is also the _AUTOSCALE_BASELINE_MM baseline B3 divides by, which is why autoscale is a no-op at the default nozzle. Detail page: Feature scale anchor.

hue_interp — circular hue lookup

Wrap-aware linear interpolation of a per-hue value array, used by C2 to query the chroma envelope at any OKLab hue angle.

interpolate_circular_degrees(query_degrees, sample_degrees, sample_values) (hue_interp.py:19) linearly interpolates sample_values (indexed by hue bin centres) at arbitrary query hues, wrapping continuously across the 360°→0° seam. Mechanics: queries are normalised mod 360 (:62); a single sample short-circuits to a constant (:64-65); otherwise the sorted bins are wrap-extended by one bin on each side (last −360°, first +360°, :79-80) so a plain np.interp handles the seam without per-query branching (:82). Output is float32, same shape as the query (:82-83). Its only live caller is C2 (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:13, used at :41) — confirmed via grep; the docstring notes it sits next to feature_scale.py as shared Wing-C infrastructure (:9-10).

How they reach the solve (liveness)



































SubjectStatusEvidenceAll five operators wired into live solveliverun_preprocessing_pipeline called at pipeline/runner.py:761, inside the same run_pipeline that runs the staged backend (pipeline/runner.py:846).All five ship disabledconfirmeddefault_enabled = False per class + app/modules.json:4-8 all false.feature_scale helperliveimported and called by B1 (b1_printscale_bilateral.py:8,196) and B3 (b3_tv_flatten.py:14,203).hue_interp helperliveimported and called by C2 (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:13,41).C1/C2 palette requirementenforcedraise ValueError if palette_metadata is None (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:314-317, c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:441-444).
See also: generator.preprocessing.runner (chain execution + domain conversions), Protect subject blending (the aggressive/gentle blend B1/B3/C1/C2 all use), Module management (how to enable per-run), Color domains (srgb_f32 / oklab_f32 definitions).

generator/exporting-print-files.title: Exporting Print Files
generator/exporting-print-files.content:
Exporting Print Files

In one sentence: export turns a completed solve’s per-pixel layer thicknesses into printable 3D geometry — a white base, one object per colour filament, and a white cap — written as STL or 3MF for your slicer, with a separate AMS swap plan telling you when to change filament.

What export produces
A finished export folder contains, per object, a watertight mesh (one STL each, or all of them bundled into a single .3mf), plus an export_manifest.json describing every object, its material, the coordinate frame, and a quality/build report. The objects are always: a white base plate, one z-slab object per colour filament, and the white cap (possibly split into several bodies). Each object is tagged with the material it prints in (build_export_manifest, post_solve_export.py:1820; per-object record at post_solve_export.py:1875).
The contract lives in generator.mesh.post_solve_export (Prisma/generator/mesh/post_solve_export.py), deliberately kept clear of any FastAPI/UI concern. The webapp calls into it through one entry point, export_solve_bundle (post_solve_export.py:2120).
How you drive it (the webapp)
Export runs in the background so the UI can poll progress. The flow is:



































HTTP routeWhat it doesCodePOST /api/export/files/startkicks off a background export job, returns a job_idserver.py:5666GET /api/export/files/statuspolls stage/progress and, when done, the resultserver.py:5745POST /api/export/files/cancelrequests cancellation of a running exportserver.py:5764GET /api/export/swap-instructionsreturns the AMS swap plan + M600 G-codeserver.py:5774POST /api/export/filessynchronous variant retained for direct API/test callersserver.py:5651
The request body (ExportFilesPayload, server.py:742) has four export knobs, plus an optional card_id target selector (covered below):

geometry_source — "field_derived" (default) or "exact_raster" (server.py:743).
field_scale — must be one of 2, 4, 8, 16; default 4 (server.py:744, server.py:754). Only affects the field-derived white cap.
output_format — "3mf" (default) or "stls" (server.py:745, server.py:761).
validate_written_meshes — re-load each written mesh and re-check topology after writing (off by default; server.py:746).

Staleness guard: re-solve before exporting
If a solve-owned setting changed since the last solve, export refuses with HTTP 409 and the message “Solve is stale … Re-solve before exporting.” The check compares the current solve-owned fingerprint against the one captured at solve time (server.py:5443–5450). The swap-instructions endpoint enforces the same guard (server.py:5781–5788). This only fires for the live current target — exporting a saved card by card_id skips it.
The two geometry sources
Export can build the geometry two ways (GeometrySource, post_solve_export.py:55). Field-derived is the default; exact-raster is the faithful-to-the-solve alternative.























SourceColour stacks + baseWhite capEntry pointfield_derived (default)exact rectilinear solve-grid objectsreconstructed as a smoother field, optionally on a finer grid (field_scale)build_field_derived_mesh_bundle_mixed_resolution, post_solve_export.py:1634exact_rasterexact rectilinear solve-grid objectsone rectilinear cell per solve pixel — matches the solve exactlybuild_exact_raster_mesh_bundle, post_solve_export.py:1407
A key fact that holds for both sources: the colour stacks and white base are always exact solve-grid geometry. They are built the same way regardless of geometry_source (_base_and_color_objects, post_solve_export.py:1291, called from both builders at post_solve_export.py:1423 and post_solve_export.py:1706). The geometry source only changes how the white cap is built.
Because the colour layers are exact, the colour part of the print is blocky at the solve resolution — by design. This is the same fidelity rule the preview honours: the geometry never fakes detail the solve didn’t produce. See Thickness map and the white base / cap budget in How a Solve Works.
Why field-derived is the default
In the field-derived path, the combined colour-top “witness” surface is nearest-neighbour upsampled to the field grid (_nearest_upsample_map, post_solve_export.py:2067; lifted at post_solve_export.py:1721), and the reconstructed white cap is meshed on that finer grid via the hybrid white-cap builder. The result is a cap that can carry sub-pixel luminance detail and a smoother top surface than a per-pixel staircase, without disturbing the exact colour layers underneath. field_scale (2/4/8/16) sets how much finer the cap grid is than the solve grid.
The exact-raster path skips reconstruction entirely: it meshes the cap as one rectilinear interval on top of the colour floor (post_solve_export.py:1434), then falls through topology-safety strategies (below) only if that single body would weld badly.
The post-solve export contract
export_solve_bundle (post_solve_export.py:2120) is the single integration point. It is fed a materialized solve bundle — not the live session — and walks nine named stages (DEFAULT_EXPORT_STAGES, post_solve_export.py:187), each surfaced as an ExportProgressEvent (post_solve_export.py:88) the UI polls. The stages: load bundle → detect solve mode → prepare material maps → build geometry source → build colour/base meshes → build white-cap meshes → serialize outputs → validate meshes → write manifest.
What the solve owns vs. what export adds
Export reads, never re-derives, the solve’s geometry. Before the bundle is built, the server materializes the solve’s Thickness maps through _prepare_export_materialization (server.py:835) → prepare_export_material_maps. That step also pins mandatory product safety settings on the config (_force_mandatory_product_settings, server.py:847): the minimum white-cap thickness is snapped up to a whole number of layers, printability enforcement and cap-continuity cleanup are forced on, etc. These guarantee every viewer-facing surface keeps at least one white skin layer — a hard print constraint.
From the materialized bundle, export_solve_bundle reads three settings out of the solve’s own metadata (it raises rather than guessing if they’re missing — _first_config_float, post_solve_export.py:1952):

























SettingLookup keysMeaningpitch_mmpitch_mm, evaluation_pitch_mm, solver_fine_pitch_mm, solve_grid_pitch_mmsolve-grid XY pitchlayer_height_mmlayer_height_mm, layer_heightprint layer height (typically 0.08 mm)d_wb_mmd_wb_mm, d_wb, white_base_thickness_mmwhite base thickness (typically 0.20 mm)
These flow into a RectilinearExportConfig (post_solve_export.py:200) and a GeometryExportPolicy (generator.mesh.geometry_policy) that all builders share. The defaults that originally shaped these come from PipelineConfig (pipeline/state.py:58): layer height 0.08 mm, white base 0.20 mm (d_wb), total height budget ~3 mm (t_max), cap variable for luminance.
Solve mode is auto-detected, not a toggle
Standard vs. luminance behaviour is detected from run/bundle metadata (detect_solve_mode_from_metadata, post_solve_export.py:253) — preferring the luminance_mode flag, with an array-presence fallback for old bundles. The webapp deliberately does not expose solve mode as an export option.
Optional border frame
If the solve was configured with a border, export wraps the content in a white frame and shifts all content objects inward by the border width (_with_export_border, post_solve_export.py:1178). The border prints in the white-cap material and is reported as a separate __border__ object. Border dimensions are read from solve metadata unless overridden (post_solve_export.py:2191–2226).
How the white cap is built (mesh internals → see linked page)
The cap is the most involved object and the only one whose construction differs by geometry source. The short version:

Field-derived: the reconstructed cap field is meshed by the hybrid builder (generator.mesh.hybrid_white_cap) on the finer grid; reconstruction itself lives in generator.mesh.field_white_reconstruction.
Exact-raster: the cap is a single rectilinear interval if it welds cleanly; otherwise export tries, in order, a topology-risk quarantine split, then an adaptive Z-partition, then per-level slabs — each a same-material body that keeps the geometry exact while avoiding non-manifold pinches after STL vertex welding (post_solve_export.py:1454–1509; topology_risk_column_mask from generator.mesh.rectilinear_interval).

Colour stacks get the same quarantine/slab fallbacks if a single colour body would weld badly (_build_color_quarantine_parts / _build_color_z_slab_parts, post_solve_export.py:1102, post_solve_export.py:985).
The full per-cell meshing, the rectilinear interval mesher, and the cap reconstruction math are out of scope here — they live in From solve to mesh the export pipeline.
Quality gates and the manifest
Every built mesh is topology-checked (_quality_for, post_solve_export.py:324; check_mesh_quality from generator.mesh.quality). A part “passes” only if it is watertight with zero open edges and zero pinch edges (_quality_passes, post_solve_export.py:328), and colour/cap parts additionally re-check quality after a strict STL-style re-weld (_strict_processed_quality, post_solve_export.py:336). Parts that still fail are quarantined into their own bodies rather than silently shipped.
The manifest’s top-level status is "ready" only if no object has open edges, pinch edges, or a watertight failure; otherwise "mesh_quality_failed" (post_solve_export.py:1833–1844). With validate_written_meshes=true, export additionally re-loads each written file from disk and re-checks it (_reload_quality_for_path, post_solve_export.py:2096).
STL vs 3MF

STL (output_format="stls"): each object becomes one .stl under …/stls/ (write_export_mesh_bundle_as_stls, called at post_solve_export.py:2344). The manifest names every file and its material so you can assign filaments in the slicer by hand.
3MF (output_format="3mf", the default): all objects are packaged into a single {export_id}.3mf with filament assignments and material display names baked in (server.py:5546–5555), so OrcaSlicer opens it with materials already mapped. The single-file name keeps multiple lithophanes from colliding in one slicer project.

Both formats are handled symmetrically by generator.mesh.export_serializers.
AMS swap instructions (M600)
A multi-colour lithophane usually needs more colour filaments than your AMS has slots. The solver groups colours into swap groups that each fit, stacked by Z height, so you load one group, print up to its top, pause, swap to the next group, and continue. White base and white cap stay in fixed slots the whole print.
GET /api/export/swap-instructions (server.py:5774) returns this plan. It is computed live, not stored: AMS capacity is read from the current printer profile (ams_slots, white_slots — server.py:5800–5802), and the groups are re-reconciled against that capacity (reconcile_export_groups, server.py:5807) so changing your AMS after solving regroups correctly without a re-solve.
The response carries two artifacts, both built in generator.swap:

Human-readable instructions (generate_swap_instructions, swap.py:272) — a text block with print dimensions, total height, per-group AMS slot assignments, the exact remove/load actions at each pause, and the white-cap section. Fixed slots are annotated [FIXED white base — do not change] (swap.py:382–396).
Pause G-code (generate_orcaslicer_pause_gcode, swap.py:618) — one M600 ; pause for filament change per swap, each annotated with the approximate layer and Z height (swap.py:632–637).

How M600 maps to your print
For each boundary between consecutive groups, the swap height is the previous group’s z_end, and the layer is round(z_end / layer_height) (swap.py:402–403, swap.py:633). You add an OrcaSlicer pause (which emits M600) at that layer; when the printer pauses, you make the listed slot changes and resume. N groups means N-1 mid-print swaps. If everything fits in one AMS load, there are zero swaps and the G-code is just a ; No filament swaps needed comment (swap.py:628).

Note on the default AMS count: generate_swap_instructions defaults ams_slots=8 (2×AMS) when called directly (swap.py:283), but the live webapp passes the printer profile’s ams_slots, falling back to 4 if unset (server.py:5801). The number you see comes from your selected printer, not the function default.

See also

How a Solve Works — produces the thickness maps export consumes.
From solve to mesh the export pipeline — the per-cell meshing internals routed out of this page.
Thickness map — the exact structure export reads.

generator/how-a-solve-works.title: How a Solve Works
generator/how-a-solve-works.content:
How a Solve Works

In one sentence: a solve takes your source image and a palette of calibrated filaments and produces, for every pixel, how thick each filament should be so the backlit print matches the image — measured in OKLab, the colour space that tracks human perception.

This page follows one solve from the button press to the finished result. See Pipeline Map for the same thing as a diagram, and The Joint LUT and Staged Solve for the deep dive on the inversion itself.
Where a solve begins
When you press Solve in the web app, the server endpoint start_solve (server.py:4654) runs the solve on a background thread. It first translates your session settings into a typed SolveConfig via _build_solve_config (server.py:984) — palette, white base/cap, layer height, resolution, the chosen colour model, gamut mode, and the dozens of staged-backend knobs — then calls solve_full (server.py:4740 is the call site; solve_full itself is facade.py:967).
solve_full is one of three entry points in the generator.facade:





























Entry pointUsed forQuality presetServer call sitesolve_preview (facade.py:897)fast low-res gamut checkPREVIEW_PRESET (15 layers, no grouping)server.py:3998 (/api/gamut-preview)solve_full (facade.py:967)the real production solveFULL_PRESET (full layers + grouping)server.py:4740 (/api/solve/start)solve_compare (facade.py:992)batch preview across several palettesCOMPARE_PRESETserver.py:4094 (/api/palette/compare)
All three resolve their pluggable slots (grouping + preprocessing) via _resolve_pipeline_slots (facade.py:584), translate SolveConfig into a PipelineConfig via _to_pipeline_config (facade.py:612), then funnel into the same orchestrator: run_pipeline (runner.py:587). The preset just toggles how many stages run and how deep they go — only solve_full/solve_compare enable the grouping stage (runner.py:597), and the preset’s grouping_enabled flag gates it.
There is a fourth facade entry, solve_preview_progressive (facade.py:924); its docstring says the progressive-solve HTTP feature was removed, and it survives only as the test vehicle that threads a SnapshotPublisher into the preprocessing preview hook. It is not on the production solve path.
The pipeline spine
run_pipeline runs a fixed sequence of stages (runner.py:587). The stage count is computed up front: five for a preview, six when grouping is enabled (runner.py:602). Before any stage runs, the runner stamps a __solve_identity__ diagnostic recording every setting the solve will use (runner.py:616) — palette, whites, layer height, gamut mode, ingress toggle, the resolved preprocessor list, and more. That record is what makes a finished run reproducible and is carried all the way out to the UI.
1. Load
This stage does three jobs, in order.
Profiles + appearance provider. It validates the palette (validate_palette, runner.py:654) and loads the spline profiles for every colour filament plus the white base and white cap (runner.py:656–667). The cap profile is the base profile when base and cap are the same filament. It then builds the Appearance provider via create_appearance_provider (runner.py:670) — the swappable colour model the rest of the solve queries. Which provider you get is set by appearance_model_provider (default "historical_spline"); the photo-stack provider is the alternative. A __appearance_provider__ diagnostic records its kind and fingerprint (runner.py:678).
The F1 preprocessing slot. If — and only if — the resolved preprocessor chain is non-empty, preprocessing runs here (runner.py:695–774), after profile load (so palette-aware operators can resolve filament context) and before the target cloud is computed (so targets are derived from the post-preprocess raster). The chain is built by _resolve_preprocessing_from_state (facade.py:547): it walks the registry of operators, keeps the ones turned on in module state, and sorts them by each operator’s order (ties broken by import path). When the chain runs, run_preprocessing_pipeline (preprocessing/runner.py:210) replaces state.image with the processed raster and stashes the original in state.source_image (runner.py:768). When the chain is empty it is a legal no-op — the original raster passes straight through and state.source_image stays None (runner.py:695).

What ships enabled: there are five built-in F1 operators — a1_bilateral_denoise, b1_printscale_bilateral, b3_tv_flatten, c1_achievable_tonemap, c2_soft_gamut_compress — and every one ships with default_enabled = False (e.g. preprocessing/operators/a1_bilateral_denoise.py:73). So the slot is fully wired and live, but on a default solve the chain is empty and preprocessing does nothing until you enable an operator in the module panel. This is the slot, not a guarantee that anything runs in it.

The optional subject-protect mask also lives in this block (runner.py:714–752): when protect_subject_enabled is set and at least one enabled operator declares supports_protect_mask, a foreground mask is resolved (default provider rembg) and threaded into the chain so operators can spare the subject.
The target cloud. Finally the runner computes the target cloud — the per-pixel colours the solve aims for, in OKLab — via compute_solve_target_cloud (runner.py:779, defined pipeline/target_cloud.py:64). This is also where Model-domain ingress is applied: image_to_target converts source pixels through the Camera Transform inverse LUT (when model_domain_ingress is on, the default) so targets live in the same colour space the model was calibrated in (target_cloud.py:72).
Observation grid vs. solve grid
The target cloud is produced on two grids, and the distinction matters for everything downstream:























GridWhat it isPitch fieldStored on stateObservationone cell per image sample — the raster as loadedimage_sample_pitch_mmobserved_target_oklab (runner.py:781)Solveone cell per solver cell — the lattice the staged backend actually plans onsolver_fine_pitch_mmsolve_target_oklab (runner.py:782)
The solve grid is derived from the observation grid by project_observation_to_solve_grid (derived_views.py:125). When the two pitches are equal — the common case, both default to 0.20 mm — the projection is a zero-cost identity pass and the same array is reused (derived_views.py:154). When they differ, the observation raster is bilinearly resampled to the solve-grid shape (derived_views.py:163). All later dE comparisons, gamut mapping, and LUT queries happen on the solve grid; the observation grid is the faithful record of what the image actually sampled. Keeping them separate is what lets the solver plan at a different resolution than the image was read at without losing the source of truth.
2. Build LUTs
Builds the Joint LUT — a precomputed table mapping candidate layer recipes (a colour combination plus a white-cap height) to the OKLab colour they produce (runner.py:793–830). There are two builders, chosen by which appearance provider is active:

spline model ("historical_spline") → build_luts (lut.py, imported as _build_luts_raw, runner.py:799)
photo-stack model → build_luts_with_provider (runner.py:815)

The cap range the LUT must cover comes from _provider_lut_d_wc_max (runner.py:44): it spans the Stage 2 boundary-cap budget plus the extra steps Stage 4 may add as a detail surface, so the solver never asks for a cap height the LUT can’t score. LUTs are cached so repeat solves skip the rebuild.
3. Gamut
Some target colours sit outside what the filaments can physically reproduce. _apply_target_gamut_mapping (runner.py:67) projects those back onto the achievable set — by convex hull, by chroma compression, or not at all, per the gamut_mode setting (default "hull"; "none"/"off" skips it). An optional white-point rescale runs first, regardless of mode (runner.py:83). The remapped targets overwrite solve_target_oklab, and a __target_gamut_mapping__ diagnostic records how many targets moved and how far. See Gamut mapping.
4. Solve
The heart of it. The production path calls run_staged_backend_path (runner.py:846, defined in generator.pipeline.staged_runner at staged_runner.py:10310) — the staged backend, an internal Stage 0–5 process. Its own progress labels trace the arc (staged_runner.py:10334+):








































StageLabel emittedWhat it does0Planning solve directivescompile per-region directives; fix the solve-grid shape1Planning color regionslateral zone plan — segment the image into colour regions2Solving visible color stackschoose, per region, a printable colour-layer recipe + boundary cap3Planning filler supportfill structural/support geometry under the colour ceiling4Solving white cap structureauthor the white cap, incl. the optional detail-relief surface5(geometry attribution, optional diagnostics)emit attribution maps when requested
Throughout, candidate recipes are scored against the joint LUT in OKLab. The staged result is then copied onto the pipeline state by _finalize_staged_backend_state (runner.py:533): the Thickness map for each filament, the white-cap maps (total, boundary, detail), the canonical solved_plan for export, and a freshly recomputed per-pixel ΔE (_recompute_de_diagnostics, runner.py:577) written into state.diagnostics — never into the thickness maps.

Legacy vs. live — read this if you are tracing code. The web app you use runs the staged backend above. There is an older, separate per-pixel engine in solve.py (solve_image) — the legacy CLI engine — and run_pipeline does not call it. Grepping confirms the only production entry into the solver is run_staged_backend_path (runner.py:846); solve.py’s solve_image is reached only by the CLI engine, not by solve_full/solve_preview/solve_compare. solve.py is not dead, though: the runner imports its gamut helpers (gamut_map_hull_batch, gamut_map_batch) in stage 3 (runner.py:127, runner.py:138, runner.py:140) and the facade imports predict_image_fast for forward prediction (facade.py:31). So solve.py contributes shared utilities, but it does not solve your images. For the fuller “which of these modules is actually on the live path” map, see What Actually Runs.

5. Group (only when grouping is enabled)
config.grouping.group(...) (runner.py:855) consolidates the palette into AMS swap groups — choosing which filaments share a slot — without rewriting the geometry. The grouping module is resolved from module state in _resolve_grouping_from_state (facade.py:513): the default is GreedyGrouping, with a beam-search GroupBudgetGrouping available when the group_budget flag is set. If grouping ever substitutes pixels, the runner recomputes ΔE to keep diagnostics honest (runner.py:863).
6. Stats
_compute_stats (runner.py:305) summarises the solve into a SolveStats: mean/max ΔE, coverage (the fraction of pixels within the ΔE threshold, runner.py:353), the maximum print height (base + colour stack + cap, runner.py:347), the source RMS ΔE, and per-filament pixel/thickness stats. This is the quality readout the UI shows.
What you get out
run_pipeline returns a PipelineState, which the facade converts back into a SolveResult via _state_to_solve_result (facade.py:864). Between them they carry everything the rest of the app needs:

thickness_maps — a Thickness map per filament, plus the white-cap maps and diagnostic maps. SolveResult exposes de_map, gamut_mask, cap_map, boundary_cap, and detail_cap as convenience properties (facade.py:405–429).
solved_plan — the canonical SolvedMaterialPlan consumed by export (built in finalization, runner.py:542).
stats — the quality summary above.
diagnostics — ΔE, gamut masks, and the __solve_identity__ record of every setting the solve ran with (runner.py:616).
For full solves only, best-case palette-fit diagnostics (_compute_palette_fit_diagnostics, facade.py:784): a per-pixel “best the palette could do” image and the gap between that and what the solver actually achieved — a way to separate palette-limited error from solver-limited error.

SolveResult can also reconstruct the predicted backlit image two ways: predict_image (full composition) and predict_image_color_only (facade.py:494), which zeroes the white-cap term so the colour story isn’t drowned out by the cap’s luminance shaping — this is what the recipe viewer’s colour-only render uses.
From here, Exporting Print Files turns the thickness maps and solved plan into printable geometry.
See also

The Transmission Model — the colour model the solve inverts.
The Joint LUT and Staged Solve — how the inversion actually works.
Pipeline Map — this page as a diagram.
What Actually Runs — live vs. legacy modules across the generator.

generator/pipeline-map.title: Pipeline Map
generator/pipeline-map.content:
Pipeline Map

In one sentence: one webapp solve runs a fixed six-step spine (run_pipeline) with two pluggable slots — preprocessing before targets, grouping after the solve — and the heavy lifting in step 4 is the staged Stage 0–5 backend (run_staged_backend_path), not the legacy CLI engine.

This is the wiring diagram for one full solve. For the narrative walk-through read How a Solve Works; for the optics read The Transmission Model and The Joint LUT and Staged Solve. The Mermaid below renders natively in Obsidian and in a Quartz-published site, so it travels with the docs.
Interactive dataflow map
The clickable, multi-scale version of this diagram: start at the Overview, click a dashed node (Colour model · Staged solve · Export) to expand it in place into its inner workings, and click any step to jump straight to its page or section. ⤢ Zoom out returns to the systems view. It shows dataflow — how an image becomes a lithophane — so the API hub and dead code are off it by design. (This interactive map is published-site only; the Mermaid diagrams further down render in Obsidian too and remain the static fallback.)

Two layers: the spine, and the staged backend inside step 4
There are two nested orchestrators, and it matters which one you are looking at:

The spine — run_pipeline in pipeline/runner.py:587. Six steps: load → build LUTs → gamut → solve → group → stats. This is fixed; the steps always run in this order.
The staged backend — run_staged_backend_path in pipeline/staged_runner.py:10310. This is the spine’s step 4 (“solve”). Internally it runs its own Stage 0–5 sequence. The webapp always takes this path (runner.py:843-846); the “6-step” engine in solve.py is the legacy CLI engine and is not what the web app runs.

flowchart TD

generator/the-joint-lut-and-staged-solve.content:
The Joint LUT and Staged Solve

In one sentence: the transmission model only runs forward (recipe → colour), so the generator inverts it by precomputing a table of achievable recipes and, for each target pixel, picking the recipe whose colour is the nearest neighbour in OKLab.

This page is the conceptual bridge between the colour you want and the print recipe that makes it. It deliberately stays at that altitude — how the table is built and queried lives in The Joint LUT building and querying, and how the per-pixel ideal recipes become a printable plan lives in The staged backend (Stage 0-5).
The inversion problem
The forward model is easy: give it a stack of filament thicknesses and it returns a colour (model.py compose_stack). Solving needs the reverse — given a colour, find a stack — and there is no clean closed-form inverse. Too many filament/thickness combinations can land near the same colour, and the achievable set is a discrete, budget-constrained lattice, not a smooth function you can analytically invert.
The generator sidesteps this entirely. It enumerates the achievable recipes once, records the colour each produces, and at solve time treats inversion as a nearest-neighbour lookup: the target colour goes in, the closest precomputed entry’s recipe comes out. That table is the Joint LUT.
”Joint” — cap and colour together
Each entry fixes both a white-cap thickness and a colour-layer recipe at once, and stores the OKLab of the full stack:
oklab( T_wb × T_wc(d_wc) × ∏ T_ci(d_ci) )

Cap and colour are solved in one shot rather than in two separate passes — that is what “joint” means. Two consequences follow directly from the entry layout (lut.py:129, LUTEntry):

The white base T_wb is baked into every entry (lut.py:461, lut.py:517). The solve target is therefore the full-stack colour, and T_wb is never divided back out at query time (model.py:141 — “T_wb is NOT divided out … already included in every LUT entry”). The stale docstring at the top of lut.py:13 still describes an old target = T_source / T_wb query; the live model.py ingress contradicts it.
An entry carries its colour filament subset, the per-filament colour thicknesses, the cap thickness, and the OKLab colour — so one nearest-neighbour hit returns a complete, printable recipe including __white_cap__ (lut.py:931–lut.py:935).

Nearest neighbour in OKLab
The match runs in OKLab, a perceptually-uniform space, so “closest colour” means “closest to how the eye sees it.” Each LUT subset holds a SciPy KDTree over its OKLab points (lut.py:135); the solve queries every tree for k=1 and keeps the global best across subsets (query_luts_batch, lut.py:946). The returned ΔE is plain Euclidean OKLab distance.
One twist worth knowing as a user: chroma weight. When chroma_weight != 1.0, the L* (lightness) axis is divided by the weight before the tree is built and before each query (lut.py:976–lut.py:980), so the nearest-neighbour search prioritises hue/chroma over exact lightness. The reported ΔE is always recomputed unweighted so quality numbers stay comparable (lut.py:1029, lut.py:1038–lut.py:1040).
A pixel whose nearest entry is still far away (ΔE above de_threshold, default 0.05; state.py:72) is flagged out of gamut — no recipe reproduces it well. That flag feeds Gamut mapping; see staged_runner.py:763.
From “ideal per-pixel recipe” to a printable plan
The nearest-neighbour lookup gives the ideal recipe for each pixel in isolation. A lithophane printed that literally would be unmanufacturable — single-pixel colour islands, sub-nozzle features. So the webapp solve does not stop at the lookup. It feeds the per-pixel targets into the staged backend (run_staged_backend_path, staged_runner.py:10310, reached from runner.py:846), which groups pixels into printable colour regions, scores candidate recipes per region against this same Joint LUT, and plans the white cap — all under the active printer’s minimum feature sizes.
That is the division of labour this page bridges:

























LayerJobWhere it’s documentedTransmission modelrecipe → colour (forward)The Transmission ModelJoint LUTenumerate recipes + colours; nearest-neighbour invertThe Joint LUT building and queryingStaged backendper-pixel ideal → printable region/cap planThe staged backend (Stage 0-5)

Liveness note for developers. The webapp solve runs the staged backend, whose only LUT entry point is the batch query query_luts_batch (staged_runner.py:762). The fixed-cap and cap-curve variants in lut.py (query_luts_fixed_cap, cap_curve_lookup_batch, build_cap_curve) are not called by the staged path — their only callers are the legacy CLI engine solve.py and pipeline_cli.py (e.g. solve.py:547, pipeline_cli.py:607). Do not assume the staged solve uses them. build_hull_from_luts, by contrast, is live in the staged path (runner.py:122).
