generator/the-solve-facade.title: The Solve Facade
generator/the-solve-facade.content:
The Solve Facade

In one sentence: the facade (generator.facade, facade.py) is the thin front door to the solver — it takes a typed SolveConfig, picks a quality preset, resolves the pluggable grouping/preprocessing slots, translates everything into a PipelineConfig, and hands off to the one orchestrator (run_pipeline) that runs the staged backend.

This page is about the handoff layer, not the solve itself. For the solve walked end-to-end, see How a Solve Works; for the inversion math, The Joint LUT and Staged Solve; for the stage-by-stage diagram, Pipeline Map. Here we stay at contract altitude: what the entry points are, what they translate, and which one is dormant.
Why a facade exists
The module docstring (facade.py:2) names a stale filename (lith_facade.py) — ignore it. The real job, stated in the same header block (facade.py:4–10), holds up against the code: callers (chiefly the web server) should never reach into pipeline internals. They build one SolveConfig, call one of three functions, and get back a SolveResult. Everything between — module-state resolution, the SolveConfig → PipelineConfig translation, the conversion of the runner’s PipelineState back into a SolveResult — lives here so the rest of the app doesn’t have to know it exists.
The three live entry points
All three production entry points have the same shape: (img, config, progress=None, modules_path=None, module_state=None), returning a SolveResult (solve_compare returns a list). They differ only in the quality preset they pass and, for compare, the per-palette loop.

































Entry pointDefinedUsed forPresetServer call sitesolve_previewfacade.py:897fast low-res gamut checkPREVIEW_PRESETserver.py:3998solve_fullfacade.py:967the real production solveFULL_PRESETserver.py:4740solve_comparefacade.py:992batch preview across several palettesCOMPARE_PRESETserver.py:4094
Liveness is confirmed from callers, not docstrings. solve_preview, solve_full, and solve_compare are all imported in server.py:79–81 and invoked at the call sites above. solve_full has a second live caller in the preprocessing evaluation harness (evaluation/preprocessing_harness.py:166). These are the production solve surface.
Each one does the same four-step dance:

Resolve pluggable slots — _resolve_pipeline_slots (facade.py:584) loads module state and builds the grouping module + the ordered preprocessor chain.
Translate config — _to_pipeline_config (facade.py:612) maps SolveConfig → PipelineConfig.
Run — run_pipeline (runner.py:587) executes the staged backend.
Convert back — _state_to_solve_result (facade.py:864) turns the returned PipelineState into a SolveResult.

solve_compare (facade.py:992) wraps steps 1–4 in a loop over palettes: it loads module state once (facade.py:1004), then for each palette clones the config with the new palette via _replace_solve_config (facade.py:769), runs the four steps with palette_index/palette_count threaded into the runner for progress reporting (facade.py:1025), and catches per-palette exceptions — a failing palette becomes a {"error": ..., "palette": ...} dict in the result list rather than aborting the whole batch (facade.py:1031). Empty palettes short-circuit to an error dict before solving (facade.py:1007).
Quality presets
A QualityPreset is a tiny named record — name, max_layers, grouping_enabled (state.py:31). Three are defined as module constants:

































Presetnamemax_layersgrouping_enabledDefinedPREVIEW_PRESET"preview"15Falsestate.py:39FULL_PRESET"full"None (auto)Truestate.py:45COMPARE_PRESET"compare"15Truestate.py:51
The preset is the only thing distinguishing the three entry points. It is passed through _to_pipeline_config onto PipelineConfig.preset (facade.py:765) and read back inside the runner. Two effects:

Layer ceiling. max_layers=15 caps preview/compare solves to a cheap low-resolution height stack; None means full solve lets the config derive it from t_max (see SolveConfig.effective_max_layers, facade.py:291).
Grouping gate. The runner only counts and runs the grouping stage when preset.grouping_enabled is true and a grouping module is actually present (runner.py:597). So even with grouping_enabled=True, a preset gets grouping only if _resolve_pipeline_slots handed one over.

Note the preset name also drives diagnostics: the palette-fit best-case diagnostics in _compute_palette_fit_diagnostics only compute when preset.name == "full" (facade.py:787), so the “solver loss” overlay is a full-solve-only artifact.
The dormant fourth entry point
solve_preview_progressive (facade.py:924) is the one to know about. Its own docstring (facade.py:932–941) says the progressive-solve HTTP feature and its mid-solve snapshot emitter were removed in the “Stage 3 cleanup,” and that the function survives only to thread an optional SnapshotPublisher (generator.pipeline.snapshot) into the preprocessing preview hook. This docstring is accurate — and verified independently from callers, not taken on faith:

No production code imports or calls it. A repo-wide grep finds it imported/called only in two tests: tests/generator/preprocessing/test_facade_threading.py:286 and tests/generator/preprocessing/test_f1_smoke.py:169.
The server’s only remaining mention of “progressive” is a static-file route comment (server.py:5914) that serves cached diagnostic/preview PNGs — there is no progressive solve endpoint.
The one other hit is a stale traceback in Prisma/output/generator.log (a log artifact, not live code).
A removal plan exists for it: Prisma/generator/docs/legacy_audit/12_WEBAPP_DEAD_BACKEND_CANDIDATES_REMOVAL_PLAN.md:59 lists removing solve_preview_progressive from facade.py.

So: DORMANT in production, retained only as a test vehicle. It runs FULL_PRESET (facade.py:943), and unlike the three live entries it forwards a snapshot_publisher into run_pipeline (facade.py:962; the runner accepts and attaches it at runner.py:593/runner.py:841). The _progressive suffix is, per its docstring, a historical artifact and a rename candidate. Do not wire new code to it without reviving the publisher path.
Resolving the pluggable slots
_resolve_pipeline_slots (facade.py:584) returns a (grouping, module_state, preprocessors) triple. It first loads module state via _load_module_state (facade.py:534) — which prefers an in-memory module_state dict, else reads modules_path through load_module_state, else returns None. The server passes modules_path=_MODULES_PATH so the live solve reads the on-disk module configuration.
Grouping — _resolve_grouping_from_state
_resolve_grouping_from_state (facade.py:513) picks the grouping module from saved state:

If module state has group_budget truthy, it builds GroupBudgetGrouping (the beam-search grouper, generator.grouping.beam_search), threading the nine grouping_* weights from SolveConfig (iterations, beam width, z-waste / overflow / swap-count / slot-stability weights, dE scoring toggles, in-group substitution) — facade.py:519–530.
Otherwise it returns GreedyGrouping (the default greedy grouper, generator.grouping.greedy_optimize) — facade.py:531.

This grouping object is only built when the preset’s grouping_enabled is true (facade.py:604); preview solves get None.

Disambiguation: the live grouping code here (generator.grouping.beam_search / generator.grouping.greedy_optimize) is not the experimental beam-search/greedy schedulers under generator.scheduling.policies. There are two unrelated beam-search and two unrelated greedy implementations in the tree — the facade wires the grouping ones.

Preprocessing — _resolve_preprocessing_from_state
_resolve_preprocessing_from_state (facade.py:547) builds the ordered list of enabled preprocessing operator instances. Unlike grouping, it is always resolved (legacy callers with no module state simply get an empty list, facade.py:561). It walks the operator registry (generator.pipeline.registry), keeps each operator whose module-state flag is on (falling back to the operator’s default_enabled, facade.py:569), passes the operator’s params block from config.preprocessing_params as constructor kwargs, then sorts by each operator’s order with ties broken by import path (facade.py:575). The chain is then threaded into the runner’s preprocessing slot. See How a Solve Works for how the chain runs inside the pipeline (and the fact that all built-in operators ship disabled by default).
The config translation — _to_pipeline_config
_to_pipeline_config (facade.py:612) is the big, boring, load-bearing function: it copies the dozens of fields from a SolveConfig (generator.facade) into a PipelineConfig (generator.pipeline.state) and attaches the resolved grouping, preprocessors, preprocessing_params, and preset. A few translation facts worth knowing:

Resolution is canonical-pitch only. The translation passes image_sample_pitch_mm and solver_fine_pitch_mm plus the stage-1 coarsening/lattice-offset fields (facade.py:696–700); there are no legacy resolution fields. The SolveConfig.__post_init__ applies a resolution backstop first (facade.py:283, via config.resolution_schema). See Settings, resolution, and the config contract and generator.config.resolution_schema.
Colour-model ingress passes through verbatim. model_domain_ingress and model_domain_ingress_lut_path ride along (facade.py:645) to the Model-domain ingress step; appearance_model_provider selects the Appearance provider (facade.py:691).
de_threshold defaults differ across layers. SolveConfig.de_threshold defaults to 0.01 (facade.py:212) while PipelineConfig.de_threshold defaults to 0.05 (state.py:72) — but the translation always copies the SolveConfig value through (facade.py:639), so the config you build wins; the PipelineConfig default only matters for direct construction.
Everything else is a near-mechanical 1:1 copy — whites, layer height, t_max/k_max, gamut mode, chroma weight, the full luminance-handler block, the staged-backend stage-2/stage-4 knobs, cap mode, protect-subject mask settings, and the printability fields. The list is long because SolveConfig is the kitchen-sink settings object; the translation is where it narrows to what the runner reads.

What comes back — SolveResult
run_pipeline returns a PipelineState; _state_to_solve_result (facade.py:864) converts it into the SolveResult dataclass (facade.py:359) that callers actually consume. The result carries the thickness maps (normalised to a typed ThicknessMaps in __post_init__, facade.py:394), the colour/white profiles, aggregate SolveStats, the original SolveConfig, the appearance provider, diagnostics (dE map, gamut mask — preferred from diagnostics, falling back to thickness maps, facade.py:405–415), grouping result, the canonical SolvedMaterialPlan, and the blueprint-triage printability report.

Disambiguation: SolveResult.blueprint_triage is the blueprint-triage PrintabilityReport (generator.pipeline.blueprint_triage.report), imported at facade.py:36. That is a different class from the mesh-side printability report (generator.mesh.printability). Don’t conflate them.

Two reconstruction methods live on SolveResult and matter for the UI’s colour views:

predict_image (facade.py:437) composes the full backlit sRGB image (base × colours × white cap) — routing through the appearance provider when it isn’t the historical spline, else predict_image_fast (generator.solve).
predict_image_color_only (facade.py:494) composes base + colours with the white cap dropped (every cap term zeroed via _cap_zeroed_thickness_maps, facade.py:474) so the cap’s luminance shaping doesn’t drown out the colour story. A zero cap thickness is the multiplicative identity in the transmission model, so this cleanly removes the term without touching the composition math. This is what feeds the recipe viewer’s colour-only render.

What this layer does not do

It does not run the legacy solve.py “6-step” engine. run_pipeline always dispatches to run_staged_backend_path (generator.pipeline.staged_runner) at runner.py:846, for every preset. The 6-step engine in generator.solve is the separate CLI engine; the webapp path is the staged backend. (predict_image_fast from solve.py is still used for fast forward prediction — that is just the composition helper, not the solve engine.)
It does not decide resolution, gamut mode, or which operators are enabled — those come in on the SolveConfig / module state. The facade only resolves and translates.
It does not persist anything. Saving runs, naming, archives, and caches are the server’s job (generator.server, generator.run_store).

Progress reporting — ProgressTracker
The facade defines a ProgressTracker (facade.py:45) — a structured progress reporter that wraps a callback and emits a dict at each stage advance and intra-stage percent update, with ETA estimation. Note the duplication: the runner has its own internal _ProgressTracker (runner.py:606), and that is the one driving the live solve’s stage callbacks; the facade entry points pass the caller’s raw progress callback straight into run_pipeline, not this class. The facade’s ProgressTracker is therefore a public helper at the facade altitude; treat its in-production use as unconfirmed here (I did not trace a live caller of the facade-level class) — the per-stage progress you see in the UI is emitted by the runner’s tracker. The emitted dict shape (stage key/label/index/count, pct, elapsed, ETA, palette index/count — facade.py:144) documents the progress contract either way, and palette_index/palette_count are the fields solve_compare populates per palette.
See also

generator/the-transmission-model.title: The Transmission Model
generator/the-transmission-model.content:
The Transmission Model

In one sentence: the transmission model answers the question the whole generator is built around — if I stack these filament layers and shine light through them, what colour comes out?

A backlit lithophane is a stack of translucent layers. Light passes through a white base, then through some coloured layers, then through a white cap. Each layer absorbs part of the light. The transmission model predicts the resulting colour so the solver can search for the stack that reproduces a target.
The model is reached through a swappable boundary — the Appearance provider (Prisma/generator/appearance_model.py). There are two implementations, and a solve uses exactly one, chosen by the appearance_model_provider config field (appearance_model.py:606).
Model 1 — the spline (multiplicative) model
This is the historical model: HistoricalSplineAppearanceProvider (appearance_model.py:82), model_kind = "historical_spline" (appearance_model.py:85).
Each filament has a spline profile — measured transmission as a function of thickness, fit with a monotone-cubic (PCHIP) interpolator over real calibration data, not a Beer-Lambert formula (lib/transmission.py:67, build_spline). predict_transmission(profile, d_mm) (Prisma/generator/model.py:63) returns the linear-RGB transmission [T_r, T_g, T_b] of one filament at thickness d. Two edge behaviours worth knowing, both in predict (lib/transmission.py:89):

























thicknessbehaviourevidenced <= 0returns [1, 1, 1] (a layer of zero thickness is perfectly transparent)lib/transmission.py:107d inside measured rangeclipped PCHIP evaluation per channellib/transmission.py:114d beyond the last knotBeer-Lambert extrapolation from the slope between the last two knotslib/transmission.py:110, _extrapolate at :120
The colour of a full stack is the product of the per-layer transmissions:
T_total = T_wb(d_wb) × ∏ T_color_i(d_i) × T_wc(d_wc)        (per RGB channel)

This is compose (lib/transmission.py:146), wrapped by compose_stack (model.py:71). Because it is a multiplication, layer order does not matter — the factors commute (lib/transmission.py:164–166). That is why the solve only has to decide how much of each filament, not the stacking order.
The spline model treats every filament independently. Real filaments interact spectrally when stacked, so compose can apply empirical pair corrections to two-filament combinations: if a corrections table is passed and the stack has ≥2 layers, it multiplies in a per-pair factor C(d_overlay) keyed by 'overlay_fid|base_fid@d' strings (lib/transmission.py:168–178). The provider itself does not pass corrections through compose; they are folded in during LUT construction instead (see The Joint LUT and Staged Solve).
Model 2 — the photo-stack model
The newer model: PhotoStackBundleAppearanceProvider (appearance_model.py:210), model_kind = "photo_stack_bundle" (appearance_model.py:224).
Instead of multiplying independent per-filament curves, this model predicts the appearance of a whole stack from a calibration bundle — an artifact fit against photographs of real printed swatches (appearance_model.py:268, load_photo_stack_bundle; see lib.photo_stack_model). It is context-aware: the prediction for a colour layer depends on what it is stacked with, which the multiplicative model cannot express. It must be constructed with an explicit candidate directory or runtime_bundle.json path — there is no implicit default (appearance_model.py:232).
It can optionally apply a corrections layer — a sibling correction_layer.json artifact that nudges the direct model toward the usable corrected model — toggled by use_corrections (appearance_model.py:226, validated at :261).

A note on naming: the code identifies these two models as historical_spline and photo_stack_bundle. The app’s Color Model selector picks between them. (A user-facing relabel of these two options was still pending at the time of writing — so this page names them by their code identity, which is unambiguous.)

The appearance-named methods are pass-through (model domain, not display)
A trap for the developer who has forgotten the backend: the photo-stack provider exposes methods whose names contain appearance — predict_stack_appearance_linear_rgb_batch (appearance_model.py:423) and predict_thickness_maps_appearance_linear_rgb (appearance_model.py:565). Since the projection-slot retirement these return model-domain RGB, not display RGB. The class docstring states it (appearance_model.py:218–221), and the code proves it: predict_thickness_maps_appearance_linear_rgb simply forwards to predict_thickness_maps_model_linear_rgb (appearance_model.py:575), and predict_thickness_maps_linear_rgb is a second alias onto the same model-domain method (appearance_model.py:596). Display conversion lives at the generator’s ingress/display boundaries (model_domain_display.py), not inside the provider. Do not read the word “appearance” as “what your eye sees.”
Image ingress: the two branches of image_to_target
Before the solver can chase a target it must convert the source sRGB image into the same colour domain the model predicts in. That is image_to_target (model.py:128), and it has exactly two branches selected by the model_domain_ingress flag (model.py:149):























model_domain_ingressbranchwhat runsevidenceTrue (default in the webapp)Camera-Transform ingresstrilinear lookup through the baked inverse 33³ LUT G = F⁻¹, mapping source sRGB → model-domain RGBmodel.py:150–151, _apply_model_domain_ingress_lut at :123, LUT applied by apply_inverse_lut (lib/camera_transform.py:356)Falselegacy sRGB-linearbit-identical srgb_to_linear(img) ** 2.2 path, no Camera Transform involvedmodel.py:152, srgb_to_linear at :108
The Camera Transform’s LUT stores oklab(T_wb × T_wc × ∏ T_colour) — the full-stack transmission including the white base. Because every LUT entry already includes T_wb, the target must be in that same space, so the ingress path does not divide T_wb back out (model.py:139–144). The default ingress LUT path is the Camera Transform data dir (model.py:28, DEFAULT_MODEL_DOMAIN_INGRESS_LUT_PATH); it resolves a CURRENT-pointed generation and verifies sha256 hashes before use (lib/camera_transform.py:333, load_inverse_lut).
The wb_profile / d_wb unused-param gotcha
image_to_target still takes wb_profile and d_wb as positional arguments, but both are unused — they are kept only for API compatibility (model.py:144, “wb_profile and d_wb are accepted for API compatibility but unused”). This is deliberate and historical: an older formulation divided T_wb out of the target, but the current LUT already bakes T_wb into every entry, so dividing it again would be wrong. Every live caller still passes them — pipeline/target_cloud.py:72 (the staged backend), solve.py:337 / :464 / :607 (the legacy CLI engine), pipeline_cli.py:594 — but the values flow into a no-op. (facade.py does not call image_to_target itself; it only forwards the ingress config down to the staged backend.) If you are touching this signature, do not start using those parameters expecting them to affect the result; they do not.
Which one is running, and how the model is reached
The provider is created once per solve by create_appearance_provider (appearance_model.py:606), from config.appearance_model_provider. The runner stores it on pipeline state (pipeline/runner.py:670). Both providers expose the same interface — most importantly predict_thickness_maps_linear_rgb, which takes the solved Thickness maps and returns the predicted per-pixel colour. The pipeline uses that to compute ΔE (the colour error) regardless of which model is active (pipeline/runner.py:185–212). For non-spline providers the runner prefers the ..._appearance_... variant when present (pipeline/runner.py:187–195) — which, per the section above, is the same model-domain output.
The choice also changes how the Joint LUT is built: the spline model uses build_luts, the photo-stack model uses build_luts_with_provider — same table shape, different way of filling each cell. Both live in lut.py (lut.py:394 / lut.py:630); the staged runner imports them under local aliases _build_luts_raw and _build_luts_with_provider (pipeline/runner.py:26–27) and dispatches between them on model_kind (pipeline/runner.py:799 vs :815).

Where the live webapp solve runs. The browser solve flows through the staged backend (pipeline/), where source conditioning is centralised in compute_solve_target_cloud (pipeline/target_cloud.py:64). The “6-step” engine in solve.py is the legacy CLI engine — it also calls image_to_target, but it is not what the web app drives.

Hand-off to the Appearance provider
This page describes what the model computes; the Appearance provider page is the contract layer — it documents the StackRequest / Layer shapes, the batch methods, the fingerprint used for cache invalidation (appearance_model.py:103 / :279), and create_appearance_provider’s aliasing of provider-kind strings (appearance_model.py:617–628, where "historical", "spline", and "historical_spline" all map to the spline provider). When you need to know how the generator talks to the model, go there; when you need to know what colour the model predicts, stay here.
From colour to error: OKLab
Whatever predicts the colour, the comparison between predicted and target happens in OKLab, not RGB. to_oklab (model.py:155) wraps linear_to_oklab (lib/transmission.py:40); the solve minimises Euclidean distance there (deltaE_ok, lib/transmission.py:59) because OKLab tracks perceived colour difference far better than RGB does, and is faster than CIEDE2000.
Colour-only preview (cap omitted)
The “colour-only” render — the same forward composition but with the white cap dropped so the cap’s luminance shaping does not drown out the colour story — is SolveResult.predict_image_color_only (facade.py:494). The cap-zeroing mechanics (_cap_zeroed_thickness_maps) are owned by SolveConfig and SolveResult reference; this page does not re-explain them.
See also

The Joint LUT and Staged Solve — how the model is inverted to find recipes.

generator/the-pipeline-orchestrator-and-.title: The pipeline orchestrator and shared state
generator/the-pipeline-orchestrator-and-.content:
The pipeline orchestrator and shared state

In one sentence: pipeline/ is the small framework layer — a single orchestration function (run_pipeline) that loads profiles, runs an optional preprocessing chain, builds LUTs, hands the heavy solve to the staged backend, and finalises one shared PipelineState carrier, with two pluggable slots (preprocessing operators and grouping) that self-register from disk and persist their on/off state to JSON.

This is the developer companion to the generator.pipeline.runner package. It covers the data carriers, the fixed-spine-plus-two-slots design, the module plugin base classes, parameter self-description, registry auto-discovery, and module on/off persistence. It also flags two seams (revalidate() and snapshot.py) that are wired but dormant in production.
Related: generation_pipeline (narrative walkthrough) · generator.facade (the entry layer above this) · generator.pipeline.staged_runner (the solve engine below it) · The staged backend solve · Module management and settings.

How to drive it (users)
You never call this package directly — you change its behaviour through the Modules panel and Settings in the generator web app (port 8010). Three knobs land here:

Preprocessing operators — a chain of optional image-cleanup / gamut steps that run on the source raster before colour solving. Several can be on at once.
Grouping strategy — picks how filaments are packed into AMS swap groups when the palette has more colours than colour slots. Exactly one is active.
Quality preset — preview vs full vs compare; controls how many layers and whether grouping runs at all.

Toggling a module in the UI writes to a JSON file (modules.json) so the choice survives a restart. The contract is enforced server-side: see Module on/off persistence below.

The shared carriers (pipeline/state.py)
Everything the pipeline produces is accumulated on one mutable object that is threaded through every stage. There are four dataclasses, all defined in pipeline/state.py.
PipelineState — the bag of solve state
pipeline/state.py:229 defines the object passed through all stages. The runner constructs it once (pipeline/runner.py:612) and mutates it in place. Fields, grouped by who fills them:





















































































FieldFilled byNotesimage, configconstructorimage is overwritten with the post-preprocess raster (pipeline/runner.py:769)profiles (ProfileSet)Load spinepipeline/runner.py:663appearance_providerLoad spinepipeline/runner.py:670lutsLUT spinepipeline/runner.py:799 / :815observed_target_oklab, solve_target_oklabrunnertwo grids; see Observation vs solve gridthickness_maps (ThicknessMaps)staged finalisecopied from the staged bundle at pipeline/runner.py:559solved_plan (SolvedMaterialPlan)staged finalisecanonical export artifact, pipeline/runner.py:542staged_resultstaged finaliseraw staged-backend bundle, pipeline/runner.py:538diagnosticsrunnerthe SOLE canonical home for __de__ / __gamut_mask__ on this path (pipeline/state.py:273)stats (SolveStats)_compute_statspipeline/runner.py:356cap_qualitystaged finalisepipeline/runner.py:581groupinggrouping slotNone unless a grouping module ransource_image, preprocessing_trace, protect_mask, preprocessing_metricspreprocessing slotonly populated when the chain is non-emptysnapshot_publisherrunner (write-only)set at pipeline/runner.py:841, never read — see Dormant seamsblueprint_triage (PrintabilityReport)reset to None on the staged path (pipeline/runner.py:555)NB: this is the blueprint_triage report class, not the unrelated mesh PrintabilityReport
The diagnostics dict is load-bearing and the comment at pipeline/state.py:266-273 is code-true: on the staged/webapp path __de__ and __gamut_mask__ live in state.diagnostics, never mirrored into thickness_maps. _compute_stats reads diagnostics first and only falls back to thickness_maps for legacy/CLI-style states (pipeline/runner.py:319-320).
PipelineConfig — the frozen request
pipeline/state.py:58 is the full parameter set for one solve. It is built by the facade’s _to_pipeline_config (facade.py:612), not by hand. Beyond the ~120 plain fields it carries three slot-related members and a set of effective_* resolver methods:

grouping: Any | None (pipeline/state.py:161) — the resolved grouping instance (or None).
preprocessors: List[Any] (pipeline/state.py:170) — the ordered list of enabled operator instances. Sorting happens in the facade resolver, not here.
preprocessing_params: Dict[str, Dict] (pipeline/state.py:171) — the FULL per-operator params dict (every registered operator’s block at its default), rides along for fingerprinting.
preset: QualityPreset (pipeline/state.py:173) — defaults to FULL_PRESET.

The effective_* methods compute derived values so callers never duplicate the arithmetic: effective_max_layers() (pipeline/state.py:183) lets the preset cap layers, effective_white_cap() falls back to the base white, effective_d_wc_max() / effective_boundary_d_wc_max() derive cap authority, colour_slots() = ams_slots - effective_white_slots(). __post_init__ (pipeline/state.py:175) applies a resolution backstop from config.resolution_schema.
ProfileSet and QualityPreset
ProfileSet (pipeline/state.py:23) is a trivial three-field bundle of loaded filament profiles: colour_profiles, wb_profile, wc_profile. QualityPreset (pipeline/state.py:31) carries name, max_layers, and grouping_enabled. Three named instances exist:





























Presetmax_layersgrouping_enabledAnchorPREVIEW_PRESET15Falsepipeline/state.py:39FULL_PRESETNone (unbounded)Truepipeline/state.py:45COMPARE_PRESET15Truepipeline/state.py:51
These are the only two things QualityPreset controls: a layer ceiling and whether the grouping slot runs.

The orchestrator: fixed spine plus two slots (pipeline/runner.py)
run_pipeline (pipeline/runner.py:587) is the whole orchestration. The structure is a fixed spine of always-run stages with two pluggable slots woven in. Reading the function top to bottom:

































































#StageKindAnchor1Load — validate palette, load profiles, create appearance providerspinepipeline/runner.py:645-687—F1 Preprocessing — run the enabled operator chain, overwrite state.imageslotpipeline/runner.py:689-7742Compute observation + solve OKLab target cloudsspinepipeline/runner.py:776-782—Configure luminance handler runtime (default-off)spinepipeline/runner.py:788-7913Build LUTs — historical-spline path or provider pathspinepipeline/runner.py:793-8304Gamut — _apply_target_gamut_mapping (incl. optional white rescale)spinepipeline/runner.py:831-8335Solve — run_staged_backend_path then _finalize_staged_backend_statespinepipeline/runner.py:843-851—Grouping — config.grouping.group(state, ...)slotpipeline/runner.py:852-8636Stats — _compute_statsspinepipeline/runner.py:864-867
Two facts that the stale module header hides (cite the line anchors, not the header):

The webapp solve is the STAGED backend. Step 5 calls run_staged_backend_path from pipeline.staged_runner (pipeline/runner.py:843-846). It does not run solve.py’s legacy “6-step” CLI engine. _finalize_staged_backend_state (pipeline/runner.py:533) copies exactly one staged result bundle onto the legacy-facing state fields, and recomputes dE via _recompute_de_diagnostics straight into state.diagnostics (pipeline/runner.py:577).
Only the two slots are optional. The preprocessing slot is a legal no-op when config.preprocessors is empty (pipeline/runner.py:695 — the whole block is guarded). The grouping slot runs only when preset.grouping_enabled and config.grouping is not None (pipeline/runner.py:597-600), and the stage count bumps from 5 to 6 accordingly (pipeline/runner.py:602-604).

Observation vs solve grid
The runner is the single owner of target-cloud computation (pipeline/runner.py:776-782). observed_target_oklab lives on the observation grid (image_sample_pitch_mm); solve_target_oklab is projected onto the solve grid (solver_fine_pitch_mm) and is what the solve path and dE recomputation both consume. The white-point rescale and gamut map reassign solve_target_oklab in place (pipeline/runner.py:91, :146), so it is not necessarily the original projection array.
Progress reporting
_ProgressTracker (pipeline/runner.py:259) wraps the optional progress callback into the WebSocket stage protocol — advance(key, label) per stage, update_pct(done, total) for in-stage progress. It emits a dict with stage, stage_index, stage_count, elapsed_s, and palette index/count. No callback ⇒ tracker is None and nothing is emitted.

The module plugin contract (pipeline/base.py)
Two abstract base classes define what a pluggable module is. Both are ABCs with one abstract method and a describe() that serialises the module for the UI.
PreprocessingModule (F1)
pipeline/base.py:73. An image preprocessing operator. Class attributes the slot runner reads:













































AttributeMeaningAnchorname, descriptionidentity / UI textpipeline/base.py:88-89params: Dict[str, ParamDef]self-described tunablespipeline/base.py:90default_enabled: booldefault on/offpipeline/base.py:91input_domain / output_domain (ColorDomain)colour-domain contract; the slot runner inserts conversions between adjacent operators whose domains differpipeline/base.py:92-93order: floatposition in the chain; conventional bands Wing A 100–199, B 200–299, C 300–399, D 400–499; ties resolve by lex import pathpipeline/base.py:94required_context: FrozenSet[ContextKey]optional shared services (e.g. palette metadata) the runner resolves before apply()pipeline/base.py:95supports_protect_mask: boolwhether the operator consumes a subject-protect maskpipeline/base.py:96
Abstract method: apply(image, *, context, progress) -> PreprocessingResult (pipeline/base.py:99). The live operators all live under preprocessing/operators/ and self-register — e.g. a1_bilateral_denoise, b1_printscale_bilateral, b3_tv_flatten, c1_achievable_tonemap, c2_soft_gamut_compress (each @register_preprocessing at e.g. preprocessing/operators/a1_bilateral_denoise.py:35). See generator.preprocessing.
GroupingModule
pipeline/base.py:122. An AMS grouping strategy. Same name / description / params / default_enabled attributes, with abstract method group(state, progress) -> None (pipeline/base.py:130) that mutates state in place. Two live implementations:























Classnamedefault_enabledAnchorGreedyGroupinggreedy_optimizeTruegrouping/greedy_optimize.py:35GroupBudgetGroupinggroup_budgetFalsegrouping/beam_search.py:436
GreedyGrouping partitions filaments into swap groups by brightness order (no-op when the palette fits one load). GroupBudgetGrouping is a beam search minimising wasted Z-band volume and exposes tuning params (grouping_priority, grouping_de_scoring, …) via ParamDef. Disambiguation: this group_budget beam search is the live grouping module — distinct from the experimental scheduling beam-search referenced elsewhere in the codebase. The facade’s _resolve_grouping_from_state (facade.py:513) instantiates GroupBudgetGrouping only if module state has group_budget on, else falls back to GreedyGrouping.

Asymmetry worth knowing: pipeline/__init__.py re-exports GroupingModule, register_grouping, get_grouping, list_groupings — but not PreprocessingModule or any of the preprocessing registry helpers (pipeline/__init__.py:2-26). Preprocessing operators import the registry decorator directly from pipeline.registry; grouping is the slot the package surfaces publicly.

ParamDef — parameter self-description
pipeline/base.py:24. A dataclass that lets a module describe one tunable to both the solver and the frontend renderer in one place. Core fields: name, label, type ("int" | "float" | "bool" | "choice" | "html" | "computed_text"), default, plus choices/choice_labels/min/max/description. UI-only fields: unit, tooltip, group, show_when (conditional visibility keyed on another param’s value), and order (pipeline/base.py:40-45). to_dict() (pipeline/base.py:47) emits the JSON the API/UI consumes, omitting None-valued optional keys. This is why the Modules panel can render parameter forms without any hand-written per-module frontend code.

Registry and auto-discovery (pipeline/registry.py)
The registry is two module-level dicts — _GROUPINGS and _PREPROCESSORS (pipeline/registry.py:15-16) — populated by class decorators at import time:

@register_grouping (pipeline/registry.py:117) stores cls under cls.name.
@register_preprocessing (pipeline/registry.py:123) stores cls and adds its name to PREPROCESSING_MODULE_IDS.

Two different discovery strategies:
Grouping is hand-listed. _KNOWN_GROUPING_MODULES (pipeline/registry.py:18) names the two modules to import and _KNOWN_GROUPING_NAMES = {"greedy_optimize", "group_budget"} (pipeline/registry.py:22) is the expected set. _ensure_store_populated (pipeline/registry.py:66) re-imports them when the store is empty or partial, with care to avoid creating duplicate class objects.
Preprocessing is filesystem-driven. _discover_preprocessing_operators (pipeline/registry.py:33) walks preprocessing.operators with pkgutil.iter_modules, imports every public (non-_, non-package) submodule in lex-sorted order (pipeline/registry.py:52-62), and that import position becomes each operator’s order tiebreaker. An empty operators/ package is legal — the slot becomes a no-op (pipeline/registry.py:40). Discovery runs once per process: _ensure_preprocessing_populated (pipeline/registry.py:98) re-discovers only when _PREPROCESSORS is empty.
Public accessors all call _ensure_registry_populated first: get_grouping / get_preprocessing (pipeline/registry.py:132 / :137), list_groupings / list_preprocessings (:142 / :147), and list_all_modules (pipeline/registry.py:159) which instantiates each class via cls.__new__ and returns its describe() dict. _clear_registry (pipeline/registry.py:152) is testing-only.

Module on/off persistence (pipeline/modules.py)
pipeline/modules.py reads and writes the JSON file of {module_name: enabled} flags. This is fully live — the generator server wires every endpoint to it.

























FunctionBehaviourAnchorload_module_state(path)read JSON, fill missing keys with defaults, normalisepipeline/modules.py:66save_module_state(path, state)normalise then writepipeline/modules.py:75toggle_module(path, id, enabled)flip one flag, validate the id, normalise, persist, return full statepipeline/modules.py:83
Two normalisation rules enforce the slot contract:

Grouping is exclusive. _normalise_grouping_slot (pipeline/modules.py:15) collapses the grouping flags to exactly one active module: if none are on, it picks the default_enabled one (greedy_optimize); if several are on, a non-default selection wins.
Preprocessing is non-exclusive. _get_all_defaults (pipeline/modules.py:51) collects every module’s default_enabled; preprocessing operators each contribute independently and several may be on at once. The zero-enabled case is a legal no-op.

The server side (all reading _MODULES_PATH): the modules-list endpoint (server.py:2904), the toggle endpoint calling toggle_module (server.py:2915-2921), a bulk save calling save_module_state (server.py:2932), and several solve paths that snapshot load_module_state into the run record (e.g. server.py:2066, :2144, :2175). The facade’s _load_module_state (facade.py:534) is the resolver-side reader that feeds _resolve_pipeline_slots (facade.py:584), turning the flag dict into resolved grouping + preprocessors for PipelineConfig.

Dormant and test-only seams
Two seams in this package are wired but not exercised by the production webapp solve. Both confirmed by grepping callers.
revalidate() — wired, narrow production use, mostly test-facing
revalidate(state) (pipeline/runner.py:250) recomputes __de__ from the current thickness maps against the solve-grid target, writing straight into state.diagnostics['__de__'] (Task 5.4 — no longer touches thickness_maps). It is a thin wrapper over _recompute_de_diagnostics (pipeline/runner.py:165).
Liveness: inside run_pipeline, the solve path calls _recompute_de_diagnostics directly during staged finalisation (pipeline/runner.py:577), not revalidate. revalidate itself is invoked in production only after a grouping run that actually substituted pixels — config.grouping.group() is followed by a conditional _recompute_de_diagnostics guarded on n_substituted_pixels > 0 (pipeline/runner.py:856-863; that branch calls _recompute_de_diagnostics, not the wrapper). The public revalidate symbol is re-exported (pipeline/__init__.py:7) and its direct callers are the test suite: tests/generator/test_pipeline_runner.py:64/:77/:91 and tests/generator/test_phase3_observation_solve_grid.py:189/:221. Historically it was the post-refinement dE hook for the now-removed refinements slot. Status: live function on a narrow grouping branch; otherwise a test/compatibility seam.
snapshot.py / SnapshotPublisher — one live hook, one dormant field
SnapshotPublisher (pipeline/snapshot.py:27) writes preprocessed source-image preview PNGs and their URLs into a shared progress dict via publish_image_preview (pipeline/snapshot.py:47). Liveness, two halves:

The preview hook is live but only reachable via a dormant facade entry point. publish_image_preview is called by the preprocessing runner per enabled operator (preprocessing/runner.py:281), which receives the publisher as a direct parameter (preprocessing/runner.py:216, threaded from pipeline/runner.py:766). A publisher reaches run_pipeline only through facade.solve_preview_progressive(..., publisher=...) (facade.py:930, :962). That facade function has no production caller — grep finds only its own definition (facade.py:924); the production webapp uses solve_full (server.py:4740), which never passes a publisher. Its own docstring marks it “currently dormant in production, exercised by the preprocessing preview tests” (facade.py:938-939).
The state.snapshot_publisher field is write-only and dead. The runner assigns it (pipeline/runner.py:841) but nothing reads it back — grepping .snapshot_publisher across Prisma/ finds only that single write. The live preview path threads its publisher as a function parameter, not via this field. The progressive-solve snapshot emitter (maybe_publish) was removed in the Stage 3 cleanup; the field’s docstring at pipeline/state.py:277-281 is code-true about this. A standing removal candidate is documented in Prisma/generator/docs/legacy_audit/12_WEBAPP_DEAD_BACKEND_CANDIDATES_REMOVAL_PLAN.md. Status: publish_image_preview hook = live but production-dormant (test-only entry); state.snapshot_publisher field = dead (write-only).

generator/what-actually-runs.title: What Actually Runs
generator/what-actually-runs.content:
What Actually Runs

In one sentence: this is the single liveness map for the generator backend — which solve path actually executes, which modules are legacy or dormant, and which symbols survive only as test scaffolding — with every verdict confirmed by grepping the call graph, not by reading docstrings (most of which are stale).

The generator backend is large and has accreted dead ends: removed features that left remnant functions, experimental subsystems wired only into tests, and two whole modules that look live but no production caller touches. Module headers and docstrings are an unreliable guide — many still cite filenames and ports that no longer exist (see Stale headers — do not trust them). This page is the authority. Other liveness/printability pages link here rather than re-deriving each verdict.
How to read the status column:

LIVE — on the production solve or export path; runs on a normal web-app solve.
LEGACY — real, working code, but only reachable through the old CLI engine, not the web app.
DORMANT — imported and constructable, but no production path invokes it; wired only to tests/scripts.
REMNANT — a leftover of a removed feature; survives because something cheap still references it.
SUSPECTED INERT — strong evidence of no live caller, but the reference graph is subtle and a prior audit was burned by missing callers; treat as a hint, re-verify before deleting.

The map




























































SubjectStatusEvidence (caller-confirmed)Staged backend (run_staged_backend_path)LIVE — the only solve enginerunner.py:843-846 calls it unconditionally for every preset; runner.py is reached by all three facade entries, which server.py imports (server.py:79-81) and calls at server.py:3998, 4094, 4740.solve_image (solve.py:410)LEGACY — CLI engine onlySole caller is pipeline_cli.py:634 (imported pipeline_cli.py:46). No web-app path imports it.blueprint_triage package (analyze_triage/apply_fixes)DORMANT — test-only; state field always Nonestate.blueprint_triage is set to None in runner.py:555 and never otherwise written on the live path; analyze_triage/apply_fixes have only test callers (tests/generator/blueprint_triage*).scheduling package (Prisma/generator/scheduling/)DORMANT — experimental, offlineNo production module imports it; the only reference in source is a comment (state.py:256). Driven only by tests/scripts.geometry package (extract_regions, simplify_regions, ColourRegion)DORMANTUsed only inside its own package (geometry/__init__.py:13-15, geometry/simplify.py:133). No external production caller imports geometry.mesh.build_printability_report + the mesh.PrintabilityReport/classification ladderSUSPECTED INERTModule’s own note at printability.py:1061-1070. Grepping the call graph: the only caller of build_printability_report (printability.py:1071) is tests/generator/test_mesh_printability.py. scripts/characterize_mesh_printability.py touches only the lower-level summarize_printability (printability.py:727), not the export roll-up. Re-verify exhaustively before touching.mesh.canonical_mesh (canonical_triangle_array)SUSPECTED INERTReached only via its canonical_mesh_hash wrapper, whose sole non-test caller is scripts/benchmark_mesh_export_heavy_options.py:123; no Prisma/generator source path outside canonical_mesh.py consumes it.Reference-bundle replay (photo-stack default bundle)rejected for live — replay onlyappearance_model.py:232-236 raises unless an explicit live candidate/runtime path is given; a reference path is “for replay only”.solve_preview_progressive (facade.py:924)REMNANT of removed progressive solveNot imported by server.py; only test callers (tests/generator/preprocessing/test_facade_threading.py, test_f1_smoke.py). Docstring at facade.py:935-942 says the HTTP feature and its emitter were removed.SnapshotPublisher.maybe_publishREMOVEDThe progressive-solve snapshot emitter was deleted in the Stage 3 cleanup (snapshot.py:6); no runner call site remains in runner.py.
The live solve path, end to end
When you press Solve, server.py calls one of three facade functions — never solve_image:

























Facade entryServer call sitePresetsolve_preview (facade.py:897)server.py:3998PREVIEW_PRESETsolve_full (facade.py:967)server.py:4740FULL_PRESETsolve_compare (facade.py:992)server.py:4094COMPARE_PRESET
All three translate their SolveConfig to a PipelineConfig and funnel into run_pipeline (runner.py:587). Inside run_pipeline, after the load / LUT / gamut stages, the solve stage does exactly one thing: it imports and calls run_staged_backend_path (runner.py:843-846). There is no branch here — the staged backend is not one solver among several, it is the solver. _finalize_staged_backend_state (runner.py:533) then copies that one result bundle onto the legacy-facing PipelineState fields the rest of the app reads. See How a Solve Works for the stage-by-stage walk and The Joint LUT and Staged Solve for what the staged backend does internally.

The “6-step” engine in solve.py is not this. solve.py’s module docstring (solve.py:2-18) describes a “joint LUT + two-pass cap smoothing” pipeline in six numbered steps. That is the legacy CLI engine (solve_image, solve.py:410), reached only through pipeline_cli.py. The web app never runs it. A few utilities from solve.py are still imported by the live runner (e.g. gamut_map_hull_batch, gamut_map_batch at runner.py:127, 138, 140, and predict_image_fast re-exported through generator.facade), but the solve_image orchestration body is legacy.

Dormant and inert subsystems
blueprint_triage (printability triage) — dormant, and not the mesh report
pipeline/blueprint_triage/ is a full printability-triage subsystem (analyze_triage, plan_fixes, apply_fixes, its own PrintabilityReport/PrintabilityError). On the live path it never runs: _finalize_staged_backend_state sets state.blueprint_triage = None (runner.py:555) and nothing on the staged path writes a real report; application.py:13-14 likewise only ever clears it. The facade carries the field through for compatibility (facade.py:392, 890) and the server reads it (server.py:4643, 4793) but always finds None. Its analysis/apply functions are exercised solely by tests/generator/blueprint_triage*.

Two unrelated PrintabilityReport classes. pipeline/blueprint_triage/report.py defines one (a triage report, with PrintabilityError, at report.py:180); mesh/printability.py:680 defines a completely different one (an export-facing mesh summary). They share a name and nothing else — printability.py:1069-1070 warns against conflating them. When a page says “PrintabilityReport,” it must say which.

scheduling — experimental offline layer scheduling
Prisma/generator/scheduling/ evaluates post-solve layer-swap schedules under fixed-budget policies (scheduling/__init__.py). No production module imports it — the only mention in source is a forward-looking comment in state.py:256. It is offline/experimental research code driven by tests.

Two beam-searches, two greedies. The live grouping module is grouping/beam_search.py (GroupBudgetGrouping, beam_search.py:436) / grouping/greedy_optimize.py (GreedyGrouping, greedy_optimize.py:35), selected in facade.py:515-531 (greedy is the default; the budget/beam variant only when module state opts in). The scheduling package has its own setup_beam_search_policy / layer_sparse_greedy_policy (scheduling/__init__.py:48-50) — same names, different subsystem, not on the solve path.

geometry — dormant region containers
Prisma/generator/geometry/ extracts vector ColourRegion polygons from a SolvedMaterialPlan (geometry/extract.py:210) and simplifies them (geometry/simplify.py). The package is internally consistent (__init__.py re-exports extract_regions/simplify_regions) but no module outside the package imports it — it is dormant. (The unrelated mesh/geometry_policy.py and assorted shapely.geometry imports are a different thing.)
mesh printability + canonical mesh — suspected inert
mesh/printability.py is a measurement-only toolkit (footprint alignment, inter-mesh seal, thin-island risk). The low-level measurement functions may be consumed by other mesh code, but the export-facing roll-up — build_printability_report (printability.py:1071) and the pass/warn/fallback/block + next_action=do_not_export classification ladder (in _classify_printability_summary, printability.py:1016-1038) — is flagged suspected inert in a code comment at printability.py:1061-1070. The code comment lists both the dedicated test and scripts/characterize_mesh_printability.py as callers, but grepping confirms the script imports only summarize_printability / render_summary_markdown (printability.py:727, 1139), not build_printability_report itself — so the export roll-up’s sole confirmed caller is tests/generator/test_mesh_printability.py. That comment is deliberately cautious because an earlier audit declared this “dead” after missing real references. Treat “inert” here as a hint, not a fact, and re-verify across tests, scripts, the config chain, and the separate blueprint_triage module before removing anything.
mesh/canonical_mesh.py (canonical_triangle_array, canonical_mesh.py:43) computes an order-insensitive geometry hash for output-equivalence checks. It is reached only through its canonical_mesh_hash wrapper (canonical_mesh.py:76), whose only non-test reference in the tree is scripts/benchmark_mesh_export_heavy_options.py; no Prisma/generator source path calls it on a live export — suspected inert by the same standard.
Reference-bundle replay — rejected for live solves
The photo-stack Appearance provider (PhotoStackBundleAppearanceProvider, appearance_model.py:210) requires an explicit live calibration candidate or its runtime_bundle.json. Passing a bare reference bundle path is allowed only as replay; the constructor raises otherwise (appearance_model.py:232-236: “select a live calibration candidate or pass a reference path for replay only”). So a default/reference bundle is never the live appearance model — the default provider is "historical_spline" (SolveConfig.appearance_model_provider, facade.py:241; wired into the runner at runner.py:670-671).
Removed-feature remnants
The progressive solve feature (mid-solve snapshots streamed to the browser) was deleted in the Stage 3 cleanup. What survives:

solve_preview_progressive (facade.py:924) — not imported by server.py (absent from the server.py:79-81 import block). Its docstring (facade.py:935-942) explains it is retained only as the facade-level vehicle that threads a SnapshotPublisher into the preprocessing preview hook, dormant in production, exercised by tests/generator/preprocessing/test_facade_threading.py and test_f1_smoke.py. Computationally it is identical to solve_full (both use FULL_PRESET); the _progressive suffix is a historical artifact and a queued rename candidate.
SnapshotPublisher.maybe_publish — the actual snapshot emitter — was removed; snapshot.py:6 records this and no maybe_publish call site remains in runner.py. The surviving publish_image_preview / snapshot_publisher threading (runner.py:593, 766, 841) is the preprocessing image-preview path, deliberately preserved as a cheap dormant hook, not the removed progressive-solve renderer.

Stale headers — do not trust them
Liveness can never be read off a module header in this codebase; cite line anchors instead. Confirmed stale headers:



































FileHeader saysRealitysolve.py:2lith_solver.pyfile is Prisma/generator/solve.pyfacade.py:2lith_facade.pyfile is Prisma/generator/facade.pymodel.py:2lith_model.pyfile is Prisma/generator/model.pyserver.py:1-9”unified_generator/pipeline”, “port 8001”real dir Prisma/generator, port 8010grouping/__init__.py:1, pipeline/base.py:1, pipeline/registry.py:1, pipeline/state.py:1# lithophane_generator/... pathsall under Prisma/generator/
Likewise, solve.py’s six-step pipeline docstring and the appearance-model “appearance-named” method docstrings describe shapes that no longer hold: the appearance methods are pass-through (they return model-domain values, not display-converted ones) after the projection-slot retirement (appearance_model.py:218-221). When in doubt, grep the caller.
Related pages

The Joint LUT and Staged Solve — what the staged backend does inside.
Exporting Print Files — the export path (and where mesh printability would sit if it were live).

home.content:
Prisma — Generator Documentation
Prisma turns an ordinary image into a stack of coloured filament layers that, when backlit, reproduce the image’s colours — a colour lithophane. The generator is the half of Prisma that does this: you give it a photo and a palette of calibrated filaments, and it produces print files (STL / 3MF) for your slicer.
This vault documents how the generator works, built from its source code — every claim cites a file:line so you can verify it. It covers the generator only; the calibration app is deferred. See README for how to open and publish this vault.

output/ams-grouping-and-swap-planning.title: AMS grouping and swap planning
output/ams-grouping-and-swap-planning.content:
AMS grouping and swap planning

In one sentence: when the solved palette needs more colour filaments than fit in one AMS load, the generator partitions them into sequential swap groups (default greedy, optional Z-waste beam search), clips any over-budget thickness into the white cap, and emits human-readable swap instructions plus OrcaSlicer M600 pauses at export time.

This page covers everything that happens to solved layers after the colour stack is solved but before (and at) export, when the palette is too big for a single AMS. It serves both the user driving the wizard and the developer who has forgotten how swap.py and the grouping modules fit together.
Related: From solve to mesh the export pipeline · generator.swap · generator.grouping.greedy_optimize · generator.grouping.beam_search · generator.pipeline.runner · generator.facade · Print constraints

The slot budget
A printer has a fixed number of AMS slots. Some are reserved for white; the rest hold colour. The budget is computed on the solve config:

ams_slots (default 4) and white_slots (default 1) — pipeline/state.py:96, pipeline/state.py:97.
effective_white_slots() bumps the white reservation to 2 when the white base and white cap are different filaments (they need two physical slots), otherwise keeps white_slots — pipeline/state.py:220.
colour_slots() = ams_slots - effective_white_slots() — pipeline/state.py:226.

So with the default 4-slot / single-white setup you get 3 colour slots. Pick a white cap filament that differs from the base and you drop to 2 colour slots (one extra slot is spent on the second white). The same accessors exist on the facade SolveConfig (facade.py:326, facade.py:331) and are wired into the modules through state.config.
Grouping only triggers when the palette overflows. Each grouping module first filters the palette to active filaments — those present in the thickness maps with at least one pixel above 1e-9 mm — and returns immediately (a no-op) when len(active_fids) <= colour_slots (grouping/greedy_optimize.py:61, grouping/beam_search.py:568). If everything fits in one load, nothing on this page happens.

Where grouping runs in the pipeline
The webapp solve runs the staged backend (run_staged_backend_path), then runs the grouping module as a distinct post-solve step. In generator.pipeline.runner:
result = run_staged_backend_path(state, ...)      # runner.py:846
_finalize_staged_backend_state(state, result)     # runner.py:851
if has_grouping:
    config.grouping.group(state, progress)         # runner.py:855

Grouping does not run inside the staged solver — it is a separate module invoked afterwards (pipeline/runner.py:855). If it substitutes any pixels (n_substituted_pixels > 0), dE diagnostics are recomputed so state.diagnostics stays honest (pipeline/runner.py:856).
Which module runs
The module is chosen in facade._resolve_grouping_from_state (facade.py:513):




















ConditionModuleRegistry namedefaultGreedyGrouping (facade.py:531)greedy_optimize (grouping/greedy_optimize.py:45)module state has group_budget truthyGroupBudgetGrouping (facade.py:520)group_budget (grouping/beam_search.py:447)
Grouping is resolved only when preset.grouping_enabled (facade.py:606); otherwise the grouping module is None. GreedyGrouping.default_enabled = True (grouping/greedy_optimize.py:47); GroupBudgetGrouping.default_enabled = False (grouping/beam_search.py:449) — the beam search is opt-in.

Two engines, one helper. There is also a legacy CLI engine (pipeline_cli.run, pipeline_cli.py:402) whose Step 4c calls swap.optimize_grouping directly (pipeline_cli.py:701). That is the command-line path, not the webapp. The webapp reaches the same greedy algorithm through the GreedyGrouping module wrapper. Both bottom out in swap.optimize_grouping.


Default greedy partitioner
GreedyGrouping.group delegates to swap.optimize_grouping (grouping/greedy_optimize.py:64), passing colour_slots, effective_max_layers(), the spline profiles, and the loaded filament registry. The result replaces state.thickness_maps with the substituted maps and stores the GroupingResult on state.grouping (grouping/greedy_optimize.py:76, grouping/greedy_optimize.py:77).
Inside optimize_grouping (swap.py:481):

Active set, sorted by brightness. Active filaments are sorted dark-first by default (group_order="dark_first", swap.py:490), using approximate luminance from the registry hex value — 0.2126·R + 0.7152·G + 0.0722·B (swap.py:543). "light_first" reverses it (swap.py:551). Missing/unparseable hex falls back to luminance 128.0 (swap.py:546).
Chunk into groups. plan_filament_groups slices the sorted ordering into consecutive groups of at most colour_slots (swap.py:553, sliced at swap.py:65).
Budget clip → white cap. For each filament, any pixel whose thickness exceeds budget_mm = max_layers * layer_height is clipped to the budget, and the excess is added to the white-cap map MapKey.WHITE_CAP (swap.py:566–swap.py:572). This is the white-cap overflow substitution: out-of-budget colour becomes white so total Z stays bounded. n_substituted_pixels counts every clipped pixel (swap.py:573).
The greedy optimiser returns total_de_cost = 0.0 — it does not estimate colour cost (swap.py:579).

Greedy is order-only: it sorts by brightness and chunks. It does not consider whether group-mates are spatially complementary.

Optional Z-waste beam-search packer
GroupBudgetGrouping (grouping/beam_search.py:436, registry name group_budget) explores many groupings and scores them by Z-waste instead of just chunking a sorted list. Enable it by setting group_budget in module state (facade.py:518).
Cost = Z-waste + band overflow + swap count + (optional) slot stability (_cost_group_budget, grouping/beam_search.py:125):

Z-waste — for each group, the band height is the max per-pixel sum of the group’s filaments; waste is band·n_pixels − sum — unused volume inside the loaded band (grouping/beam_search.py:160–grouping/beam_search.py:164). Spatially complementary filaments (thick at different pixels) pack tighter and waste less.
Band overflow — how far the summed group band heights exceed the colour budget max_layers·layer_height (grouping/beam_search.py:147, grouping/beam_search.py:167).
Swap count — len(groups) - 1 (grouping/beam_search.py:168).
Slot stability — penalises slot occupants changing between consecutive groups, only when its weight > 0 (grouping/beam_search.py:175, computed in _slot_stability_cost at grouping/beam_search.py:195).

Search structure (grouping/beam_search.py:561):

Seed several diverse orderings — dark-first, light-first, alphabetical, an interleaved dark/light comb (only when ≥4 filaments), and reverse-alphabetical (_seed_orderings, grouping/beam_search.py:77). Each is chunked and scored into the beam (grouping/beam_search.py:575).
Local search for up to max_iterations (default 10, grouping/beam_search.py:500) over a beam of width beam_width (default 16, grouping/beam_search.py:501): mutate by swapping/moving filaments between adjacent groups (_mutate_groups, grouping/beam_search.py:367), re-score, keep the best, and stop early when no improvement (grouping/beam_search.py:611).
Optional dE re-rank — when de_scoring is on, the top candidates are re-ranked with an OKLab dE estimate of the colour lost to white-cap promotion (_estimate_substitution_de, grouping/beam_search.py:217; applied at grouping/beam_search.py:618).
Apply the winner: build FilamentGroups via plan_filament_groups (grouping/beam_search.py:646) and clip overflow.

Overflow handling has two modes here. Default is the same per-filament clip-to-white-cap as greedy (_apply_substitutions, grouping/beam_search.py:290, called at grouping/beam_search.py:656). With in_group_substitution on, overflow is first offered to other filaments in the same group that have room, and only the leftover goes to white cap (_apply_substitutions_in_group, grouping/beam_search.py:313, called at grouping/beam_search.py:652) — this preserves more colour. The winning metric score is stored as total_de_cost on the result (grouping/beam_search.py:665).
User-facing parameters
The wizard exposes these on the group_budget module (grouping/beam_search.py:450):






























ParamEffectAnchorgrouping_priorityPreset that sets the four cost weightsgrouping/beam_search.py:451grouping_de_scoringRe-rank including colour-loss estimategrouping/beam_search.py:468grouping_de_cost_weightScales the dE term (needs dE scoring)grouping/beam_search.py:477grouping_in_group_subRedistribute overflow before white capgrouping/beam_search.py:486
grouping_priority choices map to weight presets in PRIORITY_PRESETS (grouping/beam_search.py:417):








































Priorityz_wasteoverflowswap_countslot_stabilitybalanced1.05.00.50.1fewer_groups0.55.03.00.1better_packing3.05.00.20.1fewer_slot_changes1.05.00.53.0
Explicit weight kwargs still override the preset for testing/back-compat (grouping/beam_search.py:530–grouping/beam_search.py:541).

FilamentGroup geometry
Both modules represent the plan as a list of FilamentGroup dataclasses (swap.py:18):






























FieldMeaningAnchorgroup_index0-based group orderswap.py:21filamentsfilament IDs in this groupswap.py:22z_start / z_endmm — bottom/top of this group’s colour bandswap.py:23, swap.py:24slot_assignmentsfilament_id → AMS slot (1-based)swap.py:25
plan_filament_groups (swap.py:28) builds them: it re-filters to active filaments (swap.py:55), chunks into groups of colour_slots = ams_slots - white_slots (swap.py:50, swap.py:65), then walks the ordering accumulating a per-pixel cumulative stack starting at the white-base floor d_wb (swap.py:79). Each group’s z_start is the running cumulative.max() when its first filament begins (swap.py:94) and z_end is the max after its last filament (swap.py:101). Slots are assigned 1..colour_slots by position within the group (swap.py:109); white is implicitly the last slot (swap.py:104). Note plan_filament_groups takes ams_slots/white_slots directly, so callers pass colour_slots + 1 when they only know the colour budget (e.g. swap.py:529).

Export-time swap planning
Group geometry and swap instructions are produced at export time in server.get_swap_instructions — the GET /api/export/swap-instructions endpoint (server.py:5774). The solve-time grouping on state.grouping is only a starting point; export re-derives the plan against the current printer state. Sequence:

Materialise export thickness maps and ordering — _prepare_export_materialization (server.py:835, called server.py:5793). Export can legitimately activate filaments the solve omitted.
Read AMS capacity from current config, not the cached solve — ams_slots/white_slots come from _cfg() because the user may have changed printers after solving (server.py:5800–server.py:5802).
Reconcile groups — reconcile_export_groups (swap.py:114, called server.py:5807). It keeps the solve-time layout when it still fits the current hardware, appends any export-only active filaments to the tail (swap.py:214), and falls back to a fresh plan_filament_groups when the old layout is too big or has too many groups for the current AMS (swap.py:168, swap.py:178). If AMS/white slot counts changed since the solve, the base groups are discarded first (server.py:5805, server.py:5806).
Generate instructions — generate_swap_instructions (swap.py:272, called server.py:5822).
Generate pause G-code — generate_orcaslicer_pause_gcode (swap.py:618, called server.py:5835).

Instruction text and M600
generate_swap_instructions (swap.py:272) emits a formatted plan: print dimensions, total height, per-group AMS slot assignments, and one SWAP block between consecutive groups. The swap height is the previous group’s z_end, converted to an approximate layer via round(swap_z / layer_height) (swap.py:403). For each swap it diffs the two groups’ slot_assignments and prints exactly which slot to unload/load (swap.py:413–swap.py:423), while reminding the user the white base/cap slots never change (swap.py:425–swap.py:429).
White slot bookkeeping: the base lives in the last AMS slot (base_slot = ams_slots, swap.py:354); when the cap is a different filament it takes ams_slots - 1, otherwise base and cap share the last slot (swap.py:355). Total lithophane height honours a per-pixel color_ceiling_map + wc_map surface when supplied, so the tallest colour stack and the thickest local cap need not coincide (swap.py:330–swap.py:339).
The actual pause command is M600. generate_orcaslicer_pause_gcode returns M600 ; pause for filament change at each between-group Z (swap.py:636), and generate_swap_instructions also embeds the same M600 snippet inline in its G-code section (swap.py:459). With a single group it returns "; No filament swaps needed" (swap.py:628). The number of mid-print swaps is always len(groups) - 1 (swap.py:353).

compute_filler_map — legacy CLI only
compute_filler_map (swap.py:583) pads every pixel to a uniform colour-stack height for a translucent filler filament. It has exactly one caller: the legacy CLI engine pipeline_cli.run, Step 4d, gated on filler_filament is not None (pipeline_cli.py:717). The webapp/staged backend never calls it — neither grouping module references it, and the __filler__ sentinel it writes is documented as “legacy CLI-only” (thickness_maps.py:15). Treat it as CLI-only / unused by the web app, not dead: it is reachable from python pipeline_cli.py ... --filler .... (The prompt’s “no observed caller” is too strong — the caller is the CLI engine, not the webapp solve path.)

Quick reference
