solver/staged-artifacts-and-the-solvedma.title: Staged artifacts and the SolvedMaterialPlan contract
solver/staged-artifacts-and-the-solvedma.content:
In one sentence: the live webapp solve runs a five-stage staged backend that emits a StagedBackendResult lineage, and a small bridge projects its final recipe map into the canonical solve-owned SolvedMaterialPlan (immutable segment geometry + mutable stack assignment + cap heights) from which every downstream raster — labels, per-filament thickness, predicted render — is one-way derived, never authored.

This page is the data-shape reference for the Solver output. It serves two readers: a USER who wants to know what a “solve” actually produces, and a DEVELOPER who has forgotten how the backend’s artifacts fit together. It is built from the four contract modules, not their docstrings (several of which are stale — e.g. solved_material_plan.py:11-14 still claims the plan “remains None at runtime”, which is false; see Liveness below).
Related: generator.pipeline.staged_runner · generator.pipeline.runner · The staged backend solve path · Blueprint triage · Region geometry extraction · Layer scheduling

Two layers of artifact, one direction of truth
A finished solve produces artifacts at two altitudes:























LayerLives whereOwnsMutabilityStage plans (Stage 0–5)StagedBackendResult on state.staged_resultthe staged backend’s internal raster blueprintbuilt once per stage, then read-only downstreamCanonical planSolvedMaterialPlan on state.solved_plansegment geometry + stack assignment + cap heightsgeometry frozen, stack assignment mutable
The rule that holds the whole system together: truth flows one way. The staged backend authors raster blueprints; the bridge condenses the final blueprint into the canonical plan; the derived-views layer projects the plan back out into legacy rasters for consumers that still want them. Nothing downstream writes truth back into the plan’s geometry. This is the “one-way ownership” pattern documented in pipeline/derived_views.py:1-20.

The five stage plans
The staged backend (run_staged_backend_path, pipeline/staged_runner.py:10310) builds one authoritative plan object per stage. Each is a dataclass in pipeline/staged_artifacts.py. They are assembled in order inside the runner:















































StagePlan dataclassBuilt atCarries (selected fields)0QuantizedDirectiveSetcompiled directivesdirectives, planning_lattice_pitch_mm, solver_shape (staged_artifacts.py:21)1LateralZonePlanstaged_runner.py:10352zone_label_map, zone_flat_indices, adjacency_edges, target_oklab_mean_by_zone (:113)2VisibleRecipeRawGeometryPlanstaged_runner.py:10403zone_recipe_labels, fine_recipe_label_map, recipe_table, raw_color_ceiling_mm, implied_cap_height_mm, gamut_mask (:263)3FillerGeometryPlanstaged_runner.py:10413raw_color_ceiling_mm, filler_height_mm, color_ceiling_mm (:310)4CapSynthesisPlanstaged_runner.py:10423cap_height_mm, cap_boundary_top_mm, detail_height_mm, final_visible_top_mm, plus detail/printability summaries (:440)5CompatibilityBundlestaged_runner.py:10957thickness_maps, diagnostics, debug_maps, compatibility_label_map, boundary_label_map (:570)
Stage 5 is not a geometry plan — it is the legacy-raster projection of stages 2–4 (see The staged_bridge).
The Stage 2 recipe table — the colour blueprint
Stage 2 is where the colour decision is made. Its recipe_table is a tuple of VisibleRecipe (staged_artifacts.py:72), each a frozen thickness_by_filament tuple. The per-pixel recipe_label_map (staged_artifacts.py:295) indexes into that table — preferring the fine_recipe_label_map when present, otherwise expanding zone_recipe_labels[zone_label_map]. This recipe map is the seed for the canonical plan.

Disambiguation trap. VisibleRecipe (Stage 2, staged_artifacts.py:72) and StackDefinition (canonical plan, solved_material_plan.py:27) are near-duplicates — both are frozen (filament_id, thickness_mm) tuples normalised to drop zeros. They are NOT the same class. VisibleRecipe is the staged backend’s currency; StackDefinition is the canonical plan’s. The bridge converts one to the other at staged_bridge.py:57.


The lineage object: StagedBackendResult
All nine artifacts are bundled into a single StagedBackendResult (staged_artifacts.py:583) returned by run_staged_backend_path (staged_runner.py:10980) and parked on state.staged_result by _finalize_staged_backend_state (runner.py:538).
StagedBackendResult
├── compiled_directives    : QuantizedDirectiveSet       (Stage 0)
├── receipts               : DirectiveReceiptBook        (per-directive status)
├── planning_diagnostics   : PlanningDiagnosticsStream   (zone-level notes)
├── performance_profile    : StagedPerformanceProfile    (timings_s, counters)
├── lateral_zone_plan      : LateralZonePlan             (Stage 1)
├── visible_plan           : VisibleRecipeRawGeometryPlan (Stage 2)
├── filler_plan            : FillerGeometryPlan          (Stage 3)
├── cap_plan               : CapSynthesisPlan            (Stage 4)
└── compatibility_bundle   : CompatibilityBundle         (Stage 5)

receipts, planning_diagnostics, and performance_profile are bookkeeping, not geometry: DirectiveReceiptBook (:40) records per-directive status/stage/detail; PlanningDiagnosticsStream (:57) holds zone-scoped notes; StagedPerformanceProfile (:64) is timings_s + counters (the solve writes e.g. stage5_solved_plan_segments at runner.py:549-553 and stage5_bridge_s at staged_runner.py:10964 into it).

The canonical artifact: SolvedMaterialPlan
This is the solve’s authoritative output and the input to export, triage, scheduling, and region geometry. Defined at solved_material_plan.py:74.
Shape













































FieldTypeMeaningsegment_id_map(H, W) intimmutable geometry identity; dense ids 0..n_segments-1segment_stack_id(n_segments,) intmutable assignment: which stack_table entry each segment usesstack_tabletuple[StackDefinition, ...]canonical, de-duplicated set of colour stackscap_height_map(H, W) float32fine-grid white-cap height, mmimage_domain_width_mm / height_mmfloatphysical extentimage_sample_pitch_mm / solver_fine_pitch_mmfloatobservation-grid and solve-grid cell sizescolor_region_target_mmfloatcolour-region geometry target
The central design move (solved_material_plan.py:74-91): geometry identity and material assignment are separated. A segment is a region of pixels that share an id; which material that region prints is a separate, mutable indirection through segment_stack_id → stack_table. A downstream stage that wants to reassign material (e.g. triage shortening a stack) rewrites segment_stack_id — it must never rewrite segment_id_map.
Invariants (enforced in __post_init__, :104)
These raise ValueError/TypeError at construction, so any plan you hold is already valid:

segment_id_map is 2-D (:105).
cap_height_map shares the (H, W) footprint of segment_id_map (:109).
segment_stack_id is 1-D (:115).
Segment ids are dense and contiguous 0..n_segments-1 — np.unique(segment_id_map) must equal arange(n_segments); a gap raises “missing dense segment ids” (:137-146).
Every segment_stack_id entry is a valid index into stack_table (:152-159).
Every stack_table entry is a StackDefinition (:161-166).
Geometry is frozen structurally: segment_id_map.flags.writeable = False (:169). Attempting to mutate the raster raises at the NumPy level — this is what makes the “geometry is immutable” claim a runtime guarantee, not a convention.

StackDefinition (:27)
One unique committed colour-layer stack: a frozen, sorted colour_thickness_mm tuple of (filament_id, thickness_mm). Colour content only — base-white (d_wb config scalar) and cap-white (cap_height_map) are modeled separately on the plan (:29-39). from_mapping (:43) drops zero-thickness entries so two mappings that differ only in absent-vs-zero entries hash equal; being frozen + content-sorted makes stacks hashable and de-duplicable into the canonical stack_table.
Convenience accessors on the plan: n_segments, n_stacks, shape, stack_at(segment_id) (:185), and filament_ids() (:189, deterministic sorted union across all stacks).
Where it is carried
The plan rides on the runtime state objects:

PipelineState.solved_plan (state.py:257) — populated by the solve path, “consumed by export, triage, and scheduling” per the in-code comment (state.py:254-256).
SolveResult.solved_plan on the facade (facade.py:380).


The derived-views layer (one-way)
pipeline/derived_views.py turns a SolvedMaterialPlan back into legacy rasters for consumers that haven’t migrated onto the plan. Every helper is pure: reads plan fields, returns a fresh array the caller may mutate, never writes back (derived_views.py:10-14).



































HelperReturnsLive consumer (grepped)committed_stack_label_map(plan) (:33)(H, W) label map = segment_stack_id[segment_id_map]server.py:1495 (Explorer Rich artifact), scheduling/model.py:435, cap_quality.py:60/572/624/737per_filament_thickness_maps(plan, ids=None) (:49){filament_id: (H, W) float32}; absent filaments → all-zerovia compatibility_thickness_maps belowcap_height_map_view(plan) (:97)fresh writable copy of cap_height_mapvia compatibility_thickness_mapscompatibility_thickness_maps(plan, ids=None) (:107)per-filament maps + writable "__white_cap__"blueprint_triage/application.py:48, blueprint_triage_gate tests; rebuilds state.thickness_maps after triage mutates assignmentproject_observation_to_solve_grid(...) (:125)(solve_h*solve_w, 3) OKLab on the solve gridpipeline/target_cloud.py:84 (live), palette suggest domain-alignment
committed_stack_label_map is the keystone: because the label is segment_stack_id[segment_id_map], pixels in one segment are guaranteed to share a stack id, and per_filament_thickness_maps builds every thickness raster by gathering a stack-indexed lookup through this label map (:69-90). Mutate segment_stack_id and re-derive, and the rasters update — the plan stays the single source of truth.
project_observation_to_solve_grid is OWNED here
Despite being a target-grid resampler rather than a plan view, project_observation_to_solve_grid lives in and is exported from derived_views.py (:125, :172). It maps observation-grid target OKLab onto the solve grid. The contract (:134-164):

When image_sample_pitch_mm == solver_fine_pitch_mm (the common case) it is a zero-cost identity pass — it returns the same object (:154-155).
When the pitches differ, it bilinearly resamples (scipy.ndimage.zoom, order=1) by the pitch ratio to the solve-grid shape (:157-164).

Its live caller is target_cloud.py:84, which feeds it the image_to_target OKLab cloud to produce the solve_oklab used by the solver. So this single function is the boundary between the observation grid (what the camera sampled) and the solve grid (what the solver optimises).

The staged_bridge build
pipeline/staged_bridge.py is the read-only Stage 5 adapter with two exported builders (:386).
build_solved_material_plan_for_export (:17) — staged plans → canonical plan
This is how a SolvedMaterialPlan actually comes into being on the live path. Called by _finalize_staged_backend_state (runner.py:542) with the Stage 2 visible_plan and Stage 4 cap_plan. Algorithm (:32-87):

Take visible_plan.recipe_label_map (the final fine recipe map). Validate it is 2-D, non-empty, non-negative (:34-41).
For each distinct recipe label present, convert its VisibleRecipe into a StackDefinition (:57) and de-duplicate into a canonical stack_table keyed by stack identity (:60-64) — two different recipe labels with identical colour content collapse to one stack.
Each distinct recipe label becomes one dense segment; segment_id_map paints the segment id onto every pixel of that label (:65), and segment_stack_id[segment] points at the de-duplicated stack (:66).
Adopt Stage 4’s cap_height_mm as cap_height_map (shape-checked against the recipe map, :68-74), and set the pitch/domain scalars from solver_fine_pitch_mm (:76-87).

The result satisfies every SolvedMaterialPlan invariant by construction (dense segments, valid stack indices, matching cap footprint).

Note: here a “segment” is one whole connected-label footprint — all pixels of a given recipe label share one segment id, regardless of spatial connectivity. Spatial connected-component splitting is a later concern handled by Region geometry extraction (geometry/extract.py:210), not the bridge.

build_compatibility_bundle (:90) — staged plans → legacy raster bundle
Called at staged_runner.py:10957 to populate Stage 5. It projects visible_plan + filler_plan + cap_plan into the flat raster world the legacy preview/export code expects (:98-383):

thickness_maps: per-palette-filament (H, W) rasters painted by recipe label (:103-113), plus white-layer channels "__white_cap__", "__white_boundary_cap__" (cap-boundary minus colour ceiling, floored at 0), "__white_detail_cap__" (:122-130).
diagnostics: "__gamut_mask__" (:132-134).
debug_maps: a large named dictionary of zone/recipe/ceiling/cap/detail rasters plus optional Stage 2 recipe-pressure, geometry attribution, printability-gate, substrate-repair, boundary-mutation, exterior-white-guard, and blueprint-printability maps — each guarded by a None check and copied (:135-374).
compatibility_label_map / boundary_label_map: copies of the recipe and zone label maps (:379-380).

This bundle is the legacy compatibility surface; the canonical plan (above) is the forward-looking one. Export can recover connected same-stack regions from the plan and avoid the per-pixel raster mesh path (staged_bridge.py:25-31).

Liveness — what is actually wired
Grepped, not assumed (a prior audit was burned by missing callers):

The staged backend is the live solve. runner.py:843-846 imports and calls run_staged_backend_path; this is the webapp solve, NOT solve.py’s legacy CLI “6-step” engine. Confirmed live.
SolvedMaterialPlan is populated at runtime. runner.py:542 assigns state.solved_plan on every solve. The solved_material_plan.py:11-14 docstring saying it “remains None at runtime” is stale — disregard it; trust the assignment.
All five derived-views helpers have live (non-test) consumers — see the table above; server.py, cap_quality.py, scheduling/model.py, blueprint_triage/application.py, and target_cloud.py all call into them.
extract_regions (geometry/extract.py:210) is exported from the geometry package and consumes state.solved_plan, but I found no production call site inside Prisma/generator/ — it is exercised only by tests/generator/test_phase4_region_extraction.py. Status: wired-by-export, test-covered, no production caller found (unconfirmed whether export currently routes through it).
scheduling/model.py consumes the plan (committed_stack_label_map, cap_height_map) but its derive_*/build_* case functions (model.py:375/505/526/589) are reached only from tests/generator/test_layer_scheduling.py in my grep — no production caller found. Status: plan-consumer, test-covered, production wiring unconfirmed.


Both unconfirmed items are plan consumers downstream of a populated plan — they are not dead in the contract sense; I simply could not trace a production call edge and am flagging that explicitly rather than guessing.


See also

The staged backend solve path — how run_staged_backend_path orchestrates the stages
Region geometry extraction — extract_regions, connected-component geometry off the plan
Blueprint triage — the live mutator that rewrites segment_stack_id and re-derives rasters
Layer scheduling — scheduling.model, fixed-budget cases off the plan

solver/the-joint-lut-building-and-queryi.filePath: Solver/The Joint LUT building and querying.md
solver/the-joint-lut-building-and-queryi.title: The Joint LUT building and querying
solver/the-joint-lut-building-and-queryi.content:
In one sentence: the joint LUT enumerates every printable (cap + colour) stack under a height budget, stores each stack’s OKLab colour in a chroma-weighted KD-tree, and the solver answers “which stack reproduces this pixel?” with a nearest-neighbour query.

This page covers Prisma/generator/lut.py (the spline path, the query functions, the disk cache, the convex hull, and the legacy cap-curve helpers) and Prisma/generator/photo_stack_lut.py (the vectorized photo-stack build path). For the surrounding solve flow see The Joint LUT and Staged Solve and the Joint LUT concept note. Architecture nodes: generator.lut, generator.photo_stack_lut, generator.appearance_model.
What “joint” means
Older designs solved cap thickness (luminance) and colour thickness in two separate steps. The joint LUT folds them together: a single LUTEntry enumerates combinations of (d_wc, d_c1, …, d_ck) jointly and stores oklab(T_wb × T_wc(d_wc) × ∏ T_ci(d_ci)) for each (lut.py:129–136, docstring formula lut.py:9–10). White base (d_wb) is fixed and baked into every entry, so the query target divides it out conceptually but the entries already include it. The cap dimension is carried per-entry in cap_thicknesses, and the chosen cap comes back to the caller under the reserved '__white_cap__' key.
A LUTEntry is one filament subset (size 1..k_max), not one filament. The build loops over itertools.combinations(filament_ids, k) for each k (lut.py:490–491), so a 3-filament palette with k_max=3 produces 7 entries (3 singles + 3 pairs + 1 triple). Each entry owns its own KD-tree.















































LUTEntry fieldshapemeaningsourcefilamentstuple[str,…]colour filament IDs in this subsetlut.py:131thicknesses(N, k)colour thickness per filament (mm)lut.py:132cap_thicknesses(N,)white-cap thickness d_wc (mm)lut.py:133oklab(N, 3)OKLab of full transmission, unscaledlut.py:134treeKDTreebuilt from chroma-weighted OKLablut.py:135chroma_weightfloatL* divided by this in the treelut.py:136
Entry enumeration under a height budget (stars-and-bars)
For each subset and each cap step, the remaining height budget caps how many colour layers fit: remaining_steps = max(0, min(max_layers, int((budget_mm − d_wc) / layer_height))) (lut.py:505–506). Within that, _enumerate_combos_budget(k, remaining_steps) produces all non-negative integer tuples of length k summing to ≤ remaining_steps (lut.py:221–247). This is a direct recursive stars-and-bars generation rather than itertools.product + filter — the docstring notes that for k=3, max_steps=25 it yields exactly C(28,3)=3276 tuples instead of product’s 17576 (lut.py:226–228). k=0 returns a single empty row; k=1 returns arange(max_steps+1) (lut.py:230–233).
photo_stack_lut.py keeps a local copy of this function (_enumerate_combos_budget, photo_stack_lut.py:78–97) “to avoid importing lut.py from this helper module” — same algorithm, but int16 dtype instead of int. The two implementations are independent and must stay in lockstep; the photo-stack copy is the one used when building provider LUTs.
The budget itself: if t_max is None it defaults to d_wc_max + max_layers * layer_height (lut.py:442–443). The live webapp passes t_max = config.t_max − config.d_wb (the budget after the white base) at runner.py:797, 809, 826.
Transmission → OKLab → pruning
Both build paths share the same post-processing tail:

Compose transmission. Spline path multiplies precomputed per-step transmission tables: T_wb (fixed), T_wc_cache per cap step, and colour_T_cache[fid] per layer count, all from predict_transmission (lut.py:461–479, 517–538). The product is clipped to [1e-9, 1.0] (lut.py:555).
OKLab. to_oklab converts the linear-RGB transmission array to OKLab (lut.py:556).
Prune near-duplicates. _prune_entries bins OKLab space at bin_width=0.005 and keeps one entry per bin (lut.py:351–391). Per bin it keeps the entry with lowest total colour thickness (less material), tiebroken by lowest cap thickness (brighter), via a single np.lexsort((cap_arr, total_colour, keys)) (lut.py:382). Binning packs the 3 quantised OKLab coordinates into one int64 key (lut.py:374–378).
Build KD-tree (see below) and append the LUTEntry.

OKLab indexing with chroma weighting
The KD-tree is built from OKLab, but when chroma_weight != 1.0 the L* channel is divided by the weight before tree construction (lut.py:564–569): scaled_oklab[:, 0] /= chroma_weight. Dividing L* shrinks lightness distances in the search metric, so nearest-neighbour matching prioritises colour (a, b) over lightness. A chroma_weight > 1 therefore tolerates more lightness error to nail hue/chroma. The stored oklab array stays unscaled — only the tree sees the scaled copy — so reported dE can be recomputed in true (unweighted) OKLab space.
Every query mirrors this: the target’s L* is divided by cw = luts[0].chroma_weight before tree.query, and the returned distance (which is in scaled space) is replaced with the true unweighted Euclidean OKLab distance against the stored oklab whenever cw != 1.0 (query_luts lut.py:915–943; query_luts_batch lut.py:973–981, 1029, 1038–1040). See OKLab and Chroma weight.
Querying
All query functions take the List[LUTEntry] and scan every entry’s tree, keeping the global best per pixel. There is no subset pre-filtering — the nearest stack across all subsets wins.
query_luts_batch — the live webapp query
This is the function the running webapp actually calls. It is imported and invoked in the staged backend at staged_runner.py:23 and staged_runner.py:762 (query_luts_batch(state.luts, targets)). It is the only LUT query reachable from run_staged_backend_path — the webapp solve runs the staged backend, not solve.py’s engine.

Input: (N, 3) OKLab targets. Output: a dict filament_id → (N,) float32 thickness array plus '__white_cap__', and a (N,) dE array (lut.py:946–1042). Filaments not used for a pixel get 0.0.
Parallelism: when parallel=True, n_luts > 1, and n > 1000, each entry’s tree.query runs on a ThreadPoolExecutor; SciPy’s cKDTree releases the GIL so this is real parallelism (lut.py:987–998). The reduction (picking the winning LUT per pixel) is sequential numpy (lut.py:1001–1016).
An optional on_lut_done(done, total) callback fires per entry for progress reporting (lut.py:1006–1007, 1015–1016).

query_luts — single-target
Scalar version of the above for one OKLab target; returns (thicknesses_dict, dE) (lut.py:906–943). Live in the legacy solve.py engine only (solve.py:106).
query_luts_fixed_cap — two-pass cap smoothing (legacy)
Re-solves colour layers with the cap pinned per pixel, used by the legacy two-pass smoothing. For each pixel it queries the min(20, len) nearest neighbours, then among those keeps the best whose cap_thickness matches the supplied fixed_cap within 0.5 × layer_height, falling back to the unconstrained best if none match (lut.py:1045–1143). The returned '__white_cap__' is set to the fixed cap, not the LUT entry’s (lut.py:1141). Liveness: called only from the legacy CLI engine — solve.py:547 (solve_image’s smoothing pass) and pipeline_cli.py:607 (imported at pipeline_cli.py:583, inside the solve_regions smoothing branch). Not reachable from the staged webapp path — see below.
query_cap_fixed_colour / query_cap_fixed_colour_batch — test-facing only
The duals of query_luts_fixed_cap: pin the colour stack and sweep the cap to minimise dE (lut.py:1146–1292). They do not use the LUTs (the luts arg is “accepted for API symmetry”, lut.py:1166, 1226); they recompose transmission directly via compose_stack/predict_transmission. Liveness: unwired in product code. A repo-wide grep finds no caller inside Prisma/generator/ — the only caller is tests/generator/test_query_cap_fixed_colour.py. Treat them as a tested-but-dormant utility.
Two build paths
The runner selects the path by the appearance provider’s model_kind (runner.py:798):
model_kind == "historical_spline"  →  build_luts(...)            (runner.py:799)
otherwise                          →  build_luts_with_provider() (runner.py:815)

See Appearance provider for what supplies model_kind.
Path A — build_luts (spline + pair corrections)
build_luts(colour_profiles, wb_profile, wc_profile, …) is the historical spline path (lut.py:394–599). It requires wb_profile and wc_profile (raises otherwise, lut.py:432–433), auto-derives d_wc_max via derive_d_wc_max if not given (lut.py:436–439), precomputes transmission tables, enumerates combos per subset/cap, and builds entries.
Pair corrections (k=2 only). When corrections is supplied and k_max ≥ 2, _build_pair_corr_cache restructures the fitter’s correction dict into per-(overlay, base) arrays interpolated to each layer count (lut.py:53–103, 481–486). Only single-base pairs are kept (len(bases) != 1 is skipped, lut.py:77–78); multi-base correction entries are dropped. During build, for each 2-filament subset the A-on-B and B-on-A correction curves are looked up; if both exist they are averaged, otherwise the available one is applied, indexed by the overlay filament’s layer count (lut.py:493–536). Corrections never touch k=1 or k=3 subsets. The pair-correction maths is a Theo domain concern; see Pair corrections.
Live caller: runner.py:799 (webapp, when the active provider is the historical spline) and pipeline_cli.py:545 (CLI).
Path B — build_luts_with_provider (live photo-stack model)
build_luts_with_provider(provider, …) is “the coexistence path for context-aware photo models” and returns ordinary LUTEntry objects so the query code stays shared (lut.py:630–901). It has two internal sub-paths:

model_kind == "photo_stack_bundle" (the current default model): it iterates iter_photo_stack_lut_arrays(provider, …) from photo_stack_lut.py, prunes, chroma-weights, and builds trees (lut.py:739–804). This is where the heavy vectorized appearance model runs.
Generic provider fallback: for any other non-spline provider it builds StackRequest objects per combo and calls provider.predict_stack_linear_rgb_batch(all_requests) in one batch (lut.py:806–901, StackRequest constructed at lut.py:825–836). Pair corrections are not applied on this path (no corrections argument exists in this function).

Live caller: runner.py:815 — the webapp’s normal path whenever the active model is not the historical spline. This is the path exercised by typical solves today.
The vectorized photo-stack evaluator (photo_stack_lut.py)
iter_photo_stack_lut_arrays (photo_stack_lut.py:1038–1100) yields one PhotoStackLUTArrays (raw, pre-prune) per subset. It builds cap steps, instantiates a _PhotoStackGridEvaluator, and for each subset/cap enumerates combos and calls evaluator.predict_subset(subset, combos, cap_indices) to get model-domain linear RGB, then projects to appearance via provider.project_model_linear_rgb_to_appearance before OKLab conversion (photo_stack_lut.py:1081–1091). _PhotoStackGridEvaluator (photo_stack_lut.py:152–915) is a NumPy mirror of the frozen photo-stack equations — white context, cap attenuation, multicolor interaction, ordered-tint retention, single-colour cap transfer / profile blend, two-colour endpoint corridor, and a kernel-weighted correction residual. Its physics is owned by lib.photo_stack_model.predictor and is out of scope here; the contract is just “grid-aligned counts → OKLab, identical to the row predictor” (verified by compare_vectorized_provider_predictions, photo_stack_lut.py:1103, test-facing).

Note: project_model_linear_rgb_to_appearance and the appearance-named provider methods are pass-throughs that return model-domain values after the projection-slot retirement (appearance_model.py:418–420; predict_stack_linear_rgb_batch aliases the model-domain batch, appearance_model.py:413–416). See Model-domain ingress.

predict_combo_model_linear_rgb (photo_stack_lut.py:917) and predict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_grid (photo_stack_lut.py:957) are sibling entry points to the same evaluator used at solve time (Stage-4 cap planning), not during LUT build. predict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_grid is imported and called by the staged cap planner (staged_solver_helpers.py:149, 163); it internally calls predict_combo_model_linear_rgb (photo_stack_lut.py:1020). predict_combo_model_linear_rgb is also reached from the appearance provider’s deduplicated row predictor _predict_unique_combo_model_linear_rgb (appearance_model.py:537). Neither is imported in staged_runner.py. They share the evaluator so hot paths never pay the row predictor’s per-row cost (photo_stack_lut.py:933–935).
Disk cache (npz, trees rebuilt)
LUTs are cached to data_paths.LUT_CACHE_DIR = <cache>/luts/ (lut.py:46–47; data_paths.py:54). KD-trees are never serialized — only the arrays are saved, and trees are rebuilt on load (_save_luts_to_cache lut.py:281–298; _load_luts_from_cache lut.py:301–348). Because the tree is rebuilt at load, chroma_weight is re-applied at load time (lut.py:325–330), so the same cached npz can serve different chroma weights — but the cache key still includes chroma_weight, so in practice each weight gets its own file.
Two cache-key schemes:























Pathkey functionfilenameversion/metadataspline (build_luts)_cache_key (lut.py:259–278)lut_<16hex>.npz (lut.py:452)SHA-256 over sorted filament IDs, all geometry params, per-profile checksums (_profile_checksum, lut.py:250), and a corrections checksum (_corrections_checksum, lut.py:106); no stored metadata blockprovider (build_luts_with_provider)_provider_cache_key (lut.py:602–627)lut_provider_<16hex>.npz (lut.py:695)includes a builder_version string and writes a cache_metadata dict (schema provider_lut_v2) into the npz, validated on load
The provider cache’s builder_version is PHOTO_STACK_LUT_BUILDER_VERSION ("photo_stack_lut_appearance_v2_2026_06_10", photo_stack_lut.py:64) for photo-stack bundles, else "provider_generic" (lut.py:675–679). On load, _load_luts_from_cache rejects the file if any expected_metadata key mismatches or if the metadata block is missing entirely (lut.py:309–319) — so a builder-version bump auto-invalidates stale provider caches. The provider path also fills a diagnostics dict (cache key/path/hit, lut/entry counts) for observability (lut.py:660–737, 785–793).
The spline path’s _save_luts_to_cache is called with no metadata (lut.py:591), and _load_luts_from_cache is called there without expected_metadata (lut.py:453–454), so its only guard against staleness is the hash in the filename.
Convex hull construction
build_hull_from_luts(luts) stacks every entry’s oklab, deduplicates by rounding to 4 decimals, and returns a scipy.spatial.ConvexHull of all achievable OKLab colours (lut.py:1295–1309). It is the achievable-gamut surface used for hull-mode gamut projection: out-of-gamut targets are pushed onto the nearest hull facet. Live callers: runner.py:122 (_lut_mod.build_hull_from_luts(state.luts) inside _apply_target_gamut_mapping, hull mode) and solve.py:484–485 (legacy engine). The hull feeds solve.gamut_map_hull_batch (solve.py:180), which the runner calls at runner.py:127/131. See Gamut mapping.
Legacy cap-curve helpers
A separate 1-D structure predates the joint LUT and is retained “for dual-resolution cap refinement”:

CapCurve (lut.py:120–125): maps OKLab L* → cap thickness d_wc, holding d_wc_steps, L_values, and a T_wc_table.
build_cap_curve (lut.py:162–190): builds it by stepping cap thickness and recording L*.
cap_curve_lookup_batch (lut.py:193–216): vectorised nearest-L* lookup with a broadcast-floats chunking guard.
derive_d_wc_max (lut.py:141–157): finds the cap thickness where mean transmission drops below a threshold (default 0.05) — beyond this the cap is effectively opaque. This one is not legacy: it is used by both build_cap_curve and build_luts to auto-derive d_wc_max (lut.py:174, 437).

Liveness of the cap-curve trio: build_cap_curve and cap_curve_lookup_batch are imported and used by the legacy engine only. build_cap_curve is imported and called by the CLI: pipeline_cli.py:45 imports it (from lut import build_luts, build_cap_curve) and pipeline_cli.py:653 calls it. cap_curve_lookup_batch is imported in solve.py:35–36 and called at solve.py:364 (build_cap_curve is not referenced in solve.py at all). Both solve.py (its solve_image/smooth_cap/solve_regions functions, solve.py:410/371/577) and pipeline_cli.py constitute the legacy CLI engine — pipeline_cli.py:46 imports solve_image, solve_regions, … from solve. The live webapp does not call them; it goes through run_staged_backend_path (runner.py:843–846) and queries LUTs with query_luts_batch. So CapCurve/build_cap_curve/cap_curve_lookup_batch are live in the CLI path, dormant in the webapp path.
Liveness summary

































































SymbolStatusEvidencebuild_lutslive (CLI + spline-provider webapp)pipeline_cli.py:545, runner.py:799build_luts_with_providerlive (default webapp path)runner.py:815iter_photo_stack_lut_arrayslive (photo-stack build)lut.py:744 via build_luts_with_providerquery_luts_batchlive (webapp staged backend)staged_runner.py:762query_lutslive (legacy engine)solve.py:106query_luts_fixed_caplive (legacy engine only)solve.py:547query_cap_fixed_colour / _batchunwired in product; tests onlyonly tests/generator/test_query_cap_fixed_colour.pybuild_hull_from_lutslive (gamut hull mode)runner.py:122, solve.py:485build_cap_curve / cap_curve_lookup_batch / CapCurvelive in CLI, dormant in webapppipeline_cli.py:653, solve.py:364derive_d_wc_maxlive (auto d_wc_max)lut.py:174, lut.py:437predict_combo_model_linear_rgb / predict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_gridlive (solve-time cap planning, not build)predict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_grid called at staged_solver_helpers.py:163; predict_combo_model_linear_rgb called at appearance_model.py:537 and photo_stack_lut.py:1020
Driving it (for users)
You never call these functions directly — the generator does. What you control maps to build parameters:

Palette → filament_ids / subsets (more filaments ⇒ more subsets ⇒ bigger LUT, longer first build).
k_max → how many colours may stack per pixel (1–3). Higher k_max multiplies subset count combinatorially.
Height budget (t_max, d_wb, layer height) → how many layers fit, hence how many combos per subset.
Chroma weight → favour colour accuracy over lightness in matching.

First solve of a new palette pays the build cost; subsequent solves hit the npz cache. Changing a filament’s measured profile, the pair corrections, or the photo-stack model version (builder_version) invalidates the relevant cache automatically.

solver/the-solve-target-cloud.title: The solve target cloud
solver/the-solve-target-cloud.content:
In one sentence: the solve target cloud is the single shared step that turns a loaded source image into per-pixel OKLab targets — convert source pixels into the model colour domain, flatten to OKLab, project onto the solve grid, and (optionally) rescale to the print’s paper white — so the solver and palette suggestion both compare against filament gamuts in exactly the same space.

What it is for
Three different callers need the same conditioning of the source image before they can ask “which filament stack reproduces this colour?”: the solve runner, palette suggestion, and gamut preview. If each re-implemented the colour conversion, suggestion could silently drift into a different colour-domain interpretation than the solve it is supposed to predict. pipeline/target_cloud.py is the one place that path lives, so it cannot drift (pipeline/target_cloud.py:1–8).
The module produces a frozen SolveTargetCloud dataclass carrying both grids of targets plus the metadata describing how they were built (pipeline/target_cloud.py:23–32):

































FieldMeaningobserved_oklab(H*W, 3) OKLab targets on the observation grid (one row per source pixel)solve_oklab(solve_h*solve_w, 3) OKLab targets on the solve gridobservation_shape(H, W) of the loaded imagesolve_shape(solve_h, solve_w) derived from the pitch ratiodomainalways "model_oklab" (see the domain contract)model_domain_ingresswhether the Camera Transform ingress LUT was used
How it works — the four steps
compute_solve_target_cloud(image, wb_profile, config) is the entry point (pipeline/target_cloud.py:64). It expects a post-load, post-adjustment image — i.e. the source image after loading and any preprocessing has already happened upstream; the target cloud does no preprocessing of its own.
1. Ingress — source pixels into the model domain
The image goes through image_to_target() (pipeline/target_cloud.py:72, defined at model.py:128). The model_domain_ingress flag picks one of two source-pixel conversions (model.py:149–152):

Ingress ON (the default everywhere the webapp drives it — state.py:77, server.py:607, facade.py:215 all default True): the source sRGB image is run through the Camera Transform inverse LUT via _apply_model_domain_ingress_lut → apply_inverse_lut from lib.camera_transform (model.py:123–125, model.py:21). The LUT is loaded from model_domain_ingress_lut_path, defaulting to Prisma/data/camera_transform (pipeline/target_cloud.py:77–81, model.py:28). This maps display-sRGB source pixels into the model’s transmission colour domain.
Ingress OFF (legacy): a plain srgb_to_linear() gamma-2.2 conversion, bit-identical to the old path (model.py:108–115, model.py:148–152).

Note the model_domain_ingress default on the image_to_target function itself is False (model.py:133), but every runtime config that reaches it passes True explicitly, and compute_solve_target_cloud reads the config’s model_domain_ingress attribute (default True) rather than relying on that function default (pipeline/target_cloud.py:76). The wb_profile and d_wb arguments are accepted for API compatibility but unused by image_to_target — the white-base term is already baked into every LUT entry (model.py:142–146).
2. OKLab conversion
The (H, W, 3) target image is reshaped to (H*W, 3) and run through to_oklab() (pipeline/target_cloud.py:83), which calls linear_to_oklab from lib.transmission (model.py:155–160, model.py:22). This is the observed_oklab array. OKLab itself is described in OKLab; this module just calls into it.
3. Observation grid → solve grid projection
project_observation_to_solve_grid() (generator.pipeline.derived_views, derived_views.py:125) resamples the observation-grid OKLab onto the solve grid (pipeline/target_cloud.py:84–90):

When image_sample_pitch_mm == solver_fine_pitch_mm (both default 0.20 — state.py:105–106, facade.py:167–168), this is a zero-cost identity pass that returns the same array object (derived_views.py:154–155). This is the common case.
When the pitches differ, the (obs_h, obs_w, 3) raster is bilinearly resampled (scipy.ndimage.zoom, order=1) to the solve-grid shape, where ratio = image_sample_pitch_mm / solver_fine_pitch_mm and solve_h = round(obs_h * ratio) (derived_views.py:157–164).

_solve_shape_for_observation() computes the matching solve_shape with the same rounding rule, so the reported shape always agrees with the resampled array (pipeline/target_cloud.py:35–48).
4. The result
All four pieces are packed into the frozen SolveTargetCloud (pipeline/target_cloud.py:91–103), with domain set by solve_target_domain(config).
The model_oklab domain contract
solve_target_domain(config) always returns the constant MODEL_OKLAB_DOMAIN = "model_oklab" regardless of the ingress flag (pipeline/target_cloud.py:20, 51–61). The ingress flag only decides how source pixels are converted; it does not change the comparison space. Either way the solver compares these targets to model-domain LUT / gamut points, so the contract for the nearest-neighbour search is model OKLab. The flag is read (bool(getattr(config, "model_domain_ingress", True))) and deliberately discarded — it is carried on the cloud as metadata, not as a domain switch (pipeline/target_cloud.py:60).
This matters because of the projection-slot retirement: the photo-stack model’s appearance-named prediction methods are now exact model-domain pass-throughs (camera-appearance conversion only happens at ingress and display boundaries — solve.py:251–253). So “compare in model OKLab” is the whole story for the solver; there is no separate appearance space in the comparison.
Gamut white-point rescale (optional pre-step)
apply_gamut_white_rescale_to_targets() is a separate, opt-in step the callers apply after building the cloud (pipeline/target_cloud.py:106). It is gated on config.gamut_white_rescale, which defaults OFF (state.py:76, server.py:606, facade.py:214); when off (or when targets/provider are missing) it returns the targets unchanged and None for the white (pipeline/target_cloud.py:114–117).
When enabled, it delegates to two functions in generator.solve:

compute_paper_white_rgb(provider, config) (solve.py:245) — the linear-RGB appearance of the thinnest white-only stack (white base + a d_wc_min white cap) through the active provider. Returns None (so rescale is skipped) when there is no white base or the paper white is already effectively [1,1,1] (solve.py:255–279).
rescale_oklab_targets(targets_oklab, white) (solve.py:282) — a per-channel von Kries adaptation: round-trip the OKLab targets through linear RGB, multiply each channel by the paper white, convert back to OKLab (solve.py:295–297). Because OKLab↔linear is bijective, the only change is the per-channel scale that adapts the source white to the print’s paper white.

The helper returns (rescaled_targets, white_rgb) so the caller can record diagnostics (pipeline/target_cloud.py:124).
Who drives it (liveness — confirmed from callers)






























CallerWhereWhat it doesSolve runnerpipeline/runner.py:779–782Builds the cloud once as the single owner of observation-grid targets; stores observed→state.observed_target_oklab and solve_oklab→state.solve_target_oklab, which then feed The staged backend (Stage 0-5) (the runner dispatches to run_staged_backend_path at runner.py:846).Solve runner (rescale)pipeline/runner.py:83–91Applies apply_gamut_white_rescale_to_targets as the white-point pre-step inside _apply_target_gamut_mapping, before any gamut mapping.Palette suggestionpalette/suggest.py:338–346solve_target_oklab_for_signature() builds the same cloud and applies the same optional rescale, so suggestion mirrors solve ingress exactly rather than promising stable corner precision (suggest.py:330–356).Palette suggestion (domain)palette/suggest.py:101, 140, 463–464Stamps ColourSignature.domain and the gamut-backend domain with MODEL_OKLAB_DOMAIN.
All five exported symbols (pipeline/target_cloud.py:127–133) are live. Four have external importers in runner.py and suggest.py: compute_solve_target_cloud (runner.py:32, suggest.py:57), apply_gamut_white_rescale_to_targets (runner.py:31, suggest.py:56), MODEL_OKLAB_DOMAIN (suggest.py:55), and SolveTargetCloud (returned by compute_solve_target_cloud, consumed at runner.py:779–782). solve_target_domain is exported but called only internally — by compute_solve_target_cloud itself (pipeline/target_cloud.py:101); it is exercised externally through that call (and pinned by tests/generator/test_palette_suggest.py:225), not imported. None are dead.


                  
                  Not the legacy CLI engine 
                  
                

This shared path is what the staged webapp backend consumes. It is distinct from solve.py’s old “6-step” CLI engine; the runner builds the target cloud here and then hands off to run_staged_backend_path, not to the legacy engine.


Defaults at a glance



































KnobDefaultSourcemodel_domain_ingressTrue (runtime) / False (image_to_target arg)state.py:77, server.py:607, facade.py:215 / model.py:133model_domain_ingress_lut_pathPrisma/data/camera_transformpipeline/target_cloud.py:80, model.py:28image_sample_pitch_mm0.20 mmstate.py:105, facade.py:167solver_fine_pitch_mm0.20 mmstate.py:106, facade.py:168gamut_white_rescaleFalsestate.py:76, server.py:606, facade.py:214

solver/the-staged-backend-(stage-0-5).title: The staged backend (Stage 0-5)
solver/the-staged-backend-(stage-0-5).content:
In one sentence: the staged backend is the generator’s sole production solve engine — it turns a prepared image into per-filament thickness maps through six ordered passes (directives → zones → recipes → filler → cap → bridge), each handing a frozen artifact to the next.

The staged backend (Stage 0-5)
When you click Solve in the generator web app, the colour decomposition is performed by run_staged_backend_path in generator.pipeline.staged_runner, not by the older solve_image engine in solve.py (that is the legacy CLI region engine — solve.py:410 solve_image, solve.py:577 solve_regions — and is not on the webapp solve path). The webapp path is run_pipeline → the staged backend; the only caller of the staged entry point is the runner: pipeline/runner.py:843-846 imports and calls run_staged_backend_path(state, progress=progress).
The function lives at pipeline/staged_runner.py:10310. That one file is ~11,000 lines; this page stays at stage-contract altitude — what each stage consumes, what it produces, and which knobs you control — and deliberately does not narrate gate/beam/mutation internals.
How to drive it
You never call the stages directly. You configure a PipelineConfig (palette, layer height, budgets, region target, feature flags) and run a solve from the web app or pipeline_cli.py. The staged backend reads state.config and state.solve_target_oklab (the prepared OKLab targets on the solve grid) and returns a StagedBackendResult bundle. The runner then copies that bundle onto legacy-facing state (pipeline/runner.py:533 _finalize_staged_backend_state), after which filament grouping, statistics, and mesh export run as usual.
Two hard preconditions, enforced by the stages themselves:

state.solve_target_oklab must be set — Stage 1 and Stage 2 raise RuntimeError otherwise (pipeline/staged_runner.py:675-676, :760-761, :6132-6133).
The solve grid shape is taken from state.image.shape[:2]; everything downstream operates on that lattice.

The pipeline at a glance
run_staged_backend_path runs the six stages in strict order, timing each into a StagedPerformanceProfile and emitting progress callbacks (all reported under stage_index: 3, stage_count: 5, pipeline/staged_runner.py:10325-10326). Each stage is a single builder function whose output is a frozen artifact consumed by the next.















































StageBuilder (staged_runner.py)Produces (staged_artifacts.py)One-line contract0 — Directives_compile_directives :567QuantizedDirectiveSet + DirectiveReceiptBookCompile + quantize the authoritative solve lattice and cap-floor directives1 — Zones_build_stage1_zone_plan :671LateralZonePlanSegment the image into lateral colour zones on a (possibly coarsened) planning lattice2 — Recipes_build_stage2_visible_plan :6122VisibleRecipeRawGeometryPlanAssign one visible filament recipe per zone and emit raw colour-ceiling geometry3 — Filler_build_stage3_filler_plan :8992FillerGeometryPlanGeometry-only filler pass (currently a pass-through; filler height ≡ 0)4 — Cap_build_stage4_cap_plan :9598CapSynthesisPlanSynthesize the white cap, edge guards, and optional detail surface; printability gates5 — Bridgebuild_compatibility_bundle (staged_bridge.py:90)CompatibilityBundleProject staged artifacts into legacy per-filament thickness maps + debug maps
The final return value is StagedBackendResult (staged_artifacts.py:584) carrying all six artifacts plus the diagnostics stream, performance profile, and receipts (pipeline/staged_runner.py:10980-10990).

The artifact names are stable; some docstrings still call this an “experimental proof slice” (e.g. staged_artifacts.py headers, staged_runner.py:10311). That language is stale — this is the production path. Trust the caller at runner.py:846, not the docstring.


Stage 0 — Directives
_compile_directives(state) (pipeline/staged_runner.py:567) builds a tiny, explicit directive set rather than letting later stages re-derive geometry. It computes the planning lattice pitch as solver_fine_pitch_mm × stage1_coarsening_factor (:572) and quantizes the minimum visible cap (d_wc_min) to a whole number of layers (:586-591). The solver_shape it pins is the raw image shape (h, w) (:613).
Each directive is a CompiledDirective with a gate (here "require") and a scope ("image"); each gets a DirectiveReceiptEntry marked status="held", stage="stage0" (:593-607). The output QuantizedDirectiveSet (staged_artifacts.py:22) is consumed by Stage 2 as its evaluation lattice (:6159 reads compiled_directives.solver_shape). See concept-solve-lattice for how fine pitch, planning pitch, and coarsening relate.
Stage 1 — Lateral zone segmentation
_build_stage1_zone_plan(state, diagnostics) (pipeline/staged_runner.py:671) partitions the image into lateral colour zones — contiguous regions that will each receive one recipe in Stage 2.
What it does:

Optionally coarsens the planning grid by stage1_coarsening_factor (_effective_stage1_coarsening_factor, :275), block-averaging both the RGB image (_downsample_rgb_image, :344) and the flat OKLab targets (_downsample_flat_oklab_targets, :399) onto the coarse lattice, with an optional lattice offset (_stage1_lattice_offset_px).
Calls generate_stage1_zone_labels (imported from generator.pipeline.staged_solver_helpers, :709) to produce the integer zone-label raster, honouring cell_mode, the effective color_region_target_mm, smooth_boundaries, and boundary_smooth_radius.
Derives per-zone bookkeeping: flat membership indices (_zone_flat_indices, :644), per-zone OKLab mean/variance (_summarize_zone_targets, :654), and 4-neighbour adjacency with shared-edge lengths (_build_zone_adjacency, :619).

The effective region target can be widened from the printability minimum width when color_region_target_from_printability is on (_effective_color_region_target_mm, used at :697 and :10360); the requested-vs-effective values are both recorded as counters (:10361-10394). Output LateralZonePlan (staged_artifacts.py:114) carries zone_label_map, zone_flat_indices, adjacency_edges, edge lengths, per-zone means/variances, and the coarse_to_fine_scale Stage 2 will reverse. See concept-colour-zones.
Stage 2 — Recipe assignment
_build_stage2_visible_plan(...) (pipeline/staged_runner.py:6122) is the heart of the solver: it chooses one visible filament recipe per zone while balancing local colour fidelity against seam continuity. This is the single largest stage in the file.
Projection back to fine grid. If Stage 1 coarsened, the zone labels are projected back onto the fine evaluation lattice (_project_zone_labels_to_fine, :6160), optionally refined into source-edge subzones (_split_stage2_source_edge_subzones, :6174, gated by stage2_source_edge_subzones). Adjacency and per-zone variance are recomputed on this evaluation lattice (:6181-6193).
Candidate query. _query_stage2_pixel_stacks (:757) runs query_luts_batch (from generator.lut) over the OKLab targets to get a per-pixel best stack plus a per-pixel ΔE; pixels above de_threshold form the gamut_mask (:763). _vectorized_stack_ids (:6214) quantizes those thickness vectors into a discrete set of unique stack ids under effective_max_layers(). Palette ordering matters here: for the photo-stack model the palette order is preserved as-is because layers are physically ordered, whereas the legacy spline model sorts ids (:6205-6212).
Enumeration + pruning. _enumerate_zone_candidates (:767) collects, per zone, the unique stack ids that appear among that zone’s pixels and scores each candidate against the zone’s targets with _score_candidates_batch (:794); a single-candidate zone gets score 0 (:790-791). Each candidate also carries its total visible thickness (:798-804). The candidate frontier is then enriched — neighbouring zones’ strong local-best stacks are injected as extra candidates (_augment_zone_candidates_with_neighbor_local_bests, :815) so a zone can match a neighbour it would not have considered alone. This frontier is what keeps the assignment search tractable instead of enumerating the full LUT.
Coordinate-descent + beam under continuity/seam. Selection is a two-step optimization over candidate indices:

_seed_zone_recipe_labels_with_beam (:1440, called :6408) runs a small beam search (_STAGE2_BEAM_WIDTH = 12, :93) to build a good initial assignment that already respects neighbour continuity.
_optimize_zone_recipe_labels (:1901, called :6496) takes that seed and refines it: _run_coord_descent (:1681, up to _STAGE2_MAX_COORD_DESCENT_PASSES = 4, :83) followed by _repair_worst_boundary_pairs pair repair (:1960).

The objective per zone/candidate is computed in _zone_objective_breakdown (:1594): local_cost + continuity_weight × boundary_cost + retaining_wall_weight × retaining_cost (:1624-1628), where boundary_cost is the edge-length-weighted squared visible-thickness step to each neighbour’s current choice (:1617-1621) and retaining_cost penalizes excess thickness above the zone’s thinnest candidate (:1622-1623). Defaults: _STAGE2_CONTINUITY_WEIGHT = 0.12, _STAGE2_RETAINING_WALL_WEIGHT = 0.02 (:81-82); the continuity weight is overridable via _stage2_continuity_weight. “Seam” quality is the mean shared-boundary thickness step, tracked before/after by _mean_boundary_step_mm (:1637).
Output VisibleRecipeRawGeometryPlan (staged_artifacts.py:264) carries the zone_recipe_labels, the recipe_table of VisibleRecipe entries, the raw colour ceiling, the gamut mask, an optional fine_recipe_label_map (when a within-zone detail override fires), and a Stage2ObjectiveSummary. Its recipe_label_map property (:295-299) returns the fine override if present, else the zone-level labels.

VisibleRecipe vs the photo-stack StackDefinition. VisibleRecipe (staged_artifacts.py:73) is the staged backend’s committed recipe — an ordered tuple of (filament_id, thickness_mm) pairs with from_mapping/to_mapping helpers. It is structurally near-identical to but distinct from the model-layer StackDefinition; do not conflate them.

Stage 3 — Filler
_build_stage3_filler_plan(...) (pipeline/staged_runner.py:8992) is the geometry-only filler pass. In current code it is effectively a pass-through: it sets filler_height = zeros_like(raw_color_ceiling) and therefore color_ceiling_mm == raw_color_ceiling_mm (:8998-9000). It still runs every solve (called unconditionally at :10413) and emits a FillerGeometryPlan (staged_artifacts.py:311) so Stage 4 has a uniform color_ceiling_mm field to build on. The stage exists as a wired seam for support/filler logic; today it adds no height. Confirmed live but no-op: the only writer of filler_height is the np.zeros_like at :8999.
Stage 4 — Cap and detail / printability
_build_stage4_cap_plan(...) (pipeline/staged_runner.py:9598) synthesizes everything above the colour layers: the white boundary cap, edge guards, an optional detail surface, and the printability gates.
Key contract points:

Budget. The remaining cap budget is t_max − color_ceiling, clamped to effective_d_wc_max() (:9610-9614); the boundary cap is further clamped to effective_boundary_d_wc_max() (:9615-9618). The minimum cap floor is quantized to layers via _quantized_cap_floor (:9609).
Requested cap & guards. _requested_stage4_cap_maps (:9619) returns the requested boundary cap, a detail reference cap, and a boundary_edge_guard_weight map. Stage 4 supports cap_mode ∈ {"fixed", "smooth_variable"} (_STAGE4_SUPPORTED_CAP_MODES, :186); any other mode does not raise — it falls back to smooth_variable and emits a stage4_cap_mode_fallback warning diagnostic (:8758-8770).
Lateral boundary shield. When printability is enforced and a non-fixed lateral shield is required, Stage 4 honours the mandatory shield floor handed off by Stage 2 (visible_plan.mandatory_lateral_boundary_shield_floor_mm, :9633), raising a ValueError if its shape disagrees with the cap (:9636-9639).
Detail surface. Optional, gated by detail_cap_enabled (:9629) plus stage4_optical_detail_surface / stage4_independent_detail_surface (:9679-9684). Detail candidates are scored per connected zone and accepted/rejected with explicit reasons (Stage4DetailZoneSummary, staged_artifacts.py:344); rejection categories include too-small, weak-optical-gain, and weak-signal (_STAGE4_DETAIL_REJECT_*, :198-201).
Printability gates. Two optional gate families run here and surface as Stage4BoundaryCapPrintabilitySummary and Stage4DetailAuthoringPrintabilitySummary / Stage4DetailPrintabilitySummary, all None when disabled (CapSynthesisPlan fields, staged_artifacts.py:454-459).

Output CapSynthesisPlan (staged_artifacts.py:441) carries cap_boundary_top_mm, cap_height_mm, boundary_edge_guard_weight, detail_height_mm, the detail zone maps/summary, and final_visible_top_mm.

Two unrelated PrintabilityReport/printability classes. Stage 4’s printability summaries (Stage4*PrintabilitySummary) and the optional plan-level BlueprintPrintabilityDiagnostic (staged_artifacts.py:501, run via staged_printability.run_blueprint_printability_diagnostic at :10729) live in this pipeline. They are distinct from the mesh-side and blueprint_triage printability types — do not cross-reference them. The blueprint diagnostic and geometry-attribution passes are opt-in, gated by emit_blueprint_printability (:10715) and emit_geometry_attribution (:10659); they are read-only diagnostics that never change geometry.

Stage 5 — Plan bridge
build_compatibility_bundle(...) (pipeline/staged_bridge.py:90) is the read-only adapter that projects the staged artifacts back into the legacy thickness-map shape the rest of the generator (mesh export, previews, dE diagnostics) expects.
It builds one (h, w) float32 thickness map per palette filament by painting each recipe’s thickness_by_filament onto its recipe_label_map mask (staged_bridge.py:103-112), then adds three white-channel maps: __white_cap__ (full cap height), __white_boundary_cap__ (cap-above-ceiling, floored at 0), and __white_detail_cap__ (:122-130). It also exports the __gamut_mask__ diagnostic and a dictionary of debug maps (zone labels, recipe labels, colour ceiling, cap tops, detail maps, etc., :135-178). Output CompatibilityBundle (staged_artifacts.py:571) plus the per-pixel image-domain extents.
Back in the runner, _finalize_staged_backend_state (pipeline/runner.py:533) copies bundle.thickness_maps into state.thickness_maps (:559-562), routes bundle diagnostics into state.diagnostics (never into thickness maps, :567-568), merges debug maps (:570), sets state.colour_committed = True, and — separately — builds the export-facing SolvedMaterialPlan via build_solved_material_plan_for_export (:542). That is the true Stage 5 handoff to mesh generation; see concept-thickness-maps and Mesh export.

Diagnostics, receipts, and performance
Throughout, the orchestrator records:

Timings per stage into StagedPerformanceProfile.timings_s (_record_timing, :261) — stage0_compile_directives_s, stage1_zone_plan_s, the Stage 2 sub-timings (stage2_beam_seed_s, stage2_coord_descent_s, stage2_pair_repair_s), stage3_filler_s, stage4_cap_s, stage5_bridge_s, and staged_backend_total_s (:10975-10979).
Counters for grid sizes, zone counts, frontier sizes, detail accept/reject tallies, and printability findings (_set_counter, :266).
Receipts (DirectiveReceiptBook) and a diagnostics stream (PlanningDiagnosticsStream) of human-readable PlanningDiagnosticEntry notes — Stage 1 zone count, Stage 2 seam/pressure notes, printability summaries.

These are what the Color Ceiling / Recipe Viewer UI and the run-record JSON read from; the per-recipe rollups shown in the app derive from the recipe_table and the color_recipe_breakdown artifact, not from re-solving.

solver/the-vectorized-photo-stack-lut-ev.title: The vectorized photo-stack LUT evaluator
solver/the-vectorized-photo-stack-lut-ev.content:
The vectorized photo-stack LUT evaluator

In one sentence: photo_stack_lut.py re-implements the frozen photo-stack v2 colour model as pure NumPy arrays so the generator can evaluate hundreds of thousands of candidate stacks per second when building the Joint LUT and precomputing cap curves — without ever changing the model the slow row-shaped predictor exposes.

This page covers the fast path. The trustworthy-but-slow path is the row-shaped predictor on the appearance provider (predict_stack_model_linear_rgb_batch, appearance_model.py:381), which evaluates one stack per pandas row. That is fine for isolated predictions and calibration review, but LUT construction needs a different runtime shape: it sweeps a regular grid of millions of stacks. This module mirrors the same equations over array columns so that hot path never pays the per-row cost. Both routes must agree to floating-point tolerance — compare_vectorized_provider_predictions (photo_stack_lut.py:1103) exists precisely to assert that.
If you just want to drive the generator, you never call this module directly — it runs automatically whenever the active provider is a photo-stack bundle. The “how it works” sections below are for the developer who has forgotten the backend.
Why a second implementation exists
The model is nonlinear and stateful per stack: white-context optical density (OD), cap attenuation, multi-colour interaction, ordered tint retention, single-colour cap transfer, two-colour endpoint corridors, and a learned correction layer. The row predictor walks these stages one DataFrame row at a time. Re-expressing every stage as a batched array op lets one call process an entire filament subset’s grid at once.
The contract is “mirror, don’t reinvent”: every constant and helper is imported from the same lib.photo_stack_model.predictor and lib.photo_stack_model.correction_layer the row predictor uses (photo_stack_lut.py:21–photo_stack_lut.py:62). The builder version string photo_stack_lut_appearance_v2_2026_06_10 (photo_stack_lut.py:64) tags LUT caches so a model change invalidates them.






























Row-shaped predictorVectorized evaluatorWhereappearance_model.py:381_PhotoStackGridEvaluator, photo_stack_lut.py:152Shapeone stack per pandas rowone filament subset’s whole grid per callRolesource of truth / oracleinteractive-speed bulk evaluationUsed bycorner cases, off-grid, the cross-checkLUT build, cap-curve precompute, on-grid dedup
The OD-composition pipeline
predict_subset (photo_stack_lut.py:827) is the core. For one filament subset and a column of per-row layer counts plus cap indices, it composes the stack in optical-density space, where stacking is addition, then converts to linear RGB once at the end.
OD is the natural domain because transmission multiplies (T_total = ∏ T_i) and log turns products into sums. The evaluator builds total_od additively, then maps back with t_from_od (predictor.py:301), which is floor + (1 − floor)·exp(−od) — the floor models the lightbox/material light leak. layer_od (predictor.py:762) samples a filament’s measured OD curve at a thickness, with a frozen high-thickness taper.
The additive composition in predict_subset (photo_stack_lut.py:884) is:
total_od = latent_color
         + white_bulk          # white base OD + white cap OD
         + white_context       # white reacting to colour load
         + cap_attenuation     # cap surface darkening
         + interaction         # multi-colour cross terms

clipped to [0, 20], then rgb = t_from_od(total_od, floor) and lab = linear_rgb_to_oklab(rgb). After that base OKLab, OKLab-space refinements layer on (these are not OD-additive — they pull hue/chroma/lightness toward learned anchors):























































StageMethodApplies whenLatent colour OD_latent_parts photo_stack_lut.py:227alwaysWhite-context OD_white_context_od photo_stack_lut.py:258alwaysCap-attenuation OD_cap_attenuation_od photo_stack_lut.py:275alwaysMulti-colour interaction OD_multicolor_interaction_od photo_stack_lut.py:305≥2 distinct coloursOrdered tint retention_ordered_tint_retention_lab photo_stack_lut.py:401≥2 distinct coloursSingle-colour cap transfer_single_color_cap_transfer_lab photo_stack_lut.py:452exactly 1 distinct colourSingle-colour measured profile_apply_single_color_profile photo_stack_lut.py:556exactly 1 distinct colourTwo-colour endpoint corridor_endpoint_corridor_lab photo_stack_lut.py:646exactly 2 distinct coloursLearned correction residual_apply_corrections photo_stack_lut.py:739context key has training rows
The branch by distinct-colour count is dispatched at photo_stack_lut.py:889–photo_stack_lut.py:895 (len(set(active_ids)) 1 vs 2). Rows are grouped by an active-filament bitmask key (_active_key, photo_stack_lut.py:193) so every row in a group shares the same set of present colours and can run one stage path together.
The whole grid is sampled from precomputed OD tables built once in __init__: cap_od_table over cap steps (photo_stack_lut.py:178) and color_od_tables per filament over colour steps (photo_stack_lut.py:185). A row indexes these tables by its integer counts — no per-row curve sampling.
Model domain vs appearance projection
The evaluator works entirely in the model domain (flatfield-normalized model RGB). The conversion to the camera-appearance domain is a separate, explicit step applied to the finished array:

predict_combo_model_linear_rgb (photo_stack_lut.py:917) returns model-domain RGB — no projection.
iter_photo_stack_lut_arrays (photo_stack_lut.py:1038) and predict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_grid (photo_stack_lut.py:957) call provider.project_model_linear_rgb_to_appearance (photo_stack_lut.py:1090, photo_stack_lut.py:1033) after model evaluation, then OKLab.

Trap, confirmed from code: that projection is currently an exact pass-through. project_model_linear_rgb_to_appearance (appearance_model.py:418) literally return np.asarray(rgb) — its docstring calls it a “compatibility pass-through for the retired solve-domain conversion.” So today the appearance and model domains coincide here; the call sites keep the seam so a real transform could be reintroduced without touching the evaluator. Do not document this as an active colour conversion — it is a no-op slot (the docstring at photo_stack_lut.py:972 that says appearance-named methods are “now an exact model-domain pass-through” is accurate). Camera appearance is handled by the camera transform / ingress elsewhere, not here.
The inf over-budget sentinel
predict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_grid (photo_stack_lut.py:957) returns (dense, within_budget):

dense is (n_stacks, n_caps, 3) OKLab, initialized to np.inf (photo_stack_lut.py:1016) and filled only for representable cells — cells whose per-filament step count exceeds max_layers stay inf because they cannot exist on the evaluator grid (representable, photo_stack_lut.py:1013).
within_budget is a boolean mask: a cell is allowed when its total colour steps fit the height left after the cap (allowed_steps, photo_stack_lut.py:1004–photo_stack_lut.py:1012) and it is representable (photo_stack_lut.py:1014).

The split matters. The dense grid is finite at every representable cell so Stage-4 cap lookups always get a colour answer; budget enforcement is the cap planner’s job, and a missing colour answer would force the slow row predictor (docstring photo_stack_lut.py:976–photo_stack_lut.py:984). The caller _precompute_cap_oklabs_vectorized (staged_solver_helpers.py:131) materializes both views: it copies dense and stamps inf onto the over-budget cells to make the scoring view (staged_solver_helpers.py:175–staged_solver_helpers.py:176), so the zone optimizer’s nearest-cap dE (_score_stack_for_cell, staged_solver_helpers.py:180) can never pick an unprintable stack — the inf distance excludes it — while Stage-4 still reads the finite dense view. inf is the sentinel that says “exists in colour space but not in the height budget.”
This entry point is live: _precompute_cap_oklabs_vectorized is imported and called from staged_runner.py:27/staged_runner.py:6242, and the staged runner is what the webapp solve actually executes (run_staged_backend_path, staged_runner.py:10310, dispatched from runner.py:846 — not the legacy solve.py CLI engine).
The zero-cap row-provider fallback (correctness guard)
At the top of predict_subset (photo_stack_lut.py:837) is a deliberate escape hatch. Rows whose cap thickness is zero (cap_steps_d[cap_indices] <= 1e-9) are not evaluated by the fast path. They are turned into StackRequests and handed to provider.predict_stack_model_linear_rgb_batch — the canonical row predictor (photo_stack_lut.py:843–photo_stack_lut.py:859).
Why: a zero cap changes the physical evidence context. A base + colour + 0-cap stack is colour-over-white, not a sandwich — the model’s cap-transfer and white-context machinery were fit on sandwiched evidence and would mis-extrapolate at the boundary. Rather than special-case every nonlinear stage for the cap-absent geometry, the evaluator delegates that rare boundary to the oracle so the fast LUT path “cannot drift from the canonical stack predictor” (comment, photo_stack_lut.py:839–photo_stack_lut.py:842). It is a correctness guard, not a perf path — zero-cap rows are uncommon and the row cost is acceptable for them. Remaining (non-zero-cap) rows proceed through the vectorized stages.
A second, related guard lives inside _latent_parts (photo_stack_lut.py:247–photo_stack_lut.py:253): when there is no colour layer and base and cap are the same white filament, the two adjacent white layers are physically one bulk of white, so the evaluator samples the nonlinear white OD curve at the combined thickness (collapsed_same_white_od_table, photo_stack_lut.py:179) instead of summing two separate curve samples — mirroring how the provider collapses the stack.
The learned correction layer
After the geometric stages, _apply_corrections (photo_stack_lut.py:739) applies the same empirical residual the row predictor applies via apply_photo_stack_correction (appearance_model.py:404). The evaluator compiles the correction artifact’s training rows once (_compile_correction_artifact, photo_stack_lut.py:703), groups them by a context key (unordered_color_key | white_key | evidence_class), and for each target row does a Gaussian-weighted local regression over the matching group’s residuals in a scaled feature space (photo_stack_lut.py:805–photo_stack_lut.py:823), capped by norm and authority. The evidence_class (_evidence_class, photo_stack_lut.py:908) is white_only / single_color_sandwich / cross_color_multilayer_sandwich, matching the corrector’s context partitioning. This stays in OKLab and only nudges L within [0,1].
Where the evaluator is wired in (liveness)
All public entry points are reachable from the live solve, confirmed by grepping callers:









































Functionphoto_stack_lut.pyCaller (confirmed)Statusiter_photo_stack_lut_arrays:1038lut.py:740/:744 (photo-stack LUT build, gated on model_kind == "photo_stack_bundle", lut.py:739)livepredict_unique_stack_cap_oklab_grid:957staged_solver_helpers.py:149/:163 → staged_runner.py:6242livepredict_combo_model_linear_rgb:917appearance_model.py:534/:537 (on-grid dedup fast path) and internally at :1020livecompare_vectorized_provider_predictions:1103test-facing cross-check helper (docstring :1109)live, test-facing_PhotoStackGridEvaluator:152constructed by all three abovelive
The on-grid dedup in appearance_model._predict_unique_combo_model_linear_rgb (appearance_model.py:505) is notable: grid-aligned rows go through the vectorized evaluator, but off-grid thicknesses fall back to the row predictor (appearance_model.py:549–appearance_model.py:563) so callers “never lose exactness, only speed.” Same principle as the zero-cap guard — the fast path covers the grid, the oracle covers everything else.
